email_papers.title: Compositional Activation Steering Across Languages and Behaviors with Contextual Gates
email_papers.abstract: Activation steering has emerged as an effective and precise way to influence the behaviours of language models. However, composing multiple steering directions to control several behaviours simultaneously remains challenging, particularly in multilingual settings and with training-free steering vectors. We address this challenge with contextual steering, jointly training gates that adapt the strength of fixed steering directions to the current hidden state and interactions between interventions. Across a broad range of languages, behavioural attributes, and models, our approach outperforms constant-strength steering and four strong baselines, including prompting. It also better preserves general knowledge and keeps the model's internal computation closer to that of the prompted model. Our analysis further shows how jointly trained gates adapt their contributions during composition, explaining the mechanisms underlying effective compositional steering.
email_papers.content:
Abstract
Activation steering has emerged as an effective and precise way to influence the behaviours of language models. However, composing multiple steering directions to control several behaviours simultaneously remains challenging, particularly in multilingual settings and with training-free steering vectors. We address this challenge with contextual steering, jointly training gates that adapt the strength of fixed steering directions to the current hidden state and interactions between interventions. Across a broad range of languages, behavioural attributes, and models, our approach outperforms constant-strength steering and four strong baselines, including prompting. It also better preserves general knowledge and keeps the model’s internal computation closer to that of the prompted model. Our analysis further shows how jointly trained gates adapt their contributions during composition, explaining the mechanisms underlying effective compositional steering.
1

Introduction
Inference-time steering shifts a model’s activation trajectory toward a desired behaviour without updating its weights
(
Turner et al., 2025
)
. It has been used to control a range of attributes, including style
(
Konen et al., 2024
)
, factuality
(
Rimsky et al., 2024
)
, truthfulness
(
Li et al., 2023
)
, language identity
(
Gurgurov et al., 2026
)
, and refusal
(
Arditi et al., 2024
)
. For language control in particular, recent work shows that steering remains effective across variation in input language and content
(
Sterz et al., 2025
;
Chou et al., 2025
;
Michaelov et al., 2026
;
Gurgurov et al., 2026
)
, suggesting that it can serve as a form of adaptation
(
Ostermann et al., 2026
;
Xu et al., 2026
)
. Yet, most existing work considers only one attribute at a time. In realistic settings, models often need to satisfy several constraints simultaneously, such as generating text in a specified language while adhering to a behavioural requirement.
Although several approaches to compositional steering have been explored
(
Nguyen et al., 2025
;
Oozeer et al., 2025
;
Ghasemi et al., 2026
)
, effectively composing multiple attributes remains challenging, particularly in multilingual settings
(
Scalena et al., 2024
;
Kang et al., 2026
)
. A central difficulty is that interventions that work well in isolation may interact when combined in the residual stream, making their effects difficult to predict. Moreover, fixed intervention strengths cannot adapt to the current context, where an attribute may already be expressed to varying degrees. Effective composition therefore requires interventions that account for both the current hidden state and the interactions between attributes
Contextual steering offers a way to address these challenges by using gates to determine intervention strengths from the current state
(
Hsu et al., 2026
)
. We extend this idea to compositional steering by jointly training such gates for multiple attributes while keeping their steering directions fixed, allowing each gate to adapt its contribution in the presence of other interventions. We evaluate this approach across languages, behavioural attributes, and models, analyse its effects on knowledge retention, and investigate why contextual steering works by examining internal representations, output distributions, and interactions between interventions.

Methodology
Two common bottlenecks in steering are layer selection and steering-strength tuning, which are typically resolved through manual sweeps
(
Turner et al., 2025
;
Konen et al., 2024
;
Rimsky et al., 2024
)
. Our method avoids both, by applying interventions at every layer and learning a gate that determines the intervention strength from the current hidden state.

Experimental Setup
Models.
We evaluate on nine instruction-tuned models spanning five model families and three sizes: Llama-3.1-8B and Llama-3.2-3B
(

(
Jiang et al., 2023
)
, and Aya-Expanse-8B
(
Dang et al., 2024
)
.
Attributes.
We select attributes that have been widely studied in the steering literature, but mostly in isolation. We consider nine target languages from FLORES
(
NLLB Team et al., 2024
)
: English, German, Japanese, Russian, Korean, Spanish, Italian, Arabic, and Polish. We additionally evaluate seven behavioural attributes: chain-of-thought, formality, humour, truthfulness
(
Lin et al., 2022
)
, refusal
(
Arditi et al., 2024
)
, bias
(
Parrish et al., 2022
)
, and toxicity
(
Hartvigsen et al., 2022
)
. Each single attribute is steered toward one of its two poles (e.g., funny vs. serious for humour). Two-way composition pairs each of the 9 languages with each of the 14 behaviour poles (126 compositions); three-way composition pairs each language with one style pole (chain-of-thought, formality, or humour) and one safety pole (refusal, truthfulness, bias, or toxicity), for 108 triples.
Evaluation.
We evaluate every attribute and attribute combinations on held-out prompts from either CLaS-Bench
(
Gurgurov et al., 2026
)
, a parallel collection of open-ended questions across 32 languages, or an attribute-specific dataset where needed: harmful and harmless instructions for jailbreak from
Arditi et al. (2024)
, TruthfulQA
(
Lin et al., 2022
)
for truthfulness, BBQ
(
Parrish et al., 2022
)
for bias, and ToxiGen
Hartvigsen et al. (2022)
for toxicity. For most attributes, we use a mixed-language source distribution, with questions pooled across several languages rather than restricted to English. This provides a more challenging setting than using a single source language. Further details are in Appendix
A.3
.
Each attribute has a task-specific score, e.g. a FastText-LID language-fidelity score
(
Joulin et al., 2017
)

Experimental Results
We report single-, double, and tripple-attribute results, with significance tests in Appendix
I
.
4.1
Single-Attribute Results
We first evaluate language and behavioural attributes independently, averaging scores over all 9 languages and 14 behaviours for each model. Figure
2
compares prompting, constant-strength CAA, and contextual CLAS. CLAS consistently outperforms CAA across all nine models, with gains ranging from 1.3 to 21.9 points. The largest gains are observed for Aya-8B (21.9 points), Mistral-7B (20.0), and Llama-3.1-8B (17.0). The advantage is also consistent across attributes (Table
11
in Appendix
F
). Removing the anchoring objective substantially degrades performance (Appendix
B
), highlighting its importance for robust contextual steering in this setting.
CLAS also compares favourably with prompting, which we use primarily as a token-space reference rather than as a steering baseline. It outperforms prompting on seven of nine models and remains within two points on the other two. These results show that residual-stream interventions can provide competitive attribute control without modifying the model weights or relying solely on input-level instructions.
4.2
Multi-Attribute Results
We next evaluate the composition of language and behavioural steering across all languages and 14 behavioural directions. Table
1
reports scores averaged across behaviours and models, broken down by target language. Joint-CLAS substantially outperforms the other steering approaches, achieving an overall average of 82.5%, compared with 78.3% for sequential CLAS, 72.4% for prompting, and 49.6% for CAA. K-Steering achieves 43.2%, comparable to CAA, while ORBIT achieves 48.2%, outperforming K-Steering; both results are consistent with their reported performance
(
Oozeer et al., 2025
;
Ghasemi et al., 2026
)
. Joint-CLAS also performs consistently across models, reaching at least 77.1% on every model and exceeding 80% on seven of nine. Independently trained gates, in contrast, do not reliably preserve single-attribute performance. Joint-CLAS addresses this mismatch by jointly training all gates with the composed interventions active, allowing each gate to adapt to the residual stream produced by the other attributes. Sequential CLAS also improves over independent composition but remains below Joint-CLAS, highlighting the benefit of jointly optimizing interacting attributes. We investigate these interactions and their effects on the residual stream in Section
5
. The results extend to three-attribute composition. Joint-CLAS again outperforms the competing methods across models, achieving at least 80% on every model; see the radar plots in Figure
3
.
A

Conclusion
In this work, we showed that simple training-free steering vectors can be composed effectively when their interactions are accounted for through contextual steering and jointly trained gating functions. The resulting approach is robust across attribute combinations, languages, and models, while preserving more general knowledge than constant-strength composition. We further investigated why contextual steering is effective and found that gate-based interventions produce internal dynamics that remain closer to those of the prompted model, suggesting that contextual steering can achieve stronger attribute control while better preserving the model’s existing computation.

Limitations
Our approach requires computing steering directions and gates separately for each model; transferring them across models remains an interesting direction for future work. We also use next-token cross-entropy to train the gates, although contrastive or other task-specific objectives may prove more suitable. A further limitation is that joint training requires first training the single-attribute gates used for warm-starting, introducing an extra training stage, though the overall procedure remains efficient in practice (Appendix
M
).
Our experiments also focus on a single method for extracting steering directions; although difference-in-means vectors are simple and effective in our setting, it would be valuable to investigate alternatives, including SAE-derived features and probe weights.
Finally, we attempted to reproduce MAT-Steer
(
Nguyen et al., 2025
)
, but found its multi-objective optimization difficult to tune in our setting; in particular, the second attribute often had little observable effect. This is consistent with the optimization challenges of this method discussed by
Ghasemi et al. (2026)
, although it does not establish that the method is ineffective more generally.

All experiments were conducted on a shared GPU cluster using NVIDIA H100, H200, A100 (40GB/80GB), L40S, RTX A6000, and V100 GPUs, depending on availability. In total, approximately

article.headline: 联合门控让多属性激活引导可组合
article.lede: 在9个模型、9种语言与7类行为属性上，联合训练的上下文门控把双属性组合平均分从CAA的49.6%提升到82.5%。
article.problem: 激活引导在单一属性上已经相当有效，但把多个方向的干预同时叠加到残差流里时，彼此会产生难以预测的交互，单独调好的强度在组合后往往失效。固定强度的干预也无法根据当前上下文自适应——某个属性可能已经被部分表达。多语言场景下的无训练引导向量组合尤其困难。
article.method: 作者沿用「上下文引导」思路：对每个属性用差值均值提取固定的引导方向，在每一层都施加干预，并训练一个小门控从当前隐状态预测该层的干预强度，训练目标为下一词交叉熵加上向常数强度锚点回归的正则项。多属性组合时，作者把所有门控放在一起联合训练，训练时组合干预始终生效，使每个门控能感知其他属性造成的残差流变化。
article.results: 单属性设置下，CLAS在全部9个模型上优于常数强度CAA，提升幅度为1.3到21.9分，最大增益出现在Aya-8B（21.9）、Mistral-7B（20.0）和Llama-3.1-8B（17.0）；相比提示方法，CLAS在9个模型中的7个上更好，其余2个差距在2分以内。双属性组合（9种语言×14个行为极，共126对）中，Joint-CLAS平均82.5%，高于顺序训练CLAS的78.3%、提示的72.4%和CAA的49.6%，也远高于K-Steering（43.2%）与ORBIT（48.2%）；每个模型至少77.1%，9个模型中有7个超过80%。三属性组合（108组）下，Joint-CLAS在每个模型上至少达到80%。整个项目约消耗1,770 GPU小时。
article.why_it_matters: 它说明无需训练、可跨语言复用方向的「免训练引导向量」并非不能组合，关键在于用 jointly 训练的门控显式建模干预之间的交互，而不是简单相加。这为推理期同时约束语言、风格与安全属性提供了比提示更可控的轻量替代方案。
article.limitations: 引导方向与门控需要对每个模型单独计算和训练，能否跨模型迁移未知；门控用下一词交叉熵训练，对比式或任务特定目标可能更合适，且联合训练依赖先训练单属性门控做热启动，多出一个阶段。作者还只考察了差值均值一种方向提取方式，并报告无法在自己的设置下调好MAT-Steer（第二个属性常几乎无效果），但这不构成该方法普遍无效的证据。

Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) can sometimes report perturbations to their internal activations—even when the input provides no evidence that an intervention occurred. How do models detect and localize such internal changes? We study this question using a controlled task that keeps the input text fixed. We either inject a concept vector into the hidden state at one of ten token positions or apply no intervention. The model is asked to identify the perturbed position or report that no intervention occurred. Across three model families, we identify two small groups of attention heads with distinct roles in introspective reporting. Middle-layer
gate heads
influence whether the model reports a change, while
router heads
in a later layer help select the position to report. Interventions on gate heads can suppress position reports even when router heads supply location information. We further examine why reporting accuracy varies across concepts. Concept vectors that are localized more accurately produce stronger attention-score and output responses in gate heads, which is associated with better alignment of the induced key and value changes in their QK and OV computations. Together, these findings identify attention-head mechanisms supporting introspective detection and localization.

1
Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) rely on internal representations to transform inputs into outputs. Whether they can report changes to these representations is a fundamental question about their capacity for introspection. Recent experiments show that models can sometimes report interventions on their hidden activations even when the input text is held fixed
(
Lindsey, 2026
)
. Yet the underlying mechanism remains unclear: how does an internal change become an explicit report about it?
Prior work studies this question with mechanistic interpretability tools such as transcoders
(
Macar et al., 2026
)
. Transcoders replace parts of a model with a separately trained approximation, so the features they find may not reflect exactly the model’s native computation. Moreover, this work, like earlier introspection experiments
(
Lindsey, 2026
)
, relies on an LLM judge to score free-form reports, introducing a potentially unreliable layer of interpretation. We address both limitations by analyzing the model’s own attention heads and introducing a task with exact, judge-free evaluation.
We design a controlled detection-and-localization task (Figure
1
). The model sees ten labeled candidate token positions. We either add a concept vector to the hidden state at one position or make no change, keeping the input text identical. The model must output the affected position’s label or
none
. For example, if we inject a vector at candidate 6, the correct answer is
6
. We find that the model completes this report in two parts:
whether
the model reports a change and
where
it identifies that change. We score these answers using only the logits at the first output position. This prevents the model from using text it has already generated as evidence of a change and allows us to evaluate answers without an LLM judge. We ask which neurons control whether a change is reported, which determine its reported location, and how the neurons work together.
Across the Qwen
(
Yang et al., 2025
)
, LLaMA
(
Grattafiori et al., 2024
)
, and Gemma
(
Gemma Team, 2025
)
model families, we find attention heads with different roles in this task. We test these roles by replacing selected head outputs with their values from a run with or without injection, a form of activation patching
(
Vig et al., 2020
;
Meng et al., 2022
)
. We search for small groups of middle-layer heads whose outputs can increase or reduce the rate of position reports, selecting the heads in each group jointly. We call these
gate heads
. In a later layer, 1–2 heads help select the reported position; we call these
router heads
. Replacing router-head outputs with their values from a run without injection reduces position accuracy. Directing their attention to another candidate position changes which position the model reports.
We then test how these roles relate. When gate-head outputs come from an injection at one position and router-head outputs from an injection at another, the reported position usually follows the router heads, and restoring gate-head outputs to their uninjected values suppresses position reports. Supplying router outputs from an injected run does not fully restore these reports. The two groups thus play different but connected roles: gate heads affect whether the model reports a change, while router heads help select the position it reports.
Finally, we investigate why the model localizes injections more accurately
for some concepts than for others.
We analyze how gate heads use their queries to read changes in keys
and their attention weights to combine changes in values.
Compared with lower-accuracy concepts, higher-accuracy concepts show
stronger alignment in both computations, with smaller differences
in the size of the changes.
We further test whether these changes affect reporting by removing
the contributions of a few leading output components from each gate
head. This reduces position reporting, providing causal evidence
that these output components contribute to the model’s reports.
More broadly, understanding how models detect and report changes to their
internal states can inform AI safety and interpretability.

Related work
Introspective reports and their confounds.
Models can predict their own behavior better than an equally trained observer
(
Binder et al., 2025
)
, and can report injected concept vectors
(
Lindsey, 2026
)
, whose four criteria (accuracy, grounding,
internality, metacognitive representation) we adopt;
Gurnee et al. (2026)
characterize which representations are verbalizable
at all. Critiques narrow what counts as evidence:
Singh et al. (2026)
argue
the behavior is consistent with generic anomaly detection and ask for a
dissociable second-order process, and
Hahami et al. (2025)
show binary
“did something change” probes are partly a global logit shift toward
affirmative answers, though harder ten-sentence variants survive it. Our task is
built against these objections: fixed text,
none
competing with ten
position labels, and scoring only the first generated token. We do not treat
anomaly detection as an alternative to introspection: under the criteria we
adopt, detecting an internally induced change is introspective access when the
report is grounded, internal, and not a direct translation of the change into an
answer, and Section
4.4
tests the last condition.
Mechanisms of intervention awareness.
Closest to us,
Macar et al. (2026)
also report a two-stage
organization, with early “evidence carrier” features suppressing downstream
“gate” features that emit the default negative answer. Their account rests on
an external transcoder dictionary, an LLM judge over free-form replies, and
components taken by thresholding attribution scores. We instead identify
components from the model’s own structure—individual attention heads and their
query–key and output behavior—which yields a sparse circuit that recurs
across three model families and supports direct causal intervention, including a
crossed gate–router intervention that tests the gating relationship between the two components.
Rivera and Africa (2026)
show detection can be
trained in and that detection dissociates from resistance—the safety reading
being that steering is not invisible, so a steered model may comply because it
noticed.

;
Zou et al., 2023
;

;
Arditi et al., 2024
)
,
but as a calibrated stimulus rather than a control knob. Methodologically we
follow head-level circuit analysis: the QK/OV decomposition
(
Elhage et al., 2021
)
, induction heads
(

)
, the
IOI circuit and path patching
(
Wang et al., 2023
)
, causal tracing
(
Meng et al., 2022
)
, and automated discovery
(
Conmy et al., 2023
)

Testing whether the leading output modes affect reporting.
The comparisons above describe how the two concept groups differ.
We next test whether the leading OV modes contribute to the model’s
reports. For each trial and gate head, we compute their output
contributions from the unmodified clean and injected runs.
We then subtract these contributions at the final prompt position
jointly across the selected gate heads and let subsequent computation
proceed.
Removing the five leading modes per head reduces both correct-position
reports and overall position reports by amounts close to those obtained
by removing the entire value-change term
(Appendix

).
Removing the remaining modes lowers correct-position accuracy by at most
four percentage points, despite their carrying a substantial share of
the output energy.
Across all 30 evaluation clusters, increasing the number of removed modes
from five to ten changes mean correct-token probability by less than
one percentage point in every model and concept group

Together, these results show that higher localization accuracy is
associated with stronger alignment in the gate heads’ QK and OV
computations. The output ablations further show that the leading OV
modes contribute causally to reporting.
6
Discussion
Summary and implications.
Across three model families, introspective reporting in our task relies on two
small groups of attention heads with different but connected roles. Middle-layer
gate heads regulate whether the model reports a position, and router heads in a
later layer help select which position it reports. The two groups interact
through a gating mechanism: interventions on gate heads can suppress position
reports even when router heads supply location information. Across concepts,
gate heads differ more in how well their queries and attention align with an
injected change than in the size of that change. This suggests that whether an
internal change is reported depends partly on how the model reads it, not only
on how large it is.
Limitations and future work.
Our analysis covers only six task variants, one injection layer and strength per model, and models of
up to 12B parameters.
Natural next steps are to test whether gate heads also contribute to free-form
and unprompted reports, and whether the same heads respond to other kinds of
internal perturbation. We analyze attention heads because the report must carry
information across positions; how MLPs process the signal within a position
remains to be studied. Intervening directly on key–query alignment would test
whether it controls which concepts are reported. For safety, our results support
the concern that steered models may register the edit
(
Rivera and Africa, 2026
)
, and suggest gate heads as a candidate site
for monitoring such registration.
AI use statement
We used large language models to polish the wording of the manuscript and to
assist in writing experiment code. All research questions, experimental
designs, analyses, and conclusions are the authors’ own. The authors reviewed
all AI-assisted text and code, verified every reported result against the
experiment outputs, and take full responsibility for the content of this paper.
Ethics statement
This work involves no human subjects, personal data, or crowdsourced
annotation. All experiments use publicly released open-weight models and
common English vocabulary words, with no harmful content generated or
collected. We study introspection in a functional sense only and make no claim
about awareness or experience in language models. Understanding how models
detect interventions on their internal states is relevant to safety methods
based on activation steering. It can help monitor whether a model has
registered such an intervention, and we believe the benefits of this
understanding for transparency and oversight outweigh its risks.

A.1
Introspection criteria and task validity
Following the definition of
Lindsey (2026)
, we consider an
internal-state report introspective only if it satisfies four criteria.
Below, we state each criterion and explain how our task and analyses
address it, distinguishing properties of the evaluation design from
empirical evidence about the model’s reports.
•
Accuracy
requires the report to correctly describe the
model’s internal state. Our interventions provide known labels:
none
for clean trials and the intervened position for injected
trials. We evaluate correct
none
responses and correct-position
reports separately (Table
1
). These measurements
quantify report accuracy without interpreting free-form text.
•
Grounding
requires the report to causally depend on the
internal property being described, such that changing that property
would change the report. Our task manipulates hidden states while
holding the visible candidate text fixed. Comparing clean and injected
runs, and varying the injection position, tests whether reports track
the manipulated internal state. The gate and router interventions
further identify internal components that causally influence whether
the model reports an intervention and which position it reports.
Together, these analyses support a causal link between internal
perturbations and the resulting reports.
•
Internality
requires this causal influence to remain
internal; inferring an abnormal internal state from anomalies in
previously sampled outputs does not constitute introspective awareness. We evaluate only the first generated token of the decision
response. The model therefore has no previously sampled decision text
from which to infer the intervention. Because the intervention changes
hidden activations without changing the visible input, the design
excludes this external-text route from the intervention to the report.
•
Metacognitive representation
requires the report to arise
from a representation of the internal state itself rather than from a
direct translation of that state into language. Following
Lindsey (2026)
, we provide indirect evidence for this
criterion. Our task asks whether and where a perturbation occurred.
Layerwise analyses distinguish position–none separation from
position-specific representations
(Figure
2
), while gate–router
interventions show that supplied positional information is insufficient
to restore position reporting under Gate Off
(Section
4.4
). Together, these findings support
a functional metacognitive interpretation in which internal-state
information is processed and its expression in a report is regulated
before an answer is generated. This criterion does not exclude anomaly
detection, which can be the first stage of such a computation; it
excludes a direct mapping from the perturbation to a position label,
which the Gate Off result argues against.

A.5

replaced each candidate word with either the corresponding concept word or a

none

A.15
Latent position clusters across models
Projection procedure.
We take the 100 concepts of the validation set and, for each concept, inject it
separately at each of the ten candidate positions, repeating the whole procedure
over 30 validation clusters; for every run we collect the residual state at the
final prompt token, together with the corresponding clean run. For each concept
and position, the residual states are averaged over the 30 clusters, as are the
clean states, giving 1,000 injected points and one clean point per layer. These
points enter a single PCA per layer, and we plot their leading three principal
components in three dimensions. Each point is one concept injected at one
position, averaged over clusters, and its colour indicates the injected
position.

article.headline: 大模型内省报告依赖门控与路由注意力头
article.lede: 研究用固定文本的注入任务，在三类模型中找到分别控制“是否报告”和“报告哪个位置”的两组注意力头。
article.problem: 大模型有时能报告自身隐藏激活被扰动，即使输入文本没有提供任何线索。此前工作多借助 transcoder 或 LLM 裁判分析自由文本报告，前者可能偏离模型原生计算，后者引入不可靠的解释层。论文要回答：模型如何检测并定位这种内部变化。
article.method: 作者设计固定输入文本的受控任务：在十个候选 token 位置之一注入概念向量，或不做干预，模型只能从首个输出位置的 logits 回答位置标签或 none。研究覆盖 Qwen3-4B-IT、LLaMA-3.1-8B-IT 和 Gemma-3-12B-IT，用激活修补与直通估计器联合选择 32 个门控头，并定位路由头。随后用 QK/OV 分解与 SVD 分析门控头如何读取不同概念注入。
article.results: 在六种标签设置上，注入试验的平均定位准确率为 Qwen 54.49%、LLaMA 44.31%、Gemma 65.95%，均高于 10% 的均匀猜测基线；干净试验的平均 none 准确率分别为 89.44%、62.78%、87.78%。每个模型选出的 32 个门控头仅占全部注意力头的 2.8%、3.1%、4.2%；门控关闭使 none 率从 37.7%/25.3%/23.8% 升至 81.5%/60.7%/80.7%。交叉位置修补中，报告主要跟随路由头来源位置 j（38.0%/37.8%/40.1%），而非门控头来源位置 i（2.9%/3.2%/4.9%）。
article.why_it_matters: 这把“内省”从行为评分推进到可因果干预的注意力头电路，为监测激活引导是否被模型登记提供了候选位点。
article.limitations: 结论仅基于六个任务变体、每个模型一个注入层与强度，以及不超过 12B 参数的模型；自由形式、无提示报告和 MLP 的作用尚未检验。元认知表征这一标准也只有间接证据。

email_papers.title: Action Learning for Scientific Simulations
email_papers.abstract: Understanding and controlling how systems evolve is central to science and engineering, where many problems require reasoning about complete trajectories. Existing approaches typically learn local dynamics or generate trajectories, but objectives constructed from individual transitions can miss dependencies across time, while generative models do not necessarily provide a tractable objective for evaluating and optimizing arbitrary paths. We study $\textit{action learning}$, the problem of recovering a stochastic action from trajectory observations, yielding a common objective for reasoning about dynamical systems. We introduce $\textbf{LEAP}$ ($\textbf{L}$earned $\textbf{E}$nergy on $\textbf{A}$ction $\textbf{P}$aths), which anchors the unknown action to a tractable reference process and learns the remaining correction by comparing observed trajectories with reference trajectories. This construction yields a differentiable objective on path space that can capture both local dynamical structure and nonadditive dependencies across time. Once learned, the same action can be flexibly reused for path ranking and inference, mechanism steering, constrained optimization and sampling. Across stochastic physical systems, many-body orbital dynamics and molecular simulations, LEAP recovers underlying dynamics, captures dependencies across time and enables transfer across inference objectives and physical conditions. We show that $\textit{action learning}$ is a promising framework for turning trajectory observations into reusable objectives for scientific inference and control.

Abstract
Understanding and controlling how systems evolve is central to science and engineering, where many problems require reasoning about complete trajectories. Existing approaches typically learn local dynamics or generate trajectories, but objectives constructed from individual transitions can miss dependencies across time, while generative models do not necessarily provide a tractable objective for evaluating and optimizing arbitrary paths. We study
action learning
, the problem of recovering a stochastic action from trajectory observations, yielding a common objective for reasoning about dynamical systems. We introduce
LEAP
(
L
earned
E
nergy on
A
ction
P
aths), which anchors the unknown action to a tractable reference process and learns the remaining correction by comparing observed trajectories with reference trajectories. This construction yields a differentiable objective on path space that can capture both local dynamical structure and nonadditive dependencies across time. Once learned, the same action can be flexibly reused for path ranking and inference, mechanism steering, constrained optimization and sampling. Across stochastic physical systems, many-body orbital dynamics and molecular simulations, LEAP recovers underlying dynamics, captures dependencies across time and enables transfer across inference objectives and physical conditions. We show that
action learning
is a promising framework for turning trajectory observations into reusable objectives for scientific inference and control.
1
From trajectory samples to path inference
(a)
Local dynamics learning.
One-step transition laws induce a likelihood over complete trajectories.
(b)
Action learning.
LEAP learns relative path costs from complete trajectory comparisons.
Figure 1:
Local dynamics learning versus action learning.
Local models learn short-range transition laws that induce a path likelihood, whereas LEAP learns an action from complete trajectories while retaining structured local dynamics when appropriate.
Understanding how systems move between states requires reasoning about the trajectories that connect them. In molecular dynamics, two conformations may be connected by several transition routes that visit different intermediate configurations
(
Bolhuis et al., 2002
;
Shaw et al., 2010
)
; in robotics, agents act through sequences of decisions
(
Kalakrishnan et al., 2011
;
Janner et al., 2022
)
. In these settings, the object of interest is often the trajectory itself: which paths realize a transition, which mechanisms are plausible and which paths remain likely under perturbations or constraints.
Answering these questions requires reasoning about complete paths. To infer representative transitions or impose new preferences, we need an objective that assigns probabilities or costs to trajectories. When the dynamics are known, stochastic action functionals provide such an objective. In statistical physics and stochastic control, actions such as the Onsager–Machlup functional, Freidlin–Wentzell rate functional and path integral control costs define probabilities or costs on path space
(
Onsager and Machlup, 1953
;
Freidlin and Wentzell, 2012
;
Kappen, 2005
;
Adib, 2007
)
. Once the action is available, we can use it for downstream tasks like constrained inference and sampling.
In many applications, however, we do not know the action. Instead, we observe trajectories from simulations or experiments, such as molecular dynamics, sequences of state transitions, policy rollouts or logs of stochastic processes
(
Lindorff-Larsen et al., 2011
;
Shaw et al., 2010
;
Glielmo et al., 2021
)
. Classical trajectory inference methods typically assume a known action, while learned methods predict local dynamics, learn representations or generate trajectories directly
(
Chen et al., 2019
;
Li et al., 2020
;
Song et al., 2021
;
Jing et al., 2024b
)
. These objects are useful, but they do not directly give the reusable path objective needed for downstream trajectory inference. We therefore call the task of recovering an evaluable action from trajectory samples
action learning
.
Existing learned methods often model dynamics locally by fitting one-step transition laws and using the resulting local model to evaluate complete trajectories
(
Chua et al., 2018
)
. This requirement can become restrictive when trajectories are selected by global events, e.g., successful transitions or task-level constraints. A local predictor trained on such data estimates the one-step conditionals of the selected process, which can differ from the underlying dynamics. Errors in local transition log-likelihoods can also accumulate along a path and then distort the induced optimization landscape. Since path-level quantities do not have to decompose into independent local decisions, optimizing locally plausible segments can still produce a poor local minimum;
Fig.
1
shows this distinction.
We propose
LEAP
(
L
earned
E
nergy on
A
ction
P
aths), a framework for learning a stochastic action directly from trajectory samples. LEAP treats the action itself as the learning target, rather than a local predictor or trajectory generator. It anchors the unknown action to a tractable reference process and learns the remaining correction from complete trajectories, yielding an evaluable objective on path space. In structured settings, this correction recovers changes in the underlying dynamics; more generally, it can capture nonadditive interactions across transitions. Once learned, the action can be reused with preferences that were not specified during training. For example, a reward for visiting an intermediate basin can favor a different transition route, while a geometric penalty can discourage paths outside admissible regions, in both cases without retraining the learned action.
Our approach applies broadly to trajectories from dynamical systems, including molecular simulations, stochastic physical systems and logged sequential processes
(
Shaw et al., 2010
;
Kalakrishnan et al., 2011
;
Janner et al., 2022
)
. We evaluate LEAP across controlled physical systems, a
31
31
-body orbital benchmark with
186
186
-dimensional states and an alanine dipeptide molecular benchmarks. These experiments test physical recovery, nonadditive dependence across time and reuse across inference objectives, with the double well and orbital systems providing exact actions for evaluation.
Our contributions are as follows: (i) we formulate
action learning
as learning a reusable objective directly on complete trajectories; (ii) we introduce
LEAP
, which learns a stochastic action by comparing observed trajectories with samples from a tractable reference process; (iii) we establish theoretical guarantees for recovering the action and show that dependencies across time can result in trajectory objectives that cannot be represented by sums of local transition costs; and (iv) we demonstrate recovery of underlying physical dynamics from terminally selected trajectories, modeling of nonadditive dependencies in many-body systems, and reuse of a fixed learned action across molecular inference tasks and physical conditions.
1.1
Related work
Sampling trajectories from known dynamics.
Classical methods for sampling trajectories usually assume access to the dynamics, energy landscape or action. When trajectories of interest occur often, it is sufficient to just do direct simulation. When relevant paths are rare, e.g., because an energy barrier separates metastable states, methods can use known physical models to identify or sample transition pathways. The string method evolves discretized curves on an energy landscape
(
E et al., 2002
)
, while minimum action methods optimize action functionals derived from stochastic dynamics
(
Freidlin and Wentzell, 2012
)
. Stochastic control methods construct trajectory objectives from known dynamics and costs to sample rare transitions
(
Kappen, 2005
;
Todorov, 2009
;
Williams et al., 2017
;
Holdijk et al., 2023
;
Du et al., 2024
)
. More recent methods use learned force fields or pretrained generative models to get energies or dynamics for transition inference
(
Yuan et al., 2024
;
Raja et al., 2025
;
Amin et al., 2025
)
. These methods typically rely on available physical models, learned dynamics or predefined objective to perform inference. LEAP targets the complementary setting of learning the trajectory action itself from observations, enabling subsequent inference without access to the underlying target dynamics at all.
Learning from trajectories.
Learned trajectory models usually target evolution or generation. Neural differential equation and latent dynamics models learn evolution from observations
(
Chen et al., 2019
;
Kidger et al., 2021
;
Hafner et al., 2019
)
, while score-based, flow matching, diffusion and action matching methods learn vector fields or scores that transport or generate samples from state, trajectory or marginal distributions
(
Song et al., 2021
;
Jing et al., 2024b
;
Jing et al., 2024a
;
Neklyudov et al., 2023
)
. These methods model evolution or generation, but they do not generally return the stochastic action needed for path optimization, mechanism steering or Metropolis-Hastings correction. Energy-based models have also been used for planning by
learning energies over individual state transitions and composing them along a trajectory
(
Du et al., 2020
)
. Relatedly, reinforcement learning and imitation learning learn rewards or policies from demonstrations, e.g., maximum-entropy inverse reinforcement learning and adversarial imitation learning
(
Ziebart et al., 2008
;
Ho and Ermon, 2016
;
Fu et al., 2018
;
Nuti et al., 2023
)
. LEAP also learns from trajectories, but targets a different object: a stochastic action on complete paths, i.e., the trajectory-level objective used directly for optimization, control and sampling, which can then be reused across new downstream objectives.

Conclusion
In this work, we introduced
action learning
, which treats the stochastic action as a reusable learning target for trajectory data, and LEAP, which learns this action by comparing complete trajectories. In the double well setting, the learned action recovers the underlying physical drift and supports path inference under new endpoints and horizons. In the orbital benchmark, it captures interactions across trajectories induced by a persistent latent regime that cannot be represented by additive transition models. In molecular coordinates, the same learned action enables completion, temperature transfer, basin preferences and angular constraints without retraining. These experiments show that learning an objective on path space provides a common interface between trajectory data and diverse downstream inference problems, including settings where the reduced dynamics are unavailable in closed form. Looking forward, we hope action learning encourages a broader view for trajectory modeling, in particular, shifting the focus to learning reusable objectives over complete paths.
Limitations.
LEAP requires sufficient overlap between the reference and observed path distributions, as poor overlap makes the learned correction harder to estimate accurately. While the structured correction in
Eq.
9
is exact for Gaussian Markov processes with shared diffusion, state-dependent diffusion requires more likelihood ratio terms. Finally, projecting dynamics onto reduced coordinates can introduce memory and friction or diffusion that depends on the state
(
Ma et al., 2016
;
Vroylandt and Monmarché, 2022
)
. Our alanine experiments therefore learn an effective action in
(
ϕ
,
ψ
)
(\phi,\psi)
rather than the full molecular action
Impact statement
This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of Machine Learning. Learned trajectory objectives may help analyze and steer dynamical systems in science, robotics, planning and other sequential domains. As with other learned objectives, they could also be used to steer systems toward harmful outcomes, so deployment requires domain validation and careful attention to the data.

article.lede: 把随机作用量本身当作学习目标，LEAP 靠参考过程的轨迹对比学出路径代价，同一目标可复用于排序、引导与采样。
article.problem: 理解系统如何演化，常需要给整条轨迹打分的可评估目标；但已有方法多拟合单步转移律或直接生成轨迹，前者只学局部动力学、误差沿路径累积，后者不返回可用于路径优化的目标函数。更麻烦的是，当观测轨迹经过终端筛选时，局部回归拟合到的是被条件化改变的 Doob 漂移，而不是原始漂移。
article.method: LEAP 锚定一个可解析采样的高斯马尔可夫参考过程，用 InfoNCE 形式的集合比较目标区分观测轨迹与参考轨迹，学习一个中心化的路径对数密度比修正，再与参考作用量相加，得到可微的路径空间目标。模型提供三种参数化：局部（逐跃迁求和）、全局（把整条路径送入网络）与混合；学成的同一作用量可直接用于路径排序、代表性路径推断、机制引导、加约束优化与 Metropolis-Hastings 采样，无需重训。
article.results: 双井系统中，LEAP 的漂移 MSE 为 (3.3±2.7)×10^-4，远低于 Kramers-Moyal 的 0.8132±0.0030 和三次速度回归的 0.7752±0.0043；换到新端点与时间跨度后，T=4 时真实路径代价 0.2533±0.0001（解析值 0.2532），T=16 时 0.2506±0.0006（解析值 0.2500）。在 31 体、186 维的轨道基准上，LEAP-Global 的修正 NRMSE 为 0.228±0.011，而 LEAP-Local 与 Transition NCE 仍停在 1.0013 和 1.0008；扩展到 42 体、256 个跃迁（每条路径 64,764 个坐标）时为 0.111，局部模型仍为 1.0015。丙氨酸二肽在 600 K 下，给定端点加三个内部观测时，LEAP 的补全圆 MSE 为 0.0931±0.0016，优于条件 DDPM 的 0.119±0.012 与条件流匹配的 0.125±0.011。
article.why_it_matters: 把作用量当作可复用的一等学习对象后，轨迹数据能变成下游推理的通用接口：排序、引导、加约束、采样都只改推理目标而不动模型，甚至可跨温度迁移（600 K 训练在 500 K 上 AUROC 0.9579，反方向 0.9719）。这也把“学动力学”和“学可优化的路径目标”这两件事区分开来。
article.limitations: 论文承认，参考分布与观测路径分布重叠不足时，修正项难以准确估计；式 9 的结构化修正只在共享扩散的高斯马尔可夫过程下精确，状态依赖扩散需要额外似然比项；投影到 (φ,ψ) 约化坐标学到的是有效作用量而非全分子作用量。实验上也显示：仅给端点做补全时，带掩码训练的条件生成器误差（0.350–0.409）明显低于 LEAP 的 0.6225。
article.figure_caption_zh: LEAP 以可处理的参考过程为锚，从完整轨迹比较中学习中心化的路径空间修正，再与参考作用量合成可评估的 S_θ(Φ;c)。

BeNice! Closing Looping’s Inference-Memory Gap via KV-Sharing
Hayden Prairie
Affiliation:
University of California, San Diego
Affiliation:
Together AI
Jacob M. Ryan
Affiliation:
University of California, San Diego
Taylor Berg-Kirkpatrick
Affiliation:
University of California, San Diego
Daniel Y. Fu
Affiliation:
University of California, San Diego
Affiliation:
Together AI
Abstract
Looped architectures scale quality while keeping parameter count fixed by repeatedly passing activations through the same block of layers.
During inference, each recurrence generates independent
KV-caches
, causing memory to grow linearly.
To address this challenge, prior work has proposed KV-sharing (i.e., sharing KV-caches across depth),
finding that, in some cases, the KV-cache of the final recurrence can be shared with the earlier recurrences
without quality loss
, a property we denote as
KV-shareability
.
However, the mechanisms underlying KV-shareability remain poorly understood, with even identically trained looped architectures not consistently exhibiting it.
In this paper, we study how
KV-shareability
can be enabled in looped models.
We propose a two-stage method: in the first stage, we use
stochastic depth
during pretraining, which induces contractive residual dynamics that drive representations toward a common limit across recurrences. In the second stage, we propose BeNice!, a post-training method that broadcasts the final recurrence’s KV-cache into the first recurrence, training it to produce compatible residuals while preserving the original model’s quality.
As a result,
BeNice!
enables KV-shareability while matching standard finetuning’s unshared validation perplexity.
Using
BeNice!
, we show that KV-sharing is complementary to alternative KV-compression methods, composing with memory-efficient sequence mixers (e.g., multi-latent attention, Kimi delta attention) and low-precision KV-cache quantization (e.g.,
fp8
,
mxfp8
,
nvfp4
).
Finally, in simulated low-memory, long-context inference, KV-sharing improves cache hit rates by up to 31.4%, increases throughput by up to 23.6%, and reduces p90 time-to-first-token by up to 83.6%.

1
Introduction
As inference deployments move to the edge
[
43
,
45
]
and take up a large portion of compute
[
67
]
, looped architectures create a new, predictable avenue to scale quality while keeping parameter count fixed
[
20
,
50
,
41
]
.
Unfortunately, while looped architectures keep the memory overhead of parameters capped, they still create
KV-caches at each recurrence
[
50
,
80
,
19
]
,
causing memory overhead to still
grow linearly
with recurrence count at inference time.
One potential direction to reduce inference-memory overhead is KV-sharing (i.e., sharing KV-caches across recurrences).
Specifically, some recent looped models have been shown to support reuse of the final recurrence’s KV-cache for all prior recurrences with
minimal impact to quality
[
20
,
21
]
, a property we term
KV-shareability
(
Figure
1
[
right
]).
Unfortunately, the mechanisms underlying KV-shareability remain poorly understood, with more recent work reporting significant quality degradation with KV-cache reuse
[
80
,
19
]
.
Moreover, even models trained under identical setups can differ in whether they exhibit KV-shareability (see
Table
1
).
In this paper, we hypothesize that contractive recurrent dynamics drive residual states toward fixed points, whose agreement under shared and unshared KV-caches enables
KV-shareability
.
To encourage contractive residual dynamics, we train with
stochastic depth
, randomly sampling depth throughout training (
Figure
1
[
left
]).
By requiring low-loss predictions across multiple depths, stochastic depth discourages residual drift and promotes convergence across recurrences.
Contractive residual dynamics are what allow KV-shareability, which we formally analyze and empirically validate by showing that replacing intermediate caches with the final cache perturbs the attention output by a term bounded by the difference between their input residuals (see
Section
3.1
).
Unfortunately, even though
stochastic depth
creates contractive residual dynamics, it does not guarantee that residual states converge to the same fixed point with and without KV-sharing. Instead, KV-sharing sometimes introduces token-independent residual errors in the first recurrence, shifting the model’s fixed point and harming downstream quality (see
Section
3.2
).
To enable KV-shareability, we pair stochastic depth pretraining with a targeted correction of the residual errors introduced by KV-sharing. We propose a two-stage method: first,
stochastic depth
pretraining to induce contractive residual dynamics; second,
BeNice!
to correct first recurrence residual errors created from KV-sharing.
Specifically,
BeNice!
jointly optimizes both the first recurrence with KV-cache reuse and the final recurrence without reuse (
Figure
1
[
middle
]), balancing KV-shareability and base-model quality.
To further study KV-sharing with other KV-compression techniques, we extended
BeNice!
to memory-efficient sequence mixers, including multi-latent attention (MLA)
[
13
]
and Kimi delta attention (KDA)
[
65
]
, by reusing the final recurrence’s latent or state, respectively.
Overall,
BeNice!
unlocks near-lossless KV-cache reuse across recurrences, facilitating predictable quality scaling using extended looping
[
50
]
while keeping parameter count and KV-cache memory constant as depth grows.
Figure 1:
Stochastic Depth,
BeNice!
, and KV-Shareability.
(
Left
) During pretraining, stochastic depth induces contractive residual dynamics. (
Middle
)
BeNice!
post-trains by injecting the final recurrence KV-caches into the first recurrence. Together, they enable KV-shareability in looped models, retaining only the final recurrence’s KV-cache
without degrading quality
(
Right
).
We evaluate KV-shareability and
BeNice!
on end-to-end quality, compatibility with other KV compression methods, and how it accelerates inference workloads:
•
End-to-End Quality.
BeNice!
improves shared quality by up to 8.35 and 4.56 points for Core and Core-extended
[
38
]
, respectively. Compared with standard finetuning,
BeNice!
improves validation perplexity by 9.75 points when sharing, while matching quality in the unshared case.
•
Complementary to other KV Compression Methods
. To evaluate
KV-sharing
with other KV-compression methods, we study its composition with memory-efficient sequence mixers and KV-quantization. We find that KV-sharing composes with both MLA and KDA sequence mixers and low-precision KV-quantization (e.g.,
fp8
,
mxfp4
,
nvfp4
).
•
Accelerating Inference Workloads.
Under simulated long-context inference traffic, we observe that memory reductions in KV-sharing improve cache-hit rates by up to 31.4% (8.1 points), increasing throughput by up to 23.6%, and reducing p90 TTFT by up to 83.6%.

Understanding KV-shareability in Looped Models
In this section, we study
KV-shareability
in looped architectures.
To evaluate KV-shareability, we compare
shared evaluations
, which reuse the final-recurrence cache across all recurrences, against
unshared evaluations
, which retain every recurrence’s cache.
Details on reproducing accurate KV-sharing inference setups for our benchmarks are provided in
Appendix
C
.
We motivate our investigation by observing that KV-shareability is
not universal to all looped models
(see
Table
1

stochastic depth
enables contractive recurrent dynamics, which we formally analyze and empirically validate allows KV-shareability when fixed points agree under shared and unshared KV-caches (
Section
3.1
). However, stochastic depth alone is insufficient to guarantee agreement, leading to models not exhibiting KV-shareability (e.g., Parcae 1.3B in
Table
1
).
Analyzing failure cases, we find that KV-sharing creates a token-independent basis shift, causing convergence to different fixed points and degraded quality under KV-sharing (
Section
3.2
).

4.2

6
Conclusion
In this work, we study the emergence and failure points of
KV-shareability
, finding that contractive residual dynamics drive KV-caches towards a common shareable limit. To enable
KV-shareability
, we propose a two stage method: first, we use stochastic depth to induce contractive residual dynamics across recurrences; second, we provide
BeNice!
, a post-training method that corrects residual errors in the first recurrence to ensure that models approach a common limit with and without KV-sharing. KV-shareability composes with both memory-efficient sequence mixers and KV-quantization, detaches inference memory overhead from test-time recurrences, and improves throughput and TTFT in memory-constrained settings.

Appendix B
Extended Literature Review
Looped architectures have been and continue to be explored by a growing body of work. We focus on architectural differences. Here, we discuss the main categories of architectural differences, as well as other works on memory efficiency in looped models.
Middle-Looped Models.
This framework of models utilizes three blocks: a prelude block (
𝒫
\mathcal{P}
) that performs representation extraction using transformer layers, a recurrent block (
ℛ
\mathcal{R}
) that recurrently updates activations, and a coda block (
𝒞
\mathcal{C}
) that turns activations into outputs.
Bansal et al. [7]
,
Geiping et al. [20]
,
McLeish et al. [41]
, and
Prairie et al. [50]
all train middle-looped models with stochastically sampled recurrence depth during pretraining.
Schwethelm et al. [58]
trained middle-looped models with fixed recurrence depth. These architectures tend to be trained with implicit halting mechanisms to determine when to stop looping
[
7
,
20
,
41
,
50
,
58
]
, using either convergence methods like KL divergence between loops
[
7
,
41
]
, low relative differences in successive hidden states
[
20
]
, or use the mean training recurrence as the optimal inference time recurrence depth
[
50
,
58
]
. However,
Bae et al. [4]
is trained with a middle-looped architecture, but uses an explicit halting mechanism of lightweight routers to decide recurrence depth.
Fully Looped Models.
This regime of looped models loops the entire model every recurrence. While not strictly a requirement, this regime of architecture tends to pull from
Graves [23]
work on adaptive compute time (ACT), using explicit halting mechanism to determine when to stop looping.
Dehghani et al. [14]
,
Zhu et al. [80]
(Ouro),
Elbayad et al. [17]
,
Jolicoeur-Martineau [31]
, and
Fu et al. [18]
all extend this concept to language models, varying the mechanisms used for explicit halting. These halting mechanisms include prediction heads for dynamically deciding halting probabilities
[
80
,
17
]
and Q-learning as a means of determining convergence
[
31
,
14
,
23
]
. Most of these models are trained with fixed recurrence depth
[
14
,
80
,
17
,
18
]
.
KV-sharing and Memory Efficiency in Looped Models.
Huginn
[
20
,
21
]
was noted as having KV-sharing ability out-of-the-box.
Bae et al. [4]
proposed a KV-sharing variant for their model that shares first recurrence KV-cache, with some quality loss.
Deng et al. [15]
extends the Ouro
[
80
]
style looped model to use with memory-efficient sequence mixers.
Vendrell et al. [69]
proposed a KV-sharing variant of the Ouro style model that shares the first recurrence KV-cache with later recurrences in addition to maintaining a sliding window KV-cache per recurrence.

article.headline: BeNice!让循环模型复用最终KV缓存
article.lede: 两阶段训练让循环语言模型推理时只保留最终循环的KV缓存，切断缓存内存随循环次数线性增长。
article.problem: 循环架构通过重复使用同一组层，在固定参数下提升质量，但推理时为每次循环单独保存KV缓存，使KV内存随循环次数线性增长。此前一些模型可复用最终循环的KV缓存，但机制不清，且并非普遍成立。
article.method: 作者先用随机深度预训练诱导收缩性残差动态，让不同循环的表示趋于共同定点；再用BeNice!后训练，把最终循环的KV缓存广播到第一循环，并联合优化共享与不共享两条路径的交叉熵损失。
article.results: 在1.3B Parcae、Core-Extended、批大小64和上下文2048的设置下，KV共享把实测全局HBM从63.82 GB降至21.60 GB，降低66.2%；μ_rec=8时总令牌容量达到不共享的3.33倍。BeNice!使共享Core和Core-Extended分别最多提升8.35和4.56点，相比标准微调在共享时把验证困惑度改善9.75点。模拟长上下文负载中，缓存命中率最多提升31.4%（8.1点），吞吐最多提升23.6%，p90 TTFT从139.2秒降到23.2秒（降低83.6%）。
article.why_it_matters: 若该方法成立，增加测试时循环深度可提升质量而不等比增加KV缓存，对长上下文和内存受限推理尤其有意义。
article.limitations: 端到端延迟收益来自模拟的长上下文负载和由开放权重模型循环中间层构造的代理模型，并非生产部署实测。方法依赖随机深度预训练与后续微调，且KV-shareability在部分循环模型上不会自然出现，随机深度单独也不足以保证共享成功。
article.figure_caption_zh: 预训练循环模型的定点收敛：随循环深度增加，循环残差状态和注意力模式的相对变化下降。

email_papers.title: DiffusionART: Efficient, Stable and Scalable Reinforcement of Diffusion Models
email_papers.abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tunes diffusion models with black-box rewards, but reverse-process methods such as Flow-GRPO are limited in efficiency by poor credit assignment, while forward-process methods such as DiffusionNFT are efficient yet unstable without carefully tuned exponential-moving-average (EMA) off-policy training. We show that NFT-style objectives contain a hidden forward--reverse consistency force that joint positive--negative training cancels only partially, and that EMA stabilizes training through restoration rather than off-policy rollouts. We introduce DiffusionART (Diffusion Reinforcement with Aggregation-First Reward Tilting), which aggregates each prompt's rewards into a shared reward-improving direction for reverse-process states, removing the consistency force by construction, and adds a trust-region-masked second update for drift-adaptive restoration without EMA tuning. It requires no differentiable reward model, remains effective with fewer samples per prompt, and supports pairwise reward models (DiffusionART-Pairwise). Across image and video generation, DiffusionART trains efficiently and stably without per-task tuning. In particular, on HunyuanVideo-13B with equally weighted visual and motion quality rewards, DiffusionART reaches the late-stage mean reward levels of DiffusionNFT and Flow-GRPO-Fast with 12.02 and 11.72 times fewer GPU hours, respectively, while achieving 28.8% and 53.0% higher mean training rewards.

Introduction
Visual diffusion and flow-matching models
1

1
We use “diffusion” as a general term. Our paper targets rectified-flow with linear data–noise interpolation
[
Lipman et al., 2022
]
, which shares the core principles of diffusion.
are typically trained to fit the data distribution by regressing noise or velocity targets rather than to optimize downstream criteria such as visual quality, motion quality, or human preference, making reward-guided fine-tuning central to recent image and video generation tasks
[
Xu et al., 2026a
,
Gao et al., 2025
]
. We focus on online diffusion Reinforcement Learning (RL), which, unlike differentiable reward-model optimization such as ReFL
[
Xu et al., 2023
]
or offline preference learning such as Diffusion-DPO
[
Wallace et al., 2023
]
, evaluates clean samples from the evolving generator and can use black-box rewards. Because these rewards arrive only after a complete output is generated, online diffusion RL faces a credit-assignment problem: costly output-level feedback must be translated into effective updates across many denoising states
[
Liu et al., 2025a
,
Zheng et al., 2025
]
.
Within this paradigm,
reverse-process RL
[
Black et al., 2023
]
, such as Flow-GRPO and its variants
[
Liu et al., 2025a
,
Xue et al., 2025
,
He et al., 2025
,
Wang et al., 2026
]
, optimizes sampled denoising transitions via group-based endpoint reward feedback. It trains on states actually visited by the generator but requires ODE-to-SDE conversion for tractable likelihoods, and its policy gradient updates each selected transition along its own transition-level sampling noise, weighted by a trajectory-level advantage that this transition only partly determines, resulting in poor credit assignment and limiting training efficiency.
Forward-process RL
, such as DiffusionNFT
[
Zheng et al., 2025
]
, instead applies forward noising to the generated clean samples and regresses velocities with reward-weighted positive and negative objectives. It needs no transition likelihoods and is highly efficient, but it is unstable without two stabilizers: joint positive–negative training and an exponential moving average (EMA) rollout policy whose lag must be tuned for each task
[
Zheng et al., 2025
]
. Neither family is thus both efficient and stable without per-task tuning. In this paper, we focus on studying the instability of forward-process RL and developing a scalable algorithm which is both stable and efficient.
We first examine NFT-style training, starting from a puzzle: its positive and negative branches share the same ideal reward-improving direction, so either alone should suffice, yet each alone collapses (Figure
2
(a)). We find that NFT’s targets, built from forward-noised endpoints, implicitly assume that the model’s sampling velocity equals the ideal forward velocity induced by its own endpoints. The two differ in practice, and the gap introduces a hidden non-reward-improving
forward–reverse consistency force
: the positive branch pulls each state’s velocity toward the ideal forward velocity and the negative branch pushes it away. Joint training can cancel this force but only partially, since reward centering balances rewards across samples rather than at each state. The residual can destabilize training and slow the reward optimization. We further show that EMA stabilizes NFT through the
restoration force
of its lagged reference, not through off-policy rollouts, but the EMA trick must be tuned per task.
Driven by these insights, we introduce
DiffusionART
(
Diffusion
Reinforcement with
A
ggregation-First
R
eward
T
ilting). It borrows supervised velocity regression from forward-process training but applies updates to states and actions during reverse-process rollouts. It first aggregates each prompt’s samples and rewards into a shared reward-improving direction

4.1
). As this target never involves the forward velocity, the consistency force is removed by construction rather than by cross-sample cancellation, and each state receives an explicit reward-improving direction instead of a scalar advantage passed through likelihood ratios. A second update with a trust-region mask mechanism on each rollout adds a restoration force proportional to each state’s drift, replacing EMA with no schedule to tune (Section
4.2
). We summarize our main contributions as follows:

1. Diagnosing the instability of NFT-style training.
The NFT objective implicitly contains a harmful forward–reverse consistency force that joint training cancels only partially (Section
3.1
).
2. Identifying restoration as the key stabilizer.
EMA stabilizes NFT through restoration rather than off-policy data, but requires per-task tuning (Section
3.2
).
3. Aggregation-first reward tilting with adaptive restoration.
DiffusionART removes the consistency force by construction, eliminating the need for EMA with drift-adaptive restoration (Section
4
).
4. Efficient and stable training.
DiffusionART matches the strongest baseline’s efficiency on SD3.5-M without EMA or per-task tuning.

Conclusion
We studied why NFT-style forward-process diffusion post-training can be unstable and found that its objective can introduce an implicit forward–reverse
self-consistency force that is not reliably canceled across states, while stronger restoration can improve stability at the cost of slower reward optimization. DiffusionART presents a simple but effective way to systematically cancel the unstable force by aggregating endpoint reward guidance before assigning it to reverse-rollout states, and then using a second update with a trust-region mechanism to provide drift-adaptive restoration for stabilization. Experiments on image and video generation show efficient, stable reward improvement, including with pairwise feedback and small rollout groups. Beyond the algorithm, our work provides insights into forward-process training, offering a clearer understanding of diffusion reinforcement learning and a path toward scalable diffusion post-training for visual generation.

A.6
Trust-Region Masking for Image Generation
We remove only the trust-region mask, retaining normalized covariance guidance, timestep weighting, and two disjoint MSE updates. On the three SD3.5-M benchmarks and FLUX.1-dev, training remains effective without masking and can improve slightly faster (Figure
12
). On FLUX.1-dev, the no-mask run reaches a training GenEval score of 0.971 by step 180. The benefit of masking is more pronounced for video generation (Figure
8
); Appendix
A.7
examines its stabilizing effect beyond reward curves.

A.7
Trust-Region Masking Diagnostics
We further inspect the matched HunyuanVideo comparison with VQ:MQ weights of
1
:
1
1{:}1
. Without masking, training exhibits larger late-stage gradient and
velocity-drift spikes (Figure
13
), complementing the
reward curves in Figure
8
(a–b).
Although the mask constrains only the second update of each rollout, its stabilizing effect extends to subsequent first updates. Over the shared first 300 training steps, the maximum first-update gradient norm is 1.96 with masking, compared with 3.33 without it. The velocity drift measured before second updates, which reflects displacement caused by the first update, also shows much larger spikes without masking (Figure
13
). With masking, the velocity drift score stays a healthy level. These observations suggest that restricting second updates helps keep later first updates well behaved, rather than merely suppressing gradients at the masked update.

The second MSE update complements shared guidance with local feedback: its restoring force grows with each state’s displacement from the rollout prediction.
This controls drift without requiring posterior sampling, combining scalable guidance with statewise stabilization.

article.headline: 聚合奖励前置，扩散模型强化学习免 EMA 调参
article.lede: DiffusionART 先把每个 prompt 的样本与奖励聚合成共享引导方向 G(c)，再施加到反向采样状态上，取代
article.problem: 在线扩散 RL 只能在整段输出生成后拿到黑盒奖励，因而需要把输出级反馈分摊到大量去噪状态上。反向过程方法如 Flow-GRPO 训练在实际访问的状态上，但要 ODE-to-SDE 转换，且用轨迹级优势加权单步转移，信用分配差、效率受限。前向过程方法如 DiffusionNFT 无需转移似然、效率高，却依赖正负联合训练和逐任务调参的 EMA 才稳定。
article.method: 作者先给出诊断：NFT 的回归目标建立在正向加噪端点推出的“理想前向速度”上，而采样器实际用的是反向速度场，两者之差 e 使更新中混入一项前向—反向一致性力 (2q−1)e，正负分支只是跨样本部分抵消；EMA 起作用靠的是把参数拉回滞后参考的“恢复力”，而非离线数据。DiffusionART 改为先聚合：用每个 prompt 的 K 个端点与奖励估计奖励—端点协方差，经 RMS 归一化得到 G(c)，直接加在 rollout 时缓存的速度预测上作为冻结目标，从构造上消掉一致性力。随后把每个 rollout 的样本分成两个不相交 minibatch 各更新一次，第二次更新自带随状态漂移增大的恢复项；并用基于 ODE-to-SDE 参考转移的 KL 代理做信赖域掩码，屏蔽漂移过大且方向向外的更新。
article.results: 在 HunyuanVideo-13B、VQ:MQ=1:1 权重下，DiffusionART 用比 DiffusionNFT 和 Flow-GRPO-Fast 分别少 12.02× 和 11.72× 的 GPU 小时达到两者的后期平均奖励水平，最后 50 步平均奖励 13.018，比二者分别高 28.8% 和 53.0%。VQ 达到 5.5 时只需 24 步、63.4 GPU 小时，而 DiffusionNFT(EMA) 需 273 步、1401.4 GPU 小时（步数少 11.4×，GPU 小时少 22.1×）；在 TA:VQ:MQ=7:2:1 下 400 步的评测 VQ/MQ 为 8.970/4.224，比最强基线高 31.4% 和 57.4%。图生视频任务中达到 MQ 6 用 45.8 GPU 小时，Flow-GRPO-Fast 为 220.3（4.8×）。SD3.5-M 上达到 Flow-GRPO 第 500 步奖励所需步数在 GenEval、OCR、PickScore 上分别少 10.0×、5.2×、9.6×。成对奖励、K=2 时 400 步耗 260.8 GPU 小时、VQ 12.235，不逊于 K=8 的 883.3 小时、12.092。
article.why_it_matters: 它把扩散与流匹配模型的在线 RL 后训练从“每个任务调 EMA 与 β”中解放出来，并证明同一套超参可扩展到 13B/14B 视频模型和高维成对偏好奖励，为可规模化的视觉生成后训练提供了一条路径。
article.limitations: 引导 G(c) 是整个 prompt 共享的一阶奖励倾斜方向，并非逐状态的后验引导，单次更新版本会逐渐退化，必须靠第二次更新补上局部修正；作者也承认“恢复力相对引导力在参数梯度上反而更大”这一现象只给出推测，详细分析留待未来工作。此外漂移阈值 δ=10⁻⁵、ν=0.8 等为固定值未做敏感性分析，信赖域掩码在文生图上收益不明显（无掩码甚至略快），主要证据仍来自奖励模型打分的基准，缺少与人类评测的直接对照。
article.figure_caption_zh: 左：NFT 的正负分支各自带来方向相反的前向—反向一致性力、未必完全抵消；右：DiffusionART 把每个 prompt 的端点与奖励聚合成归一化引导 G(c)，直接施加到本次 rollout 经过的状态上。

DiffusionART avoids these forces by applying $G(c)$ directly at the reverse velocity. {Right:} We aggregate each prompt's endpoints and rewards into normalized guidance $G(c)$ (Equation~ {eq:art_empirical_cov}) and apply it to states visited along this rollout.

Abstract
Autonomous research agents are increasingly used to automate large portions of scientific research, yet they are prone to research integrity violations (RIVs): behaviors that compromise the validity, reproducibility, or faithfulness of the research process.
We present RIDAR, a framework for automated RIV detection and runtime intervention.
First, we introduce RIVT, a comprehensive taxonomy of 14 RIV types
spanning the full research lifecycle.
Building on RIVT, we present
RIDAR-Post-hoc
, a framework
to detect RIVs within agent trajectories.
RIDAR-Post-hoc
achieves 85.2% F1 performance on
RIV-Gold
, a benchmark for RIV detection with 60 expert-annotated trajectories.
Applying
RIDAR-Post-hoc
to
RIV-Wild
, a dataset of 300 agent trajectories across 50 distinct research tasks, we detect 3,964 RIV instances in 99.7% of trajectories, revealing the prevalence of RIVs in current agents.
Finally, we present
RIDAR-Runtime
, a framework for dynamically detecting and correcting RIVs during agent runtime.
RIDAR-Runtime
effectively reduces agent RIVs remaining at task completion by 36.8%.
Related code and data are available at
https://github.com/THU-KEG/RIDAR
.
1
Introduction
Figure 1:
An example RIV instance of test-case exploitation. In the right figure, RIDAR detects the violation and provides runtime feedback to the agent, which then corrects its behavior.
Large language model (LLM)-based autonomous research agents, which
automate extended scientific research workflows covering idea generation, experimentation, and paper writing,
have demonstrated remarkable potential for accelerating scientific discovery
(
Lu et al., 2024
;
Yamada et al., 2025
;
Lyu et al., 2026
;
Novikov et al., 2025a
;
Xin et al., 2026
)
.
As the long-horizon agentic capabilities of LLMs continue to grow
(
OpenAI, 2026
;
Anthropic, 2026
;
Z.ai, 2026
)
, research agents
produce increasingly long trajectories spanning hundreds of reasoning steps, tool calls, and observations,
making visibility and verification of process-level behavior a significant challenge.
Scientific research, however, requires valid, reproducible, and faithful research processes,
not just impressive final outputs.
Existing studies show that research agents are prone to
research integrity violations
(RIVs):
agent behaviors that compromise the methodological validity, experimental reproducibility, or evidential faithfulness
of research workflows
(
Luo et al., 2025
;
Atinafu and Cohen, 2026
;
Trehan and Chopra, 2026
;
Fei et al., 2026
)
.
Examples of research integrity violations include presenting previously published research ideas as novel, tuning methods on held-out test data, exploiting evaluator flaws to obtain higher scores, or drawing conclusions unsupported by
collected evidence.
A concrete example of agent RIV and runtime intervention is shown in Figure
1
.
As research agents begin to automate increasingly large portions of the full research lifecycle, there is an urgent call for methods to detect such violations and
intervene at runtime.
Detecting and intervening in research integrity violations faces three key challenges.
(1) Standardization challenge.
RIVs can take diverse forms across
research stages,
making it challenging to establish a
unified standard for their detection.
Existing work typically focuses on analyzing subtypes of RIVs
(
Luo et al., 2025
;
Eulig, 2026
;
Trehan and Chopra, 2026
;
Yang et al., 2026
)
or RIVs for a specific research task
(
Atinafu and Cohen, 2026
)
.
There is no comprehensive, task-agnostic standard for detecting agent RIVs across the full research lifecycle.
(2) Evidential challenge.
RIV detection cannot rely on outcome-level signals, as RIVs often occur in research processes that produce superficially successful outcomes.
Existing efforts on agent failure diagnosis typically start from a known outcome failure, such as an incorrect final answer, and trace backward across the trajectory to collect supporting evidence
(
Cemri et al., 2025
;
Zhu et al., 2025
;
Qi et al., 2026
)
.
Lacking such an outcome anchor, RIV detection instead requires a comprehensive analysis of the agent trajectory to uncover each violation and ground it in dispersed evidence.
(3) Temporal challenge.
Runtime RIV intervention is constrained to observing only a growing trajectory prefix,
requiring a balance between evidence sufficiency and feedback timeliness.
Premature feedback may disrupt normal agent execution, whereas delayed feedback can allow violations to propagate into final outputs.
While runtime intervention has proven effective in preventing unsafe agent behaviors using rule-based matching
(
Xiang et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2025
;
Wang et al., 2026d
)
,
the runtime correction of RIVs, which requires both nuanced, context-sensitive judgement beyond formalized rules and timely feedback, remains a particular challenge.
To address these challenges,
we present
RIDAR
, a framework for
R
esearch
I
ntegrity violation
D
etection
A
nd
R
untime intervention.
We first formalize the Research Integrity
Violation Taxonomy (
RIVT
),
a taxonomy of 14 violation types
spanning the full research lifecycle, including idea generation, literature review, experimentation, and paper writing.
RIVT is empirically grounded in
multi-stage
expert annotation and provides a unified standard for instance-level RIV detection across research stages.
Building on RIVT, we present
RIDAR-Post-hoc
, a post-hoc RIV detection framework for completed agent trajectories.
RIDAR-Post-hoc
performs comprehensive, evidence-grounded RIV detection via three interacting components: an Analyzer agent that examines the trajectory segment by segment and proposes candidate violations, a Verifier agent that validates each candidate, searches for omissions, and assigns RIVT types, and a rule-based middleware that handles deterministic checks and inter-agent communication.
Finally, we present
RIDAR-Runtime
, a runtime
RIV intervention
framework for monitoring and correcting violation behaviors of running research agents.
RIDAR-Runtime
balances evidential sufficiency and feedback timeliness by implementing a single resident Analyzer agent to monitor the growing trajectory prefix, identify violations, and provide feedback to the acting agent for real-time correction of problematic behaviors.
To evaluate RIDAR under realistic agentic research scenarios, we construct
RIV-Gold
, a benchmark of 60 real research agent trajectories manually annotated with RIVT violation types, with an average length of 796.6 steps per trajectory.
On
RIV-Gold
,
RIDAR-Post-hoc
achieves an instance-level F1 of 85.2%, confirming its reliability in RIV detection.
To further investigate the prevalence of RIVs in autonomous research agents, we construct
RIV-Wild
, a dataset of 300 agent trajectories collected from 6 frontier harness-model configurations across 50 distinct research tasks.
RIDAR-Post-hoc
identifies 3,964 RIV instances across 99.7% of these trajectories,
with analysis revealing how violation patterns vary across task and RIV types.
Finally, to test whether RIVs can be mitigated through runtime intervention, we construct
RIV-Live
, a 60-trajectory subset of
RIV-Wild
re-run with
RIDAR-Runtime
intervention,
each paired with its non-intervened baseline.
RIDAR-Runtime
reduces the mean number of RIVs remaining at task completion from 14.9 to 9.4, yielding a 36.8% decrease.
These results show that RIVs are widespread in current autonomous research agents and that automated runtime intervention offers an effective safeguard.
2
RIVT: Research Integrity Violation Taxonomy
Figure 2:
Overview of the 14 RIVT violation types across four stages of the research lifecycle.
To systematically characterize research integrity violations in autonomous research agents, we introduce the Research Integrity Violation Taxonomy (RIVT).
RIVT follows a multi-stage, multi-expert construction process.
First, our authors held numerous roundtable discussions to characterize the core research stages of a full research lifecycle and share violation behaviors each author has personally observed in daily use of frontier agents.
This produced four core stages, idea generation, literature review, experimentation, and paper writing, together with an initial set of candidate RIV types.
Next, we collected a small set of agent research trajectories on tasks from each author’s own expertise, and examined these trajectories to expand and refine the candidate RIV types.
We then recruited 17 experienced AI researchers to annotate the
RIV-Gold
benchmark against this draft taxonomy, allowing them to extend and refine it as their annotations surfaced new behaviors.
Details of
RIV-Gold
benchmark construction will be discussed in Section
4.1
.
Finally, we consolidated this taxonomy through a further round of discussion, yielding the final RIVT with 14 violation types.
Figure
2
shows an overview of RIVT, with full definitions in Appendix
A
.
3
RIDAR: Automated Detection and Runtime Intervention

The overall framework of RIDAR.
In this section, we present RIDAR, a framework for RIV detection and runtime intervention.

RIDAR addresses RIV detection and intervention through two frameworks:
RIDAR-Post-hoc

3.1
RIDAR-Post-hoc
Detecting RIVs in long agent trajectories poses a core tension: detection must achieve comprehensive coverage while avoiding false positives.
RIDAR-Post-hoc
resolves this tension by explicitly separating candidate proposal from validation: an Analyzer agent searches the full trajectory comprehensively to propose evidence-grounded RIV candidates, while a Verifier agent independently determines which candidates are sufficiently supported.
We assign different LLM backbones to the two agents to prevent self-preference biases
(
Panickssery et al., 2024
;
Goel et al., 2025
)
.
During detection, the Analyzer audits the full trajectory segment by segment
under an audit schema,
which organizes auditing around a reference notebook and a group of rubrics.
For each segment, the Analyzer updates the reference notebook

Even with proposal and validation separated, LLM-based auditing remains vulnerable to incomplete coverage and inaccurate evidence handling.
RIDAR-Post-hoc
therefore adds a rule-based middleware with three main functions.
First, it enforces coverage by requiring the Analyzer to process every trajectory segment, answer all rubric items, and submit every recorded candidate for validation.
Second, it performs deterministic checks of RIV findings by validating evidence spans,
structured outputs, and precision-sensitive numerical values.
Finally, it coordinates communication between the two agents through a stateful MCP server, which queues Analyzer proposals for asynchronous validation, returns Verifier feedback for candidate revision or withdrawal, routes completion review candidates, and blocks termination until all candidates are resolved.
3.2
RIDAR-Runtime
A finding that arrives after a run has ended can document a violation but cannot correct it.
We therefore extend RIV detection to enable runtime intervention before a run completes.
To ensure intervention timeliness,
RIDAR-Runtime
employs a single resident Analyzer agent paired with a rule-based Supervisor.
The Analyzer processes growing agent trajectories in windows and

To keep pace with the acting agent, the Analyzer may delegate time-consuming evidence collection tasks to background subagents while retaining the final judgment itself.
Each live finding is passed to the Supervisor, which delivers targeted feedback to the acting agent at the next available interaction point.
However, violations concerning final agent outputs often become decidable only after the agent’s last step, when no further interaction point remains.
RIDAR-Runtime
therefore introduces a
