Each substep issues one query to an external retriever, which filters candidates by score and retains at most $K$ for the {Select} stage.

page_papers.title: WorldForge V2: Eliciting Camera-Trajectory Alignment in Video Diffusion Models
page_papers.abstract: Video diffusion models have learned rich 3D/4D priors, making them promising for scene generation and video re-rendering. However, their use in spatial tasks is limited by imprecise camera control, spatial and temporal inconsistencies, and entangled camera motion with scene dynamics. Existing approaches, such as task-specific fine-tuning and post-process warping, often introduce visual artifacts, generalize poorly, or incur high computational costs. We propose WorldForge V2 to achieve accurate camera control while preserving the generative capabilities of pretrained video models. We first develop a training-free guidance framework using warped references to iteratively refine generation along a target camera path. Optical-flow analysis identifies motion-related latent channels for selective guidance, helping separate motion control from appearance. A dual-path strategy further compares guided and unguided predictions to correct artifacts from imperfect references. Together, these components guide viewpoint changes while preserving scene appearance and object motion. To reduce refinement costs, v-cache approximates the correction using the preceding denoising prediction, avoiding an additional model evaluation. We further extend motion localization from latent channels to network blocks and introduce Trajectory LoRA, which concentrates adaptation on blocks most responsive to trajectory guidance. A two-stage training strategy teaches these adapters to denoise the states encountered during guided generation, using limited supervision effectively. This enables reliable camera control with very little training data, with a single training scene already supporting generalization to unseen scenes. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations across multiple datasets show that our method achieves state-of-the-art generation quality and trajectory accuracy in camera-controlled video generation.
page_papers.content:
Abstract
Video diffusion models have learned rich 3D/4D priors, making them promising for scene generation and video re-rendering. However, their use in these spatial tasks is limited by imprecise camera control, spatial and temporal inconsistencies, and the entanglement of camera motion with scene dynamics. Existing approaches, such as task-specific fine-tuning and post-process warping, often introduce visual artifacts, generalize poorly, or incur high computational costs. We propose WorldForge V2, which aims to achieve accurate camera control while preserving the generative capabilities of pretrained video models. We first develop a training-free guidance framework using warped references to iteratively refine generation along a target camera path. Optical-flow analysis identifies motion-related latent channels for selective guidance, helping separate motion control from appearance. A dual-path strategy further compares guided and unguided predictions to correct artifacts from imperfect references. Together, these components guide viewpoint changes while preserving scene appearance and object motion. To reduce refinement costs, v-cache approximates the correction using the preceding denoising prediction, avoiding an additional model evaluation. We further extend motion localization from latent channels to network blocks and introduce Trajectory LoRA, which concentrates adaptation on blocks most responsive to trajectory guidance. A two-stage training strategy teaches these adapters to denoise the states encountered during guided generation, using limited supervision effectively. This enables reliable camera control with very little training data, with a single training scene already supporting generalization to unseen scenes. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations across multiple datasets show that our method achieves state-of-the-art generation quality and trajectory accuracy in camera-controlled video generation.
Index Terms:
Camera control, video diffusion models, 3D/4D generation.
I

Introduction
Fig. 1:
Comparison with existing methods. With limited training data and iterations, our method achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and trajectory accuracy in camera-controlled video generation.
Recent video diffusion models (VDMs) can synthesize videos with coherent motion, consistent scene content, and plausible viewpoint changes over time
[
1
,
2
,
3
]
. Trained on large-scale video data, these models acquire strong spatiotemporal priors, making them powerful backbones for spatial-intelligence tasks such as 3D/4D generation, video re-rendering, and world modeling
[
4
,
5
,
6
,
7
,
8
,
9
,
10
,
11
]
. In these applications, the camera trajectory determines how a scene is observed over time, which regions become visible, and how viewpoint changes relate to scene geometry. Effective trajectory control is therefore essential. The generated video should follow a specified camera path while preserving scene content, object motion, temporal coherence, and visual quality.
To realize such control, existing approaches broadly follow two directions. One direction adapts VDMs for camera control through additional trainable modules, pose-aware conditioning interfaces, or model fine-tuning
[
12
,
13
,
14
,
15
,
5
,
16
]
. These methods provide explicit camera control but often require large-scale trajectory–video supervision or careful fine-tuning. With limited supervision, such adaptation may weaken the visual and temporal priors of the pretrained model. Recent work has therefore explored training-free alternatives that keep the pretrained VDM fixed and inject trajectory cues only during inference
[
6
,
17
]
, including the zero-shot variant of Warp-as-History
[
18
]
. A representative route is
warping-and-repainting
, which warps already observed content along the target camera path and uses the pretrained video model to synthesize newly revealed regions. This route enables direct camera control at inference time while preserving the pretrained model, making it well suited to downstream spatial-intelligence tasks.
Despite these advantages, warping-and-repainting can introduce a denoising-state mismatch during diffusion sampling. When warped visible regions are directly combined with model-generated regions in a noisy latent, the two parts may correspond to different noise states. The warped regions are associated with externally sampled noise, whereas the generated regions follow the model’s own denoising trajectory. We refer to this mismatch as a
denoising-state domain gap
. It can lead to boundary discontinuities, geometric artifacts, noisy patches, and texture degradation. The key challenge is therefore to inject useful trajectory evidence from warped references while reducing the denoising-state gap introduced by their fusion.
To address this problem, we propose
WorldForge V2
, a camera-trajectory-control framework that helps VDMs use imperfect warped trajectory signals more effectively while preserving generation quality.
WorldForge V2 follows the warping-and-repainting route.
First, it addresses the incompatibility introduced by warped-reference fusion: direct fusion in noisy latents mixes externally noised warped regions with generated regions following the model’s current denoising state.
WorldForge V2 reduces this mismatch by fusing the warped reference into the model-predicted clean estimate and mapping the fused result back to the current denoising state, enabling training-free trajectory-aligned video generation.
Second, clean-estimate fusion provides a reliable way to inject warped references into the denoising process by reducing noisy-state mismatch.
To further improve its sampling efficiency, we introduce v-cache, which approximates the clean-estimate correction directly in noisy latents.
In this way, warped-reference guidance can retain the benefit of clean-estimate fusion while reducing the extra sampling overhead.
Finally, full-model fine-tuning and large trainable control modules involve optimizing a large number of parameters, making it difficult to use limited training data efficiently. To address this problem, we build on our pipeline and further investigate an optimization-based approach to camera-trajectory control. Since different layers in VDMs specialize in different functions, we extend the motion-channel localization used in FLF to model adaptation. We identify trajectory-sensitive blocks and apply LoRA only to these blocks. This selective adaptation provides a data-efficient alternative to broad model tuning.
First, we address the denoising-state incompatibility caused by warped-reference fusion. In direct noisy-space fusion, the warped visible regions and the model-generated regions may follow different denoising states, causing geometric artifacts, boundary discontinuities, and noisy patches. To mitigate this mismatch, Intra-Step Recursive Refinement (IRR) fuses the warped reference with the model-predicted clean estimate under the visibility mask and then re-noises the fused estimate to the current timestep. This fuse-then-renoise process associates all regions with the same Gaussian noise realization, thereby reducing their denoising-state gap.
Camera-trajectory control also faces a typical motion–appearance disentanglement problem, as enforcing camera motion may inadvertently alter object and scene appearance. To address this problem, Flow-Gated Latent Fusion (FLF) uses optical-flow cues to locate channels that are highly correlated with motion and injects trajectory guidance only into these channels, thereby reducing appearance distortion.
Finally, artifacts or misalignment in the warped reference may degrade the quality of the generated video. To mitigate this issue, we propose Dual-Path Self-Corrective Guidance (DSG). Inspired by classifier-free guidance
[
19
]
, DSG compares the trajectory-guided and unguided denoising directions. Their difference captures the update introduced by trajectory guidance, which DSG uses to suppress unreliable deviations while retaining useful trajectory constraints. Together, IRR, FLF, and DSG enable training-free trajectory-aligned video generation while reducing the adverse effects of incompatible denoising states and unreliable reference signals.
Second, the fuse-then-renoise process in IRR provides an effective way to reduce the denoising-state gap introduced by warped-reference fusion. We further improve the efficiency of this process with v-cache. Our key observation is that the correction induced by clean-estimate fusion can be approximated directly in noisy latent space from a denoising prediction already available during sampling. Based on this observation, v-cache applies the approximated correction during warped-reference fusion, allowing trajectory guidance to remain on the original denoising path. This avoids an additional model evaluation and reduces inference latency.
Finally, we further develop an optimization-based extension of our pipeline for camera-trajectory control. Existing optimization-based methods often fine-tune the full model or introduce large trainable control modules, making inefficient use of limited supervision. Since camera control mainly depends on motion-related representations, we extend the motion-channel localization idea of FLF to model adaptation. Leveraging the functional specialization of different VDM layers
[
20
]
, we identify trajectory-sensitive blocks, apply LoRA only to these blocks, and train the adapters with a two-stage optimization strategy tailored to our pipeline. This selective adaptation provides a data-efficient alternative to broad model tuning. In our experiments, we find that training data from a single scene is sufficient to enable effective trajectory following.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:
•
To address denoising-state mismatch, motion–appearance entanglement, and unreliable warped references, we develop a training-free guidance pipeline with IRR, FLF, and DSG, enabling trajectory-aligned video generation with fewer artifacts and less appearance distortion.
•
To retain the benefit of clean-estimate correction with lower sampling cost, we introduce v-cache, which approximates the correction in noisy latent space and avoids an additional model evaluation, thereby reducing inference latency.
•
To avoid data-inefficient full-model tuning, we identify trajectory-sensitive blocks, adapt only these blocks with LoRA, and optimize them using a two-stage strategy tailored to our pipeline; training data from a single scene is sufficient to enable effective trajectory following.
•
Comparative experiments on multiple public datasets demonstrate accurate camera-path control and high-quality video generation.
A preliminary version of this work was published at
CVPR 2026
[
21
]
. The source code is available at
https://github.com/Westlake-AGI-Lab/WorldForge
.
Fig. 2:
Overview of WorldForge V2.
Given a single image or video frame and a target camera trajectory, the scene geometry is reconstructed and rendered into trajectory-aligned warped frames.
WorldForge V2 first performs training-free trajectory guidance in the predicted clean latent space using IRR, FLF, and DSG.
Building on this framework, we further introduce an efficient route that directly fuses trajectory information in the noisy latent space with V-Cache, together with a trajectory-sensitive lightweight LoRA scheme for camera trajectory control using only limited training data.
The resulting video follows the specified camera path while preserving the generative capability of the pretrained video diffusion model.
II

Camera Control in Video Diffusion Models
Existing camera-control methods broadly follow two directions. Training-based methods introduce pose-aware conditioning interfaces, additional control modules, or model fine-tuning to learn camera-controlled generation
[
12
,
13
,
15
,
14
,
5
,
44
,
16
,
45
]
. These methods provide explicit camera control but usually require substantial trajectory–video supervision; when training data are limited, model adaptation may weaken the visual and temporal priors learned during pretraining. Recent work has therefore increasingly explored training-free inference-time control and lightweight adaptation, which preserve most or all of the pretrained model and inject trajectory cues through initial noise, latent transformations, rendered references, or history frames
[
8
,
6
,
17
,
46
,
47
,
18
,
48
]
. Across training-based and training-free methods, warping-and-repainting warps observed content along the target camera path and uses a VDM to generate newly revealed regions
[
49
,
50
]
. This route provides explicit geometric correspondence and integrates naturally with depth estimation, point-based rendering, and visibility masks. WorldForge V2 adopts this route and studies how warped references can be used more effectively for camera-trajectory control while reducing the artifacts introduced during denoising. Related motion-control work also uses entity-specific 3D trajectories to control object motion
[
51
]
.
II-C
Guidance and Correction Strategies in Generative Models
Guidance methods steer diffusion or flow models toward desired outputs by modifying their sampling directions. Classifier-free guidance (CFG) combines conditional and unconditional predictions to improve alignment with semantic conditions
[
19
]
. Subsequent methods further adjust the guidance direction through negative or auxiliary branches, differential predictions, adaptive rescaling, resampling, and iterative repainting
[
52
,
53
,
54
,
55
,
56
,
57
,
58
]
. In 3D/4D generation, guidance is also widely used to enforce viewpoint consistency from rendered or warped observations
[
59
,
60
,
6
,
17
,
8
]
. However, conventional guidance does not directly address the artifacts introduced by noisy warped references. WorldForge V2 explores correction strategies for warping-guided generation, including correcting warped-reference fusion in noisy latent space and using the difference between guided and unguided predictions to refine the denoising process. Together, these strategies improve the quality of trajectory-controlled videos generated under warping guidance.
II-D
Parameter-Efficient Adaptation for Camera Control
Model adaptation commonly uses trainable control branches or parameter-efficient fine-tuning. ControlNet and T2I-Adapter introduce lightweight conditioning modules, while LoRA adapts pretrained models through low-rank parameter updates
[
61
,
62
,
63
]
. These lightweight adaptation strategies have also been applied to motion learning, sparse-view synthesis, and trajectory-controlled generation with limited training data
[
64
,
65
,
18
,
45
]
. Related studies further show that motion- and camera-related representations are concentrated in particular latent channels or network layers
[
20
,
66
]
. Based on these findings, WorldForge V2 uses optical-flow cues in FLF to localize motion-related latent channels and reduce appearance interference. We further extend this idea to model adaptation by identifying trajectory-sensitive blocks and applying lightweight LoRA only to these blocks, enabling effective trajectory alignment with very limited training data.
III

Method
WorldForge V2 (Fig.
2
) aims to control camera trajectories while preserving the video priors of pretrained generation models. Given a source image or video and a target camera path, geometric warping first produces a trajectory reference and its visibility mask. WorldForge V2 then uses these signals to guide denoising and generate videos that follow the target path. Sec.
III-A
introduces the required notation and background. Sec.
III-B
presents the training-free guidance pipeline: IRR reduces the denoising-state gap through clean-estimate fusion, FLF restricts trajectory injection to motion-related latent channels, and DSG corrects the guided prediction using the model’s original denoising path. Sec.
III-C
derives a noisy-latent correction that reduces the denoising-state gap with fewer model evaluations. Finally, Sec.
III-D
identifies trajectory-sensitive network blocks and adapts them with LoRA using limited supervision, enabling data-efficient trajectory control for VDMs.
III-A

Experiments
Our experiments examine how rendered-reference guidance combines camera control with the scene priors of pretrained video models. We first evaluate the training-free framework in static 3D generation and dynamic 4D re-rendering, then study V-Cache correction and data-efficient LoRA adaptation. Transfer experiments examine the reuse of the learned control, and ablations establish the roles of guidance, block selection, and training. We denote the IRR–FLF–DSG framework as
Ours (Training-Free)
and the adapted models as
Ours (LongCat)
and
Ours (H3)
.
IV-A

Experimental Setup

Metrics
We evaluate visual quality and camera accuracy together. The training-free experiments use FID and CLIP similarity for static scenes, and FVD and CLIP-V similarity for dynamic videos. For Trajectory LoRA, we additionally evaluate target-view reconstruction with pixel-level metrics, PSNR and SSIM, and the perceptual metric LPIPS. Vis-LPIPS and Disocc-LPIPS assess preservation of visible content and completion of newly exposed regions, respectively. ATE measures overall trajectory agreement, while RPE-T and RPE-R measure local translation and rotation errors. Metric implementations are specified in the supplementary material.
IV-B
Inference-Time Camera-Trajectory Control
We evaluate whether warped-reference guidance can follow a prescribed camera path while retaining the scene priors of a frozen video backbone. For static 3D generation, we compare with See3D
[
49
]
, ViewCrafter
[
4
]
, ViewExtrapolator
[
17
]
, TrajectoryAttention
[
15
]
, TrajectoryCrafter
[
5
]
, and NVS-Solver
[
6
]

[
14
]
does not directly accept warped reference videos as trajectory inputs and is therefore included only in the qualitative comparison.

Method

Conclusion
We presented WorldForge V2 for accurate camera control while preserving the generative capabilities of pretrained video models. Our training-free guidance uses warped references to iteratively refine generation along the requested camera path, with motion-aware channel selection and self-correction preserving scene appearance and object motion. Building on this guidance, v-cache reuses denoising predictions to approximate the refinement correction, reducing sampling cost. Trajectory LoRA extends motion localization from latent channels to network blocks and combines selective adaptation with two-stage training, enabling pretrained video models to learn reliable trajectory control from very few trajectory–video pairs. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations across multiple datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art generation quality and trajectory accuracy in camera-controlled video generation. Future work will explore long-horizon, real-time streaming generation with camera control to support the development of interactive world models.

article.headline: WorldForge V2：免训练实现相机轨迹控制
article.lede: 新框架 WorldForge V2 把 warp 参考融入去噪干净估计，免训练地为视频扩散模型提供相机轨迹控制。
article.problem: 现有 warping-and-repainting 路线在噪声潜空间直接融合 warp 内容时会引入「去噪状态域差」：warp 区域绑定外部采样噪声，模型生成区域则跟随自身去噪轨迹，两者不一致会造成边界断裂、几何伪影、噪声块与纹理退化。同时，相机运动与物体、场景外观相互纠缠，强制视角变化容易连带改写外观；而依赖大规模轨迹—视频对的有监督微调在数据有限时会削弱预训练先验。
article.method: 作者提出 IRR（Intra-Step Recursive Refinement）：在可见性掩码下把 warp 参考与模型预测的干净估计融合，再重新加噪回当前时间步，使两区域共享同一噪声实现以缩小去噪状态差。FLF 用光流线索定位与运动强相关的潜通道，只在这些通道注入轨迹引导以减少外观失真；DSG 借鉴 CFG，比较引导与无引导预测之差来压制不可靠参考带来的偏差。效率侧，v-cache 复用采样中已有的去噪预测在噪声潜空间近似该修正，省去一次额外模型评估；Trajectory LoRA 把运动定位从潜通道扩展到网络块，只对轨迹敏感块加 LoRA，并用两阶段训练适配引导生成中出现的状态。
article.results: 原文在多个公开数据集上做了静态 3D 生成与动态 4D 重渲染对比，指标包括 FID、CLIP、FVD、CLIP-V、PSNR、SSIM、LPIPS、Vis-LPIPS、Disocc-LPIPS、ATE、RPE-T、RPE-R，并宣称在生成质量与轨迹精度上达到 SOTA。但本次提供的正文中相关表格只剩表头、数值全部缺失，论文未给出具体数字，因此无法核验具体提升幅度。可引用的定量陈述仅有一处定性描述：单个场景的训练数据已足以支撑对未见场景的泛化。
article.why_it_matters: 把相机控制做成免训练引导、再叠加极小数据的块级 LoRA，意味着 3D/4D 生成、视频重渲染和世界模型这类空间任务可以在不牺牲预训练视频先验的前提下获得可控视角，降低了适配成本。
article.limitations: 全文没有任何可核对的定量结果与消融数值，SOTA 断言目前无法验证；方法仍依赖深度估计与几何 warp 的质量，v-cache 只是对干净估计修正的近似，「单场景即可泛化」也只有作者自述，尚缺多场景统计支撑。
article.figure_caption_zh: 不同参考插入策略下的噪声状态一致性：直接插入会在可见区与模型生成区之间留下推断噪声均值与对数方差的间隙，并伴随噪声块与结构断裂；IRR 缩小了这些间隙，V-Cache 在近似其修正的同时保持连续表面与清晰几何细节。

FrontierCS 2: A Benchmark for Computer Science R&D
Abstract
Website
\href
https://frontier-cs.orgfrontier-cs.org
Code
\href
https://github.com/FrontierCS/FrontierCS-2github.com/FrontierCS/FrontierCS-2
Abstract
Can LLM agents make contributions to frontier computer science R&D? We introduce FrontierCS 2, a benchmark of 48 open-ended tasks. We take a paper and the code its authors released and delete the paper’s contribution. The deleted code becomes the human reference that sets the bar.
Earlier open-ended benchmarks give each agent a problem statement and grade one program after the run. FrontierCS 2 places the agent inside a research environment. The agent inherits a working repository and may submit a patch at any point. For each patch, a judge returns a development-suite score but keeps the evaluator, the held-out final suite and the reference private, and grades the final submission on that suite against the reference.
The tasks span 13 domains, from machine-learning systems and high-performance computing to databases, security and robotics. Beyond these 48 tasks, FrontierCS 2 keeps a private set of more than 100 tasks, to be announced in the future.
We evaluate 12 agents. The best one is Claude Opus 5.5, passing 58% of its runs. No run passes on 16 tasks. A higher score is not the same as a pass: most runs that beat the reference on the combined final score still fall short on some metric or workload. On a shared capability scale for agents and tasks, the median task is roughly as difficult as what the strongest agent can handle.

Introduction
Figure 1:
Pass rate.
Share of each agent’s runs whose final submission beats the human reference on every metric and held-out workload; the harness is in gray.
Consider a researcher who picks up a published system to make it better. They inherit a working codebase, change one component, test the change on the workloads the paper reported, and are judged against the paper’s own implementation. Much of research and development in computer science looks like this. We ask whether an LLM agent can do the same.
Existing open-ended benchmarks answer a narrower question. On FrontierCS

(

Benchmarks that do place the agent in a real environment are narrow in another way. SWE-bench

In this paper, we evaluate agents against the published code itself, inside the repository it came from, across computer science. FrontierCS 2 is the second version of FrontierCS (
\Cref
tab:fcs-versions). We take the code a paper’s authors released, delete the paper’s contribution, and ask the agent to rebuild it so that it beats the original (
\Cref
fig:overview). We call the deleted code the human reference and measure it on the paper’s own workloads (
\Cref
sec:method). The agent works as a researcher would. It edits the code, submits a patch whenever it likes, and gets back a score on a development suite from a judge. The evaluator, the held-out final suite and the human reference stay with the judge (
\Cref
sec:scoring). At the end, the agent names one patch as final, and the judge grades that patch on the held-out suite. A run passes only when the patch beats the human reference on every metric and every held-out workload.
We evaluate 12 models, each paired with one agent harness, with one run per task. The best agent, Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, passes 58% of its runs, and every other agent passes fewer than half of its runs (
\Cref
fig:pass-rate). No agent passes any of 16 tasks. To compare agents and tasks on one scale, we fit the FrontierCS Capabilities Index (FCI) together with a matching difficulty index. The median task sits at about the strongest agent’s FCI (
\Cref
sec:exp-eci). The leading agent also changes with the cost budget per run (
\Cref
sec:scaling).
In summary, our contributions are:

Task building
Figure 2:
FrontierCS 2 task building.
We delete the paper’s contribution from its own repository and give the agent what remains. The judge keeps the deleted code as the human reference, the pass thresholds measured from it on the paper’s workloads, and a final suite with held-out workloads.
We build the tasks by subtraction from the code the paper’s authors released (
\Cref
fig:construction,tab:sources).

We locate the code that implements the paper’s contribution, delete it, and leave everything it depends on unchanged. Take SVG-EAR
(
29
)
, which we build from the Sparse VideoGen repository
2
2
2
\url
https://github.com/svg-project/Sparse-VideoGen
. We delete the error-aware attention class and three of its routines. These routines average each cluster, choose the cluster pairs to compute, and compute those pairs while estimating the rest. The agent receives this repository with the deleted functions still declared and called, and it must write them. It may edit only the files that held the contribution. The human reference is a private patch that restores the deleted code. Subtraction gives each task built this way an oracle that already runs in its repository on the paper’s own workloads.
We set each metric’s pass threshold from the reference’s own measurements on the workloads the paper reported. For SVG-EAR, latency must be at most 0.96 times the reference’s latency, PSNR must stay within 0.25 dB of the reference value, SSIM within 0.01 and LPIPS within 0.005. The judge scores every submission on a development suite of these workloads. Only the final submission is scored on a final suite, which adds held-out instances the agent never sees (different seeds, queries or input graphs).
4
Judge
Figure 3:
FrontierCS 2 judge.
Each colored box is a sandbox. The agent’s sandbox reaches only the driver. The agent sees only a development-suite score and a sanitized message per patch; all that decides its result stays with the judge.
The agent and the judge hold separate information (
\Cref
fig:evaluation). The agent holds the repository; the judge holds the evaluator, the held-out final suite and the human reference. The agent has five hours and may submit a patch to the allowed files at any time. The judge returns the patch’s score on the development suite and a message that counts the development workloads meeting each metric’s threshold, without the reference score or the evaluator’s raw output.
They also run apart, each in its own sandbox, linked only by a driver started for the run. The agent’s sandbox reaches no network but the driver, which forwards its model calls and patches, so it cannot download the authors’ code. On GPU tasks, the agent may start a development GPU through the driver, while only the judge uses the GPU that measures the patch against the human reference. Some tasks also give the judge test sandboxes: on Continuum
(
30
)
, a vLLM serving task, they run SWE-bench episodes against the patched vLLM.
Development-suite scores guide the agent and do not count toward its result. At the end of the run, the agent names one submission as final, and the judge evaluates that patch alone on the held-out suite. We do not pick its best development-suite submission for it, since choosing the patch is part of a researcher’s work. We say a submission beats the reference on a metric when it meets that metric’s threshold. A run passes when its final submission beats the reference on every metric across every held-out workload. The judge also assigns a final score from 0 to 100 on a scale each task defines.

Evaluation results
5.1
Experimental setup
Figure 4:
Pass rate and cost.
Each point is one agent: pass rate on the y-axis against mean cost per run in US$ on a log-scale x-axis. GPT-6.1 Sol passes less often than GPT-6 Astra and sits far to its left on the cost axis.
Agents.
An agent pairs a model with a harness, the program that runs the model’s tool calls and submits its patches to the judge. We evaluate 12 models, each in one harness. We name each agent by its model, but the harness is part of what we measure.
\Cref
tab:agents lists each agent’s harness, version, reasoning effort and output limit.
Tasks and runs.
A run is one agent on one task, from the starting repository to its final submission. Each of the 12 reported agents runs each task once. The provider refused two Gemini 4 Argon runs before a final submission. Like every run without a passing final submission, they count as failures, in the pass rate and in FCI alike.
Metrics.
Our main metric is the pass rate, the share of an agent’s runs that pass. We also report an agent’s mean score, its mean margin over the human reference. This is the average over its runs of the final score minus the reference’s score on the same task (0 is a tie).
\Cref
fig:pass-cost sets each agent’s pass rate against its mean cost per run. A higher final score does not mean a pass, and a pass does not need a higher score (
\Cref
fig:score-ref). Most runs whose final score exceeds the human reference’s miss a threshold on at least one metric or workload. Conversely, some passing runs score at or below the reference’s final score, since the final score is one number on each task’s own scale, while a pass needs every metric to hold at once.

Each faint point is one run’s final score minus the human reference’s on the same task, one row per agent; the line spans each agent’s range and the dot marks its mean. The vertical line at 0 marks a tie.
5.2
FrontierCS Capabilities Index (FCI)
The FrontierCS Capabilities Index (FCI) puts the agents on one capability scale, and the FrontierCS Difficulty Index (FDI) puts the tasks on the same scale. FCI adapts Epoch AI’s Epoch Capabilities Index
(
31
)
, an item response model. We fit it to per-metric outcomes and to score margins over the human reference, rather than to raw scores.
One joint fit takes two observations from every run: which of the task’s metrics the run beats the human reference on, and the margin of its final score over the reference’s. The metric outcomes tell the fit how hard each part of a task is, and the margin tells it how close a failed run came. Both share one fitted run effect, which says how far that run lands above or below its agent’s strength.
Each agent has one strength, which we report as its FCI: ten points per logit, with Kimi K2.7 at 0. Kimi K2.7, run in Kimi Code, is a thirteenth agent that serves only as this 0 point: its runs enter the fit, but we do not report it. A task’s FDI is the FCI at which an agent passes it half the time. The human reference has no FCI, since its code cannot beat itself. Intervals are 90% bootstrap intervals over the tasks, and
\Cref
app:fci gives each step of the fit.
Figure 6:
FrontierCS Capabilities Index.
Each bar shows an agent’s FCI from 0 with its 90% bootstrap interval as a whisker. The intervals separate only agents that sit far apart on the capability scale.
Claude Opus 5.5 leads FCI, followed by GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, and Step 5 Preview is last (
\Cref
fig:fci); FCI and the pass rate order the agents almost alike. The tasks span a wider range of difficulty than the agents do: the median task sits at about the strongest agent’s FCI. Each task’s FDI is uncertain, however, so we do not order individual tasks by it. FDI measures how hard a task is to pass, and across tasks it follows the pass rate closely.

Case studies
6.1
Two checksums shrink private lookups
Figure 8:
QuarterPIR bytes per lookup.
Bytes per private lookup on the 67-million-entry database; the x-axis starts at 1,200. Muse Wonder 1.0’s checksums remove far more of the reference’s bytes than any other passing run does. Kimi K3, far below the rest and not passing, is left out. Step 5 Preview’s run timed out.
Private information retrieval lets a client read one entry of a database held by a server, without the server learning which entry it read. QuarterPIR
(
32
)
makes this cheap. The client first builds a compact summary of the database; afterwards, each lookup costs one short request and one short reply. In our task the agent rewrites how the server answers requests, and it may also change the messages and the client. A run passes if every lookup returns the right entry and the run beats the human reference on the bytes each lookup sends, on every timing, and on the memory the client keeps.
In the human reference, every reply carries values the client rarely needs. Along with the answer, the server returns one parity value for each group of the database. The client needs only one of them, to correct the hint it refreshed after its previous lookup. Asking for that one alone, however, would tell the server where its previous lookup went. Muse Wonder 1.0 replaces these values with two checksums, the construction that lets a RAID-6 disk array rebuild two failed disks. Since the client already knows the only two groups in which its own values can differ from the server’s, two checksums are enough to recover the one it needs. This shrinks every reply, and therefore every lookup. Privacy is unchanged, because the task lets the server see only a public function of the request the authors’ client would send.
Muse Wonder 1.0’s run passes with a final score above the human reference’s. Most agents pass this task, but no other passing run shrinks the lookup by nearly as much (
\Cref
fig:case-quarterpir). We found this idea only by reading the patches, since neither of our measures picks it out. A pass counts the same whether a run saves a few bytes or the most. GPT-6.1 Sol even scores slightly higher than Muse Wonder 1.0 with a far smaller saving.
6.2
Two faster clocks for a packet scheduler
Figure 9:
BBQ clock period and circuit size.
Each point is one agent’s circuit on the largest tree, 4,096 priorities. The x-axis gives its size in lookup tables and the y-axis its clock period, with shorter, faster clocks at the top; the grey dot marks the human reference. Claude Opus 5.5’s circuit has the shortest clock period and is among the largest. Agents without a correct circuit at this size are left out.
A network switch or network card has to decide, for every packet it sends, which waiting packet goes next. Programmable schedulers express this decision as a priority queue: each packet carries a priority, and the queue must hand out the most urgent one millions of times per second. BBQ
(
33
)
builds such a queue as an FPGA circuit. It marks the occupied priorities in a tree of bitmaps. Each bit keeps a count of the packets below it, so that the bit can be cleared when its last packet leaves. In our task the agent rewrites the logic of the tree’s levels. A run passes if the circuit is correct and beats the human reference on throughput and on worst-case latency at every tree size, including a larger one that the agent never sees during development.
On the smaller trees, the slowest step of each clock cycle in the human reference begins with a counter read from on-chip memory. The operation just ahead may have changed the same counter a moment earlier. The circuit therefore has to check the value it read against recent updates before it can use it. Gemini 4 Argon keeps the memories but settles that check while the read is still in flight, leaving little work for when the value arrives. Claude Opus 5.5 takes the other route. It moves every counter from memory into registers and updates a whole level of the tree in a single cycle, so that on the development trees no operation waits for a read.
Only these two and GPT-6.1 Sol pass, and the two designs trade speed for size (
\Cref
fig:case-bbq). Both handle more operations per second than the human reference on every tree. On the largest tree, however, the circuit of Claude Opus 5.5 uses the most lookup tables of the passing circuits. Its design also does not serve trees as large as those BBQ was designed for. Gemini 4 Argon keeps roughly the human reference’s circuit size and memory layout. Registers alone do not explain Claude Opus 5.5’s clock. Other agents also move the counters into registers, and on the largest tree they end up slower than the human reference. The final score ranks Claude Opus 5.5 first, because it rewards speed and ignores circuit size.
6.3
A measured budget for sparse video attention
Figure 10:
SVG-EAR time and PSNR.
Each run’s mean time per clip and mean PSNR against full attention on the held-out clips, with the human reference’s in grey; the x-axes start at 600 s and 16 dB. Only GPT-6 Astra is both faster and closer to full attention than the human reference on average, and it still fails. Step 5 Preview, far slower, is off the chart.
Video diffusion models spend most of their time in attention. SVG-EAR
(
29
)
, our running example in
\Cref
sec:method, computes some blocks of attention exactly and estimates the rest from cluster centroids. Within a fixed budget, it computes the blocks whose estimates would err the most. A run passes only if every held-out clip is faster than with the human reference and stays within narrow bands of its PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS.
No run passes, and GPT-6 Astra comes closest. It keeps the authors’ design but measures the error instead of predicting it. Every few denoising steps, it computes the exact attention of a few real queries and rebuilds their output under several budgets. Each attention head then runs with the smallest budget whose error stays under a bound. Astra also corrects a bias of the centroid estimate that the paper leaves in. Its videos come out faster than the human reference’s on every clip and, on average, closer to full attention (
\Cref
fig:case-svgear). It still fails on image quality in two clips. Speed was not the obstacle on this task. Most runs beat the reference’s time on every clip, and no run stays within every image band.
7
Conclusion
We built FrontierCS 2 to ask whether LLM agents can make contributions to frontier computer science R&D. Each task measures an agent against the code that researchers released with their paper, in that code’s own repository. Beyond these 48 tasks, FrontierCS 2 keeps a private set of more than 100 tasks, to be announced in the future.
The case studies show what the pass and the final score capture and what they miss. On SVG-EAR, a run faster than the human reference on every clip and closer to full attention on average still fails on image quality in two clips (
\Cref
sec:case-svgear). On QuarterPIR, neither measure separates the run that removes far more bytes per lookup from the other passing runs (
\Cref
sec:case). On BBQ, the final score ranks the largest passing circuit first, because it ignores circuit size (
\Cref
sec:case-bbq). We think benchmarks like this one will need to report such side costs next to the pass.
FCI and FDI are the measures we recommend for benchmarks like this one. They place agents and tasks on one scale, use every metric outcome and score margin of a run rather than one number, and come with intervals that show which differences the data support (
\Cref
sec:exp-eci).

article.headline: FrontierCS 2：让智能体重建论文代码
article.lede: 新基准从论文仓库删除关键贡献，要求智能体提交补丁并超越作者原码；最强代理通过58%的运行。
article.problem: 现有开放式编码基准多给一个问题陈述、只评分一次，或仅在机器学习领域用测试与排行榜衡量；缺少在真实仓库中直接与作者代码比较、跨计算机科学领域的研发型任务。FrontierCS 2 据此追问：LLM 智能体能否在论文自己的代码库中做出前沿计算机科学研发贡献。
article.method: 任务通过“减法”构建：取论文作者发布的代码，删除实现论文贡献的部分，保留依赖与调用，并把删除代码作为人类参考。智能体获得可运行仓库，在五小时内可随时提交补丁；法官返回开发集分数，但隐藏评估器、留出最终集和参考。最终提交只在留出工作负载上逐指标与人类参考比较，全部指标和工作负载都超过参考才算一次运行通过。
article.results: 论文评估了12个智能体，最佳为Claude Opus 5.5，通过其58%的运行，其余智能体通过率均低于一半；有16个任务没有任何一次运行通过。基准包含48个任务，覆盖13个计算机科学领域，另有超过100个私有任务待后续公布。中位任务的难度约等于最强智能体的FCI水平。
article.why_it_matters: 它把智能体评估从一次性程序题推进到真实仓库中的研究式改动，并以作者原始代码作为标尺，覆盖数据库、高性能计算、安全、机器人等13个领域，更接近计算机科学研发实践。
article.limitations: 局限在于每个被报告的智能体在每项任务上只运行一次，且不同智能体使用不同harness；案例研究还显示通过率和最终分数会忽略电路大小、每次查询字节缩减幅度等侧成本，FCI的90%区间也只能分开差距较大的智能体。

Rethinking Sequence Compression with
Test-time Regression
Sihan Yang   Jie Huang   Hanxuan Li   Yifan Guo   Weigao Sun   Yiran Zhong   Weiyang Liu
The Chinese University of Hong Kong   Independent Researcher   Token Foundry
Alibaba Group
*
Corresponding author
spherelab.ai/ttr-compressor
Abstract
Sequence compression is a fundamental operation and a critical information bottleneck in efficient language and multimodal models, and yet prevailing approaches based on pooling or learned projections remain underperforming.
We revisit sequence compression through the lens of test-time regression: input tokens define a regression problem whose fitted coefficients form the compressed representation.
Importantly, the regression problem is learned end-to-end via backpropagation, while its coefficients are computed efficiently in closed form during the forward pass.
This leads to TTR-Compressor, a general alternative to conventional pooling and projection-based compression.
We evaluate TTR-Compressor as the compressor for block-wise sparse attention and the visual token merger for multimodal large language models.
On block-wise sparse attention, TTR-Compressor improves RULER performance over attention-based compressors by a large margin.
For visual token merging, it consistently outperforms the standard MLP merger and matches its performance with 55.6% fewer visual tokens.
These results establish test-time regression as an effective primitive for sequence compression in efficient language and multimodal models.
Figure 1:
Overview of TTR-Compressor.
(a) Unlike pooling and projection, which process tokens independently, TTR-Compressor fits all tokens jointly and thereby captures the interplay among them. (b) TTR-Compressor outperforms existing methods on both block-wise sparse attention and visual token merging.
1
Introduction
Sequence compression is a ubiquitous operation in modern efficient large model architectures
(
Qwen Team, 2026b
;
DeepSeek-AI, 2026
)
, and yet remains surprisingly underexplored. For example, block-wise sparse attention compresses each token block into a summary vector used to score and select relevant blocks
(
Jiang et al., 2024
;
Lu et al., 2025
;
Yuan et al., 2025
)
, while multimodal large language models (MLLMs) merge neighboring visual features into compact tokens before feeding them into the language backbone
(
Wang et al., 2025
;
Bai et al., 2025
;
Team et al., 2026a
)
. In both settings, the compressor acts as a critical information bottleneck. Once information is discarded, it cannot be recovered downstream.
One would expect compression to be a carefully designed architectural component. However, most models rely on simple mechanisms, such as parameter-free pooling, learned projections over concatenated tokens, or at best, attention-weighted pooling.
We argue that these default compressors share a fundamental structural limitation,
i.e.
,
they aggregate tokens using weights that do not account for inter-token relationships
.
Mean pooling uses uniform weights, linear projection uses fixed position-dependent weights, and attention-weighted pooling scores each token independently.
As a result, redundant tokens can reinforce one another, while distinctive information is diluted.
From a statistical perspective, these methods primarily exploit
first-order
token statistics while ignoring
second-order
inter-token correlations, the very structure that reveals which information is redundant and which is distinctive.
We introduce a fundamentally different compression strategy. Rather than asking
which weighted average
best summarizes a set of tokens, we let the tokens define a regression problem
and take its
fitted coefficients
as the summary. Specifically, our proposed TTR-Compressor, constructs a self-supervised ridge-regression problem directly from the input tokens, requiring no external labels, and uses its closed-form solution as the compressed representation.
This formulation creates a natural division: the outer training loop meta-learns
which
regression problem produces task-useful representations, while the inner closed-form solution determines
how
that problem should be fitted to each input. The key distinction from conventional pooling and projection arises from the Gram matrix in the regression solution.
By explicitly capturing inter-token correlations, TTR-Compressor fits correlated tokens jointly, so redundant evidence has diminishing rather than purely additive influence.
This input-adaptive behavior cannot be reproduced by a fixed projection or additive token combination.
Moreover, learning the regularizer removes the need for ridge hyperparameter tuning in large-scale pretraining. Because the compression window is typically smaller than the channel dimension (
i.e.
,
T
<
d
T<d
), we solve the dual problem with an efficient
T
×
T
T\times T
Cholesky factorization.
Thus, TTR-Compressor incurs minimal overhead and introduces only
2
​
d
2d
learnable parameters per compressor, making it an effective drop-in replacement for sequence compression.
We evaluate TTR-Compressor on two applications that impose fundamentally different requirements on compression. In
block-wise sparse attention
, the compressed summary must act as a faithful
retrieval key
. In this setting, TTR-Compressor consistently outperforms traditional baselines on RULER
(
Hsieh et al., 2024
)
retrieval tasks, surpassing sophisticated attention-based compressors
(
Hu et al., 2026
)
by a considerable margin. In
visual token merging
, by contrast, the compressed summary must preserve a faithful
representation
. Here, TTR-Compressor consistently outperforms the widely used MLP merger across diverse compression ratios, and achieves comparable performance with 55.6% fewer visual tokens. Our contributions are summarized below:
•
A novel compression framework.
We introduce a test-time regression framework for sequence compression, reframing token summarization as an instance-adaptive optimization problem.
•
A practical operator.
We derive an efficient dual closed-form solution and eliminate hyperparameter tuning, making TTR-Compressor fully practical and scalable for large-scale pretraining.
•
Empirical effectiveness.
As a drop-in component in large models, TTR-Compressor consistently outperforms conventional baselines in both block-wise sparse attention and visual token merging.
2
Related Work
Sequence compression.
Compressing a sequence of tokens into a single vector is a fundamental operation across modern architectures, with applications ranging from multimodal token reduction
(
Bolya et al., 2022
;
Li et al., 2023
;
Yao et al., 2024
;
Cha et al., 2024
;
Chu et al., 2024
)
to block-wise sparse attention
(
Jiang et al., 2024
;
Lu et al., 2025
;
Gao et al., 2024
;
Lai et al., 2025
)
.
Existing compression operators largely fall into three paradigms:
(1)
parameter-free pooling
, such as mean pooling;
(2)
concatenation followed by learned projection
; and
(3)
attention-based compression
, which summarizes tokens via attention-weighted averaging
(
Mohtashami & Jaggi, 2023
;
Yang et al., 2025b
)
.
A fundamental limitation of these families is that they compute token combinations without explicitly accounting for the inter-token correlations.
In contrast, TTR-Compressor derives its representation as the solution to a linear system whose Gram matrix directly encodes these correlations, providing an expressive, drop-in replacement for the operators above.
Test-time regression and test-time training.
The idea of adapting part of a network on each input at inference time dates back to fast-weight programmers
(
Schmidhuber, 1992
;
Schlag et al., 2021
)
and was revived as test-time training (TTT), first for robustness under distribution shift
(
Sun et al., 2020
)
and then as sequence-modeling layers whose hidden states are small models updated by gradient descent on a self-supervised loss
(
Sun et al., 2024
;
Behrouz et al., 2026b
;
Behrouz et al., 2026a
;
Han et al., 2026
)
. In-Place TTT
(
Feng et al., 2026
)
further extends this paradigm by directly adapting the existing MLP projection weights of pretrained Transformers. A parallel line of work reinterprets linear attention and its descendants (
e.g.
, DeltaNet
(
Yang et al., 2024
)
, Gated DeltaNet
(
Yang et al., 2025c
)
, Longhorn
(
Liu et al., 2025
)
, Titans
(
Behrouz et al., 2026b
)
) as online regression: each layer maintains a key-to-value regressor that is refined with one gradient or delta-rule step per token and read out by the query. MesaNet
(
von Oswald et al., 2026
)
pushes the inner optimization to convergence, solving the problem at every time step with conjugate gradients, while LaCT
(
Zhang et al., 2026
)
updates fast weights over large, unordered chunks to improve hardware utilization.
TTR-Compressor differs from these methods in two fundamental ways. First, because compression operates independently on small, disjoint blocks without cross-block dependencies, the regression admits an efficient,
exact closed-form solution
via a single
T
×
T
T\times T
dual solve. This avoids both iterative gradient-based inner optimization (as in TTT, ViT
3
, In-Place TTT, and MesaNet) and single-step approximations (such as delta-rule updates). Second, rather than using test-time regression to produce input-dependent model weights
(
Bertinetto et al., 2018
;
Sun et al., 2020
)
or a fast-weight memory that is subsequently queried
(
Schlag et al., 2021
;
Yang et al., 2025c
;
Behrouz et al., 2026b
)
, we use regression to directly yield a
representation
of a token block. Specifically, the fitted coefficients themselves serve as the compressed representation (
e.g.
, a visual token or a retrieval key).

5
Applications and Experimental Results
We evaluate TTR-Compressor in two settings: block-wise sparse attention for efficient language modeling, where compressed representations guide context selection, and visual token merging for efficient multimodal understanding, where they serve as the visual input to the language backbone.
5.1
Block-wise Sparse Attention
Architecture and Baselines.
Block-wise sparse attention partitions the context into blocks, scores their compressed representations against each query, and attends to tokens in selected blocks alongside a local window. The compressor therefore determines which distant information remains accessible: an uninformative summary can prevent a relevant block from being selected, regardless of the quality of its individual token representations.
We adopt HiLS-Attention
(
Hu et al., 2026
)
as a base framework and vary only the compressor. HiLS-Attention has three effective architectural components: hierarchical softmax attention, which combines within-block attention with learned block-level weights; low-rank query calibration, which adapts queries for scoring compressed representations; and HoPE, which applies RoPE to only a subset of feature dimensions to support length extrapolation. We compare four compressors: mean pooling, concat & projection, the attention-weighted pooling used in the original HiLS-Attention, and TTR-Compressor. Full attention and sliding-window attention serve as additional references.

We train 345M-parameter language models on the FineWeb dataset
(
Penedo et al., 2024
)
with an 8K context length. Training runs for 30,000 optimization steps with a global batch size of 128 sequences, corresponding to approximately 30B tokens, and uses AdamW with a learning rate of
3
×

Evaluation covers two complementary aspects. First, since queries use the compressed representations to retrieve relevant blocks, retrieval accuracy directly reflects compression quality. Following
(
Hatamizadeh et al., 2026

Results.
As shown in Table
1
, the choice of compressor largely determines retrieval quality. TTR-Compressor outperforms all baselines by a large margin, and its advantage persists when extrapolating to 16K and 32K. We attribute this to its second-order modeling: pooling and projection add up tokens independently, so the redundant context that fills most of a block drowns out the few informative tokens. The Gram matrix in TTR-Compressor fits correlated tokens jointly and reduces the influence of redundant evidence, so the resulting key keeps the distinctive content that queries need to find. The convolutional variant brings a further gain, reaching 12.24 points over the strongest baseline, as convolution makes the regression targets more informative and thus improves compression quality. On the benchmarks in Table
2

Concat & Projection has substantially more parameters than the other compressors, which may benefit pretraining. TTR-Compressor performs well and on par with full attention.

We attribute the strong performance of TTR-Compressor to its second-order modeling. The MLP merger concatenates the features in each group and maps them with fixed weights, so the mixing does not depend on how the features relate to each other. When most features in a group are redundant, such as background patches, they dominate the merged token and wash out fine-grained details. 6
Concluding Remarks
In this work, we revisit sequence compression, a pervasive yet often overlooked bottleneck in modern architectures, through the lens of test-time regression. Instead of relying on fixed pooling or learned projections, we formulate token compression as an instance-adaptive ridge regression problem, allowing the compressed representation to be solved directly from each input sequence.
By exploiting inter-token correlations through second-order interactions, TTR-Compressor offers a more expressive way to preserve sequence information while remaining lightweight and parameter-efficient. Its dual-form solution further makes this formulation scalable in practice.
Empirically, TTR-Compressor performs strongly across both block-wise sparse attention and multimodal token reduction, improving long-context retrieval while matching standard visual mergers with significantly fewer tokens.
More broadly, our results suggest that sequence compression need not be viewed as static aggregation, but as an input-dependent inference problem that adapts to the structure of each sequence. We expect this perspective establishes test-time regression as a simple, expressive, and scalable primitive for efficient foundation models.

E.1
Scaling Up Model Size and Training Budget
To further verify that the advantage of TTR-Compressor is not merely an artifact of the smaller-scale setting used in the main paper, we scale up both the model size and the training budget. Specifically, we train a 1B-parameter model on 100B tokens and evaluate it on the same RULER subtasks across context lengths ranging from 4K to 32K. For comparison, we also scale up Attention-Weighted Pooling—the strongest baseline among all compression methods evaluated in the main paper’s 345M-parameter experiments—to the same 1B-parameter, 100B-token setting.

article.headline: 用测试时回归重做序列压缩
article.lede: TTR-Compressor用闭式岭回归压缩token块，在稀疏注意力与视觉token合并上优于池化/MLP基线。
article.problem: 现有序列压缩多依赖均值池化、拼接后投影或注意力加权池化。这些方法按不依赖token间关系的权重聚合，主要利用一阶统计量，冗余token可能相互强化而独特信息被稀释。
article.method: 作者把压缩窗口内的token构造成自监督岭回归问题：key为归一化token，target由可学习投影生成，拟合系数即压缩表示。回归目标的外层参数通过任务损失端到端学习，内层用T×T对偶Cholesky闭式求解；正则项改为可学习对角矩阵，每个压缩器仅2d个可学习参数。
article.results: 在345M模型、8K训练的RULER上，TTR-Compressor平均0.5092，注意力加权池化为0.3920，带卷积版0.5144，论文称卷积版比最强基线高12.24分。视觉token合并2×2平均从MLP的54.93升至55.92（卷积版56.03）；3×3从52.27升至54.30（卷积版54.85），卷积版比MLP在OCRBench、InfoVQA、ChartQA分别高4.10、4.54、3.56，平均高2.58。摘要另称以55.6%更少视觉token匹配MLP。
article.why_it_matters: 它把压缩从固定聚合变成输入自适应的推理问题，且对偶解只解T×T系统、参数少，可作为池化/投影的即插即用替代。若在更大模型和更多任务上成立，可能影响长上下文稀疏注意力和多模态token缩减的设计。
article.limitations: 视觉2×2平均提升仅从54.93到55.92，语言主实验为345M参数，附录扩到1B/100B后平均0.7996对0.735，仍需更多架构验证。key归一化消融从0.5092降到0.2531，说明方法对实现细节敏感，且部分零样本评测未激活稀疏注意力。
article.figure_caption_zh: TTR-Compressor总览：内层把序列压缩写成测试时岭回归并用精确对偶Cholesky求解得到表示h*，回归参数由任务梯度端到端学习；通过Gram矩阵联合耦合token，冗余token的相对影响下降。

figure.caption: {Overview of TTR-Compressor.} (a) Bilevel learning: The inner solve formulates sequence compression as test-time ridge regression with an exact dual Cholesky solve to obtain the representation $ {h}^*$, while the regression parameters are learned end-to-end via task gradients. (b) Input-dependent second-order adaptation: By jointly coupling tokens through the Gram matrix, TTR naturally diminishes the relative influence of redundant tokens compared to additive pooling. For intuitive illustration, we set $ {D}= {I}$ and uniform targets $ {v}= {1}$; as typically learned in practice, a smaller regularizer $ {D}$ further amplifies this deduplication effect, yielding an even higher relative share for distinct tokens.

page_papers.title: Disentangling Dual Image References in Frequency Aware Diffusion Models for Personalized Generation
page_papers.abstract: Personalized image generation aims to synthesize text-driven images conditioned on reference images, while mainly casting the generation as image customization for foreground and style transfer for background. Previous arts of diffusion models suffers from the text misalignment with background for image customization and foreground for style transfer during the denoising process. Such facts, as we observed, rooted from the entanglement among hybrid frequency bands during the denoising process. To address such salient limitation, in this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle these Dual image references within Frequency-aware Diffusion Models, dubbed Dual-FDM, to simultaneously tackle two crucial personalized image generation tasks: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. For customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference. For color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference. Both the substituted frequency bands are used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image.Extensive experiments validate the superiority of Dual-FDM over the state-of-the-art diffusion models for personalized image generation. Our code can be accessed from https://github.com/htyjers/Dual-FDM.

Disentangling Dual Image References in Frequency Aware Diffusion Models for Personalized Generation
Haipeng Liu
Yang Wang
†
†
thanks:
Yang Wang is the corresponding author
Meng Wang
Affiliation:
School of Computer Science and Information Engineering

Hefei University of Technology, China
Email:
hpliu_hfut@hotmail.com
yangwang@hfut.edu.cn
eric.mengwang@gmail.com
Abstract
Personalized image generation aims to synthesize text-driven images conditioned on reference images, while mainly casting the generation as image customization for foreground and style transfer for background. Previous arts of diffusion models suffers from the text misalignment with background for image customization and foreground for style transfer during the denoising process. Such facts, as we observed, rooted from the entanglement among hybrid frequency bands during the denoising process. In particular, the low-frequency band primarily captures color information, mid-frequency band encodes global structure, while high-frequency band corresponds to local texture.
Besides, the early (high-noise) denoising stage mainly focuses on the low-and-mid frequency bands, while the late (low-noise) denoising stage progressively exhibits the high-frequency band, resulting in the dominance of low-and-mid over high frequency bands, especially when entangled within a single image reference, tends to reinforce each other at the early stage, hence the pitfall of overwhelming suppression of text prompt guidance. To address such salient limitation, in this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle these
Dual
image references within
F
requency-aware
D
iffusion
M
odels, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, to simultaneously tackle two crucial personalized image generation tasks: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. For customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference. For color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference. Both the substituted frequency bands are used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image.
We further compute the ratio of information entropy of the substituted frequency bands to adaptively modulate the denoising timesteps between the early and late stages. Extensive experiments validate the superiority of
Dual-FDM
over the state-of-the-art diffusion models for personalized image generation. Our code can be accessed from
https://github.com/htyjers/Dual-FDM
.

1
Introduction
Figure 2
:
(a) Comparison of the generated results, as well as the attention score map of text prompts and image references, between IP-Adapter
Ye et al. (2023)
and MS-Diffusion

for image customization. (b) Comparison of the generated results between InstantStyle

for style transfer. (c) Comparison of generated results guided by different frequency band of the image reference.
Personalized image generation focuses on synthesizing text-driven images conditioned on reference images, which enjoys remarkable progress, benefiting from the powerful denosing capabilities of Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs)
Ho et al. (2020)
;
Liu et al. (2024)
;
Liu et al. (2025a)
,
e.g.
, Stable Diffusion
Rombach et al. (2022)
;
Esser et al. (2024)
;
Podell et al. (2023)
;
Qian et al. (2022)
;
Qian et al. (2023)
;
Wang et al. (2024c)
. Typically, the personalized image generation involves two key subtasks,
i.e.
,
image customization
and
style transfer
. Given text prompts, image customization
Xiao et al. (2025)
;
Zeng et al. (2024)
;
Pang et al. (2024)
;
Gal et al. (2022)
;
Ruiz et al. (2023)
;
Kumari et al. (2023)
;
Liu et al. (2025b)
;
Ma et al. (2024)
;
Li et al. (2024)
;
Li et al. (2023)
;
Liu et al. (2022)
;
Cao et al. (2026)
;
Jiang et al. (2026)
aims to generate images by substituting the foreground semantics in the text prompts with the foreground extracted from the reference images, while preserving the background of the text prompts. In contrast, style transfer
Qin et al. (2025)
;
Rout et al. (2025)
;
Liu et al. (2023)
;
Sohn et al. (2023)
;
Zhu et al. (2025)
;
Qi et al. (2024)
;
Hertz et al. (2024)
;
Lei et al. (2025)
;
Gao et al. (2024)
;
Xing et al. (2024)
;
Wang et al. (2024b)
;
Wang et al. (2024a)
;
Jeong et al. (2024)
;
Wang et al. (2022)
focuses on disentangling style (
background
) from reference images and aligning the foreground with the text prompt. However, prior arts have struggled to align the generated image with the text prompts within each individual subtask.
Figure 3
:
Illustration of our proposed
Dual-FDM
pipeline (a); For customization style transfer (b), we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference, named
Dual-FDM
cust
(Sec.
2.3
). For the color style transfer (c), we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference, named
Dual-FDM
cost
(Sec.
2.4
). Each of the two personalized image generation tasks are conducted in the early and late stage of the whole denoising process guided by text prompts as illustrated in Eq. (
1
).
For image customization, substantial efforts
Ye et al. (2023)
;
Aiello et al. (2025)
;
Huang et al. (2025b)
aim to
emphasize dense image references of the foreground while overwhelming sparse text prompts of the background, especially for complex ones
,
e.g.
, a degraded “
flower wreath
” and the missing “
coffee
” in the IP-Adapter
Ye et al. (2023)
of Fig.
2
(a). Building on this, layout-based methods
Wang et al. (2025)
;
Huang et al. (2025b)
;
Zhang et al. (2024)
exploit spatial layouts to explicitly constrain reference concepts to the foreground, while assigning background regions to text prompts.
This preserves the foreground identity, but the explicit separation of foreground and background in the layout disrupts overall consistency, leading to the misalignment with (complex / long) text prompts.
As illustrated in the MS-Diffusion
Wang et al. (2025)
of Fig.
2
(a), the generated spatial arrangement of “
flower wreath
” and “
coffee
” diverges from the prompt and instead resembles
“A flower wreath around a dog near a coffee”
.
When coming to style transfer, during the early stage of the denoising process with high-level noise, the foreground is reconstructed from sparse text prompts,
the dense style information intended for the background often leaks into the foreground, resulting in misalignment with the text prompts
,
e.g.
, the incorrect number of “
woman
" in the InstantStyle
Wang et al. (2024a)
of Fig.
2
(b). To resolve such issue, StyleStudio
Lei et al. (2025)
applies style via instance normalization
Huang and Belongie (2017)
in the cross-attention layers and leverages layout to preserve foreground in the self-attention layers. Nevertheless, self-attention score maps highlight only the most salient regions, implying that the extracted layout can align only with simple text prompts (
i.e.
, “
a dog
") rather than the multi-objects (“
two pillows and one lemon
" in the StyleStudio
Lei et al. (2025)
of Fig.
2
(b)) text prompts, thereby
preventing it from handling the complex text prompts
.
So far, neither image customization nor style transfer achieves satisfactory alignment between the generated image and the text prompt for diffusion models. Such facts, as we observed, rooted from the entanglement among hybrid frequency bands. Intuitively, as shown in Fig.
2
(c), the low-frequency and mid-frequency bands capture color and global structure, while high-frequency band focuses on local texture, where different frequency bands are mainly denoised during
different
stages of the denoising process. As we observed, the early (high-noise) denoising stage mainly focuses on the low-and-mid frequency bands, while the late (low-noise) denoising stage progressively exhibits the high-frequency band (See Sec.
A
of the Appendix), the dominance of low-and-mid over high frequency bands, especially when entangled within a single image reference, suggesting reinforce each other at the early stages, resulting in an overwhelming suppression of text prompt guidance.
To resolve the text misalignment for personalization generation, we propose to solve the problem upon dual references and develop a paradigm to disentangle these
Dual
image references within
F
requency-aware
D
iffusion
M
odels, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, for two classical personalized image generation tasks in a row: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. Specifically:
•
We propose to map the foreground or background of image references into the frequency domain via Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT), where a mask is applied from left to right to progressively disentangle the low-, mid-, and high-frequency bands. Notably, for customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference, named
Dual-FDM
cust
(Fig.
1
(a)). The style reference with the mid-frequency band substituted is used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image in the decoupled cross-attention layer. For the color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference, named
Dual-FDM
cost
(Fig.
1
(b)). The style reference with the substituted low-frequency band is further utilized as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image in the decoupled cross-attention layer.
•
To pop up the foreground or background of the image reference, we utilize the key projection matrices in the decoupled cross-attention layer to represent the foreground, which are then reformulated through singular value decomposition (SVD) to derive the corresponding
background matrix
for the background.
•
For each task, we further compute the ratio of information entropy of the substituted frequency bands to adaptively modulate the denoising timesteps between the early and late stages, so as to achieve a well-balanced performance between text alignment and dual-image similarity.
Extensive experiments validate the superiority of Dual-FDM over the state-of-the-art diffusion models for personalized image generation.
2
Methodology
Central to our proposed Dual-FDM cover the following aspects: 1) how to pop up the background of the image references (Sec.
2.2
); 2) how to disentangle the mid-frequency band in customization style transfer (Sec.
2.3
); 3) how to disentangle the low-frequency band in color style transfer (Sec.
2.4
); 4) how to adaptively modulate the timesteps within the denoising process between early and late stages (Sec.
2.5
). Before shedding light on Dual-FDM, we elaborate the preliminary regarding decoupled cross-attention mechanism, which plays a pivotal role of personalized image generation.

Since CLIP is trained on real image–text (T) pairs, it is particularly sensitive to image style, which may distort text–image similarity. In addition, the generated background aligned with text prompts can interfere with the customized reference (C); hence we propose CLIP-TC, which incorporates text prompts to suppress such interference. We also provide CLIP-T (image–text similarity) and CLIP-CS (image–image reference similarity) for comparison.

To validate the superiority of

Ye et al. (2023)
,
Dreamcache
Aiello et al. (2025)
, and

Huang et al. (2025b)

Zhang et al. (2024)
,
MIP-Adapter
Huang et al. (2025b)
, and
MS-Diffusion
Wang et al. (2025)

, and

Xu et al. (2025)
.

4
Conclusion
In this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle dual image references within frequency-aware diffusion models, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, for two classical personalized image generation tasks in a row: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. Extensive experiments validate
the superiority of
Dual-FDM
over the state-of-the-art diffusion models.

High-frequency information.

,
Variance
, and
LBP Variance
, which are sensitive to edge sharpness, local contrast, and texture complexity. These metrics reflect the recovery of high-frequency details.

Appendix C
The algorithm of customization style transfer and color style transfer
Due to the page limitation, we summarize the process of customization style transfer in Algorithm
1
and color style transfer in Algorithm
2
.
To tackle the text-alignment issue in personalized image generation, in this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle these
Dual
image references within
F
requency-aware
D
iffusion
M
odels, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, for two classical personalized image generation tasks in a row: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. For customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference. For color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference. Both the substituted frequency bands are used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image.
For each task, we further compute the ratio of information entropy of the substituted frequency bands to adaptively modulate the denoising timesteps between the early and late stages.

Appendix D
More details about the implementation details
As mentioned in Sec.3.1 of the mainbody, due to page limitation, we further provide more details about the implementation details as follows:
Datasets.
We evaluate
Dual-FDM
on combined datasets covering image customization, style transfer, and text-to-image (T2I) generation:
•
Image Customization
: 1)
DreamBench
Ruiz et al. (2023)
+
TI benchmark
Gal et al. (2022)
: a well-known single-object personalized image generation dataset comprising 38 subjects, covering unique objects and pets such as backpacks, stuffed animals, dogs, cats, sunglasses, and cartoons, with each subject associated with 25 prompts; 2)
DreamBench++
Peng et al. (2025)
: the latest human-aligned personalized image generation benchmark, comprising 65 object classes, 20 human classes, and 45 animal classes. For each image, 9 text prompts are generated by GPT-4o to span a range of difficulty levels.
•
Style Transfer
: 1)
IS-Plus benchmark
Wang et al. (2024b)
: a style evaluation benchmark containing 104 images across diverse styles; 2)
StyleBench
Gao et al. (2024)
: a style evaluation benchmark covering 73 distinct styles, ranging from paintings, flat illustrations, and 3D rendering to sculptures with varying materials. For each style, 5–7 distinct images with variations are collected. In total, StyleBench contains 490 images across diverse styles.
•
T2I generation
:
T2I-CompBench++
Huang et al. (2025a)
: an enhanced benchmark for compositional text-to-image generation. T2I-CompBench++ comprises 8,000 compositional text prompts categorized into four primary groups: attribute binding, object relationships, generative numeracy, and complex compositions. These are further divided into eight sub-categories.
Based on the above, we construct several combined datasets for different joint tasks: 1) for customization style transfer (small-scale), we concatenate
DreamBench
and
TI benchmark
as the customization references, and use
IS-Plus benchmark
as the style references; 2) for customization style transfer (large-scale), we take
DreamBench++
as the customization references and
StyleBench
as the style references; 3) for color style transfer, we combine
InstantStyle-Plus
and
StyleBench
as the color and style references, while text prompts are provided by
T2I-CompBench++
for stylized image generation.
Metrics.
We consider 9 evaluation metrics from three aspects to evaluate our
Dual-FDM
:
•
Text and Image Reference Alignment
: we follow previous methods and adopt two representative models,
CLIP
2
2
2
Since CLIP is trained on real image–text (T) pairs, it is particularly sensitive to image style, which may distort text–image similarity. To alleviate this, we propose CLIP-TS by measuring similarity with style reference (S), thereby reducing the style influence . In addition, the generated background aligned with text prompts can interfere with the customized reference (C); hence we propose CLIP-TC, which incorporates text prompts to suppress such interference. We also provide CLIP-T (image–text similarity) and CLIP-CS (image–image reference similarity) for comparison.
and
DINO
Caron et al. (2021)
, for evaluation. Specifically,
CLIP-T
measures the similarity between generated images and the given text prompts;
CLIP-TC
and
CLIP-TS
evaluate the similarity between generated images and customized (or style) reference images while jointly considering the text prompts; finally,
CLIP-CS
assesses the similarity between generated images and dual-reference images.
•
Image Generation Quality
: we employ Image Reward (
IR
)
Xu et al. (2023)
to model human preferences for image quality and
HPS V2
Wu et al. (2023)
that combines perceptual studies with deep learning for comprehensive visual and semantic assessment. Both metrics measure the semantics consistency of the high-quality image generation aligned with human standards;
•
Time Complexity
: We employ the inference time (
Times
) and Video Random Access Memory (
VRAM
) consumption to evaluate the computational efficiency and memory footprint of different methods during image generation.
Model Configuration.
Our main experiments are conducted on the pre-trained IP-Adapter-Plus
Ye et al. (2023)
with SDXL
Podell et al. (2023)
model as the text-to-image diffusion model, configured with 30 sampling steps and and a fixed random seed of 42, to ensure high-quality outputs. We use the recommended hyper-parameters for each method across all images to ensure fair comparison. All experiments are implemented in PyTorch and conducted on a NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU.
