Appendix I
Limitations and Broader Impacts
Limitations.
As illustrated in Fig.
14
, for customization style transfer, when the style reference contains extremely sparse patterns (
e.g.
, line-based structures), the mid-frequency customized cues may
attenuate high-frequency style details, leading to incomplete style information
. We plan to address this issue in our future work.
Broader Impacts.
Our
Dual-FDM
can generate the personalized image according to the text prompt and reference images, our method may raise certain ethical concerns. The personalized image could potentially be misused in the creation of misleading information. We strongly advocate for the establishment of clear accountability in the use of such technologies, along with enhanced legal and technical oversight, to ensure they are applied responsibly.

The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.
•
The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.
•
The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.
•
The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.
•
If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.
•
While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.
3.
Theory assumptions and proofs
Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?
Answer:
[N/A]
Justification: We did not include theoretical results in our paper.
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that the paper does not include theoretical results.
•
All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.
•
All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.
•
The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.
•
Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.
•
Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.
4.
Experimental result reproducibility
Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?
Answer:
[Yes]
Justification: We have described the model details in the implementation details in Sec.
D
of the Appendix and carefully described the experimental metrics in the experimental chapter. The information we provide is sufficient and detailed for replication purposes.
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that the paper does not include experiments.
•
If the paper includes experiments, a
[No]
answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.
•
If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.
•
Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.
•
While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example
(a)
If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.
(b)
If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.
(c)
If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).
(d)
We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.
5.
Open access to data and code
Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material?
Answer:
[Yes]
Justification: We make a detailed description of the implementation details to ensure that they are repeatable and use publicly available personalized image generation datasets. We provide our code in the Appendix.
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that paper does not include experiments requiring code.
•
Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (
https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy
) for more details.
•
While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so
[No]
is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark).
•
The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (
https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy
) for more details.
•
The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc.
•
The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why.
•
At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable).
•
Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted.
6.
Experimental setting/details
Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results?
Answer:
[Yes]
Justification: We have carried out a detailed narration in the implementation details in Sec.
D
of the Appendix.
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that the paper does not include experiments.
•
The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them.
•
The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material.
7.
Experiment statistical significance
Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments?
Answer:
[N/A]
.
Justification: Based on our experimental experience, the reproducibility of the experiments involved in this work is high, with results that are replicable and stable, rather than simply reporting the highest outcomes. Additionally, previous related work
Ye et al. (2023)
;
Aiello et al. (2025)
;
Huang et al. (2025b)
;
Zhang et al. (2024)
;
Huang et al. (2025b)
has also not reported error bars. We thus do not run the statistical significance test.
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that the paper does not include experiments.
•
The authors should answer
[Yes]
if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper.
•
The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions).
•
The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.)
•
The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors).
•
It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean.
•
It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified.
•
For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates).
•
If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text.
8.
Experiments compute resources
Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments?
Answer:
[Yes]
Justification: We state this detailed information of computer resources in Sec.
3.1
of the Mainbody .
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that the paper does not include experiments.
•
The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage.
•
The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute.
•
The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper).
9.
Code of ethics
Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics
https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines
?
Answer:
[Yes]
Justification: We confirm that the research involved in the article complies with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics in all respects.
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.
•
If the authors answer
[No]
, they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics.
•
The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction).
10.
Broader impacts
Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed?
Answer:
[Yes]
Justification: The paper have conducted a discussion of broader impacts in the Appendix.
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.
•
If the authors answer
[N/A]
or
[No]
, they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.
•
Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.
•
The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.
•
The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.
•
If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).
11.
Safeguards
Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)?
Answer:
[N/A]
Justification: We utilize the publicly available personalized image generation dataset
Ruiz et al. (2023)
;
Wang et al. (2024b)
;
Gal et al. (2022)
;
Peng et al. (2025)
;
Gao et al. (2024)
;
Huang et al. (2025a)
and the pretrained generation models Stable Diffusion XL, there is no relevant description we will set up safeguards when we release the code of
Dual-FDM
.
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that the paper poses no such risks.
•
Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters.
•
Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.
•
We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort.
12.
Licenses for existing assets
Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected?
Answer:
[Yes]
Justification: We utilize the publicly available personalized image generation dataset
Ruiz et al. (2023)
;
Wang et al. (2024b)
;
Gal et al. (2022)
;
Peng et al. (2025)
;
Gao et al. (2024)
;
Huang et al. (2025a)
and the pretrained generation models Stable Diffusion XL, both of them state the dataset and model license.
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that the paper does not use existing assets.
•
The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset.
•
The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL.
•
The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset.
•
For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided.
•
If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets,
paperswithcode.com/datasets
has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset.
•
For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided.
•
If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators.
13.
New assets
Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets?
Answer:
[N/A]
Justification: We do not introduce new assets in the paper.
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that the paper does not release new assets.
•
Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc.
•
The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used.
•
At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file.
14.
Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects
Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)?
Answer:
[N/A]
Justification: The paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.
Guidelines:

The answer

Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper.

15.
Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects

•
Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper.

Declaration of LLM usage

article.headline: 用频域掩码解耦双重参考图的个性化生成
article.lede: Dual-FDM 在 DCT 频域用掩码分离低中高频，替换风格参考中的对应频段，兼顾定制化与色彩风格迁移。
article.problem: 个性化图像生成通常分为图像定制（保留参考图前景、背景交给文本）与风格迁移（保留风格、前景交给文本）两类子任务，但已有扩散模型在去噪过程中常出现文本错位：定制时背景被参考图压制，风格迁移时密集的风格信息泄漏到前景。作者认为根源在于混合频段的纠缠——低频主要携带颜色、中频编码全局结构、高频对应局部纹理，而高噪声的早期去噪阶段以低中频为主，低频与中频在单一参考图内相互强化，从而压制了文本提示的引导。
article.method: 方法先用解耦交叉注意力中的 key 投影矩阵表示参考图前景，并对其做奇异值分解，将奇异值取倒数重构出“背景矩阵”，以此在注意力层面提升背景、抑制前景。随后把参考图前景或背景经 DCT 变换到频域，用由坐标和阈值定义的掩码切出低/中/高频段：定制化风格迁移（Dual-FDM_cust）用定制参考前景的中频替换风格参考背景的中频；色彩风格迁移（Dual-FDM_cost）用色彩参考前景与背景的低频替换风格参考背景的低频。替换后的频段作为 key 和 value 重建去噪图像的 query，并通过替换频段的信息熵比值自适应划分早期与晚期去噪步数。
article.results: 在 DreamBench/TI benchmark 与 DreamBench++ 上，Dual-FDM_cust 的 CLIP-T 为 0.3194（MS-Diffusion 0.3123）、CLIP-TC 为 0.5031（IP-Adapter 0.4802）、Image Reward×10 为 5.3487、HPS×10 为 2.6007，均为表中最佳；作者称相对 [MS-Diffusion+CSGO] 在 CLIP-T 上领先最多 2.27%、CLIP-TC 上 7.5%、CLIP-CS 上 4.17%、HPS 上 2.24%。在 T2I-CompBench++ 的色彩风格迁移对比中，Dual-FDM_cost 在 Color、Shape、Texture 等类别取得最高 CLIP-TS/CLIP-S/DINO-S，例如 Color 类 CLIP-TS 0.5015、CLIP-S 0.7178、DINO-S 0.4970。效率方面，推理时间 10.26s、显存 12.48GB，低于 IP-Adapter 的 13.30s 与 16.92GB。
article.why_it_matters: 它把“文本对齐失败”从提示工程问题转为频段归属问题，给出了一套无需重训练、只在注意力 key/value 上做频域替换与步数调度的可插拔方案，对同时使用多张参考图（主体+风格+色彩）的生成流程有直接参考价值。
article.limitations: 作者在附录中承认，当风格参考包含极度稀疏的图案（如线稿结构）时，中频的定制线索会削弱高频风格细节，导致风格信息不完整；此外论文未报告误差棒或统计显著性检验，对比结论基于单次运行，且实验仅在 SDXL + IP-Adapter 这一底座上进行，跨底座泛化性尚不清楚。
article.figure_caption_zh: 图 1：(a) Dual-FDM_cust 以定制参考（左）与风格参考（上）生成的定制化风格迁移示例；(b) Dual-FDM_cost 以色彩参考（左）与风格参考（上）生成的色彩风格迁移示例。

page_papers.title: RoboFFT: Finetuning generative robot policy via online reinforcement learning with forward process
page_papers.abstract: Generative models, such as diffusion and flow-based models, have shown strong promise for robot policy learning by capturing complex and multimodal action distributions from demonstrations. However, policies trained solely with imitation learning often suffer from imperfect demonstrations and distributional shifts, while further improvement typically requires additional expert data. Reinforcement learning offers a natural solution through environment interaction, but effectively finetuning generative robot policies remains challenging due to the intractability of likelihood estimation. In this work, we propose RoboFFT, a forward-process reinforcement learning framework for finetuning generative robot policies, which applies forward noising to sampled actions and uses the weighted score / flow matching loss to construct a surrogate policy ratio for PPO-style updates. We evaluate RoboFFT with popular generative robot policies on representative simulation benchmarks, including long-horizon planning and sparse reward settings. Extensive experiments and analysis demonstrate that RoboFFT consistently improves performance while achieving better stability and training efficiency. We further integrate RoboFFT into a real world RL framework and demonstrate its effectiveness in real world tasks. Project website: https://student-of-holmes.github.io/RoboFFT/.
page_papers.content:
RoboFFT: Finetuning generative robot policy via online reinforcement learning with forward process
Yu Li
Shenghe Hu
Yuhan Wang
Yaoxiang Pu
Haotong Zhang
Yuanpei Chen
Yaodong Yang
Abstract
Generative models, such as diffusion and flow-based models, have shown strong promise for robot policy learning by capturing complex and multimodal action distributions from demonstrations. However, policies trained solely with imitation learning often suffer from imperfect demonstrations and distributional shifts, while further improvement typically requires additional expert data.
Reinforcement learning offers a natural solution through environment interaction, but effectively finetuning generative robot policies remains challenging due to the intractability of likelihood estimation.
In this work, we propose
RoboFFT
, a forward-process reinforcement learning framework for finetuning generative robot policies, which applies forward noising to sampled actions and uses the weighted score / flow matching loss to construct a surrogate policy ratio for PPO-style updates.
We evaluate
RoboFFT
with popular generative robot policies on representative simulation benchmarks, including long-horizon planning and sparse reward settings. Extensive experiments and analysis demonstrate that
RoboFFT
consistently improves performance while achieving better stability and training efficiency. We further integrate
RoboFFT
into a real world RL framework and demonstrate its effectiveness in real world tasks. Project website:
https://student-of-holmes.github.io/RoboFFT/
.
Figure 1:
We present
RoboFFT
, an online reinforcement learning framework for finetuning generative robot policy with forward process. (a) Reverse finetuning formulates the reverse denoising process as a multi-step MDP, while forward finetuning aligns with the same objective as training by following the forward noising process.
(b) One framework across popular generative robot policy on simulation benchmarks.
(c) Real-world deployment with integration of real world RL.
(d) Improved performance in success rate, training stability and efficiency.
†
†

1

2

<yuanpei.chen312@gmail.com, yaodong.yang@pku.edu.cn>

Keywords:
Diffusion RL, Generative Robot Policy, Robot Manipulation
1
Introduction
Generative robot policies, typically based on diffusion and flow-based models
[
43
,
42
,
15
,
29
]
, have become a powerful paradigm for learning visuomotor skills from demonstrations by modeling complex and multi-modal action distributions
[
12
,
56
,
53
]
, which significantly improves robot action accuracy and robustness and yields substantial performance gains in complex manipulation tasks
[
12
,
53
]
. However, policies trained purely by imitation learning remain constrained by the quality and coverage of the demonstration data. Imperfect demonstrations, covariate shift, and insufficient exposure to deployment-time states can all limit the final task performance of behavior-cloned policies
[
13
,
40
]
. Online reinforcement learning (RL) naturally presents itself as a promising paradigm to further improve generative robot policies, as it empowers the policy to directly maximize task rewards by continuously interacting with and learning from the environment.
Applying policy gradient RL methods to generative robot policies is nevertheless nontrivial. Unlike autoregressive policies, whose token likelihoods are tractable, diffusion and flow-based models typically lack a tractable exact likelihood formulation. This makes popular policy gradient objectives, such as PPO, difficult to be applied directly. Existing approaches address this issue by formulating the reverse denoising process as a multi-step MDP embedded in the high-level environment MDP, and optimizing through this two-level decision making trajectory
[
5
,
39
,
57
]
(Fig.
1
(a), left). Despite its promising results, reverse-process finetuning introduces substantial computation and memory overhead, and may suffer from gradient instability due to long denoising chains, especially in high-dimensional and long-horizon manipulation tasks.
To address these issues, we propose
RoboFFT
, a simpler yet more effective framework for online RL finetuning of generative robot manipulation policies through the
forward
noising process, inspired by recent studies from other application domains such as image generation and simple locomotion
[
52
,
59
,
34
]
. Instead of assigning credit through the reverse denoising chain,
RoboFFT
approximates the exact log-likelihood with a more computationally stable and efficient form akin to the score / flow matching loss for pretraining, yielding a principled PPO-style objective that is aligned with the imitation-learning objective while avoiding complicated likelihood computation or backpropagation through the full reverse trajectory. For flow-based policies, we further adopt SDE sampling by injecting noise into the sampling process, enabling controllable exploration during online data collection. In practice, Monte Carlo estimation, ratio-temperature calibration and further adaptations make likelihood estimation and updates robust across different policy architectures and tasks.
We evaluate
RoboFFT
on challenging robot manipulation benchmarks such as Robomimic
[
33
]
and LIBERO
[
30
]
, which pose difficulties like high-dimensional visual observation, long horizon planning and sparse reward for finetuning. Experimental results across different tasks demonstrate substantial and consistent performance improvements over pretrained diffusion and flow policies and achieve competitive or better performance compared with representative reverse and forward process finetuning baselines, while reducing optimization overhead. We further verify the applicability of our method on more complicated VLA and real world deployment settings, and study the key designs through ablations and visualizations. Our contributions are summarized as follows:
(1) We introduce
RoboFFT
, an online reinforcement learning framework that performs policy gradient finetuning in the forward noising process for generative robot policies.
(2) We carry out practical implementation of
RoboFFT
for representative generative robot policies (flow, diffusion and VLA) on challenging long-horizon, sparse-reward manipulation tasks, showing that
RoboFFT
achieves superior performance and improved training stability and efficiency.
(3) We integrate
RoboFFT
into the real world reinforcement learning framework for practical deployment and demonstrate its effectiveness over real world tasks.
(4) We carry out a systematic ablation analysis of key design choices and conduct investigative experiments to provide empirical insights for the mechanism of
RoboFFT
.
2
Related Work
2.1
Policy Gradient for Robot Manipulation
Policy gradient and actor critic methods provide a standard framework for learning continuous-control policies from interaction data
[
50
,
45
,
28
,
41
]
. Due to the
training stability with high-dimensional action spaces, they have been widely applied to a range of robotic control problems, including dexterous manipulation, legged locomotion, and agile navigation
[
48
,
9
,
10
,
1
,
17
,
21
]
. For long-horizon manipulation, however, training from scratch remains highly exploration-intensive and is often impractical. A more practical paradigm is therefore to finetune policies initialized from demonstration data. Prior studies have shown that reinforcement learning can further improve such demonstration-initialized policies beyond behavior cloning while substantially reducing the exploration burden
[
38
,
46
,
37
]
. RoboFFT follows this finetuning paradigm, while focusing on diffusion- and flow-based robot policies whose action distributions are implicitly induced by generative sampling processes, making the likelihood ratio computation required by policy gradient methods nontrivial.
2.2
RL for Generative Models
Reinforcement learning has recently been widely applied to generative model finetuning in offline
[
3
,
35
,
16
,
49
,
14
,
36
,
7
]
, offline-to-online
[
11
,
26
]
, and online settings
[
39
,
57
,
54
,
34
,
52
,
59
]
. Online finetuning for diffusion and flow models can be broadly categorized into reverse-process and forward-process approaches. Reverse-process methods formulate the denoising or sampling trajectory as a multi-step decision process, enabling tractable per-step likelihood for policy optimization
[
5
,
39
,
57
]
. While effective, optimizing through long internal sampling chains can increase computation and memory costs and may introduce training instability. Forward-process methods instead optimize policy via constructing surrogate likelihood objectives or contrastive learning, better aligning RL finetuning with generative pretraining
[
52
,
34
,
54
,
59
]
. DiffusionNFT and AWM
[
59
,
52
]
study this idea for text-to-image generation. FPO and FPO++
[
34
,
54
]
extend it to robotic control, but mainly focus on locomotion tasks. In comparison, RoboFFT studies forward-process finetuning in more challenging robotic manipulation, and covers more extensive settings including both diffusion and flow policies, VLA finetuning, and real world deployment with practical stabilization designs.

Evaluation on Real World
To evaluate the effectiveness of

We then perform multiple offline RL iterations. In each offline iteration, we perform offline PPO-style optimization on the collected rollout data, where IQL

After each offline RL update, we deploy the updated policy on the real robot to collect additional trajectories, which are added to the offline dataset for the next offline RL iteration. To stabilize policy improvement and avoid drifting away from reliable human behaviors, we combine the newly collected rollout data with the original teleoperation demonstrations and conduct imitation learning to update the base policy for the next iteration.

6
Limitations
Although
RoboFFT
enables stable online finetuning of generative robot policies through the forward noising process, it still has several limitations. First, the weighted score/flow matching loss is only a surrogate for the true action log-likelihood, and its scale may vary across noise schedules, action dimensions, and policy architectures. Therefore, additional calibration such as temperature scaling is still needed to ensure stable PPO-style updates. Second, our current framework relies on on-policy PPO, which has limited data efficiency and cannot fully reuse historical trajectories. This makes real-world deployment challenging, especially when data collection is restricted to a single robot. Although offline-to-online paradigms such as RL100
[
26
]
can partially alleviate this issue, they usually require iterative data collection and offline retraining, which remains time-consuming in practice. Future work may explore more sample-efficient variants that better leverage historical trajectories and human intervention data for safer and faster real world robot learning.
7
Conclusion
We present
RoboFFT
, a forward-process reinforcement learning framework for finetuning generative robot policies. By applying forward noising to sampled actions and using the weighted score/flow matching loss to construct a surrogate policy ratio,
RoboFFT
enables PPO-style policy optimization without requiring explicit likelihood estimation. Experiments on representative simulation benchmarks show that
RoboFFT
consistently improves popular generative robot policies on long-horizon and sparse-reward manipulation tasks, while achieving better training stability and efficiency. Further integration into a real world RL framework also demonstrates its effectiveness on real robot tasks.

Robomimic Benchmark
We use Robomimic

as the simulated manipulation benchmark throughout our main experiments. Robomimic provides sparse-reward robot manipulation tasks collected from human demonstrations, making it a suitable testbed for evaluating whether online finetuning can improve a behavior-cloned generative policy beyond its initial demonstration-trained performance. The four tasks cover different manipulation difficulties. Lift requires the robot to grasp and lift an object, while Can is a pick-and-place task where the robot must manipulate a can into the target container. Square is a more precision-sensitive assembly task in which the robot must manipulate a square nut and place it onto a positioning peg. Transport is a long-horizon bimanual manipulation task that requires coordinated control of two robot arms to move an object across the workspace. Thus, the benchmark spans both short-horizon single-arm manipulation and longer-horizon bimanual manipulation.
We consider both state-input and pixel-input variants. In the state-input setting, the policy observes low-dimensional proprioceptive and object state features. In the pixel-input setting, the policy observes RGB image(s) at

B.4
Baseline Methods and Configurations
We compare RoboFFT with representative online RL fine-tuning baselines for diffusion- and flow-based robot policies.
DPPO.
Diffusion Policy Policy Optimization
[
39
]
is a representative reverse-process fine-tuning method for diffusion policies. It formulates the reverse denoising process together with the environment interaction process as a two-level MDP, and applies PPO to optimize the Gaussian likelihoods of denoising transitions. We use DPPO as the canonical diffusion-policy RL baseline for long-horizon manipulation tasks.
ReinFlow.
ReinFlow
[
57
]
extends the reverse-process policy-gradient paradigm to flow-based policies. It injects stochasticity into the deterministic flow trajectory, turns the sampler into a discrete-time Markov process with tractable Gaussian transition probabilities, and performs PPO-style optimization over the internal sampling trajectory. We use ReinFlow as the primary flow-policy baseline.
FPO.
Flow Policy Optimization
[
34
]
is a forward-process policy-gradient method that constructs a PPO-style surrogate ratio from conditional flow matching losses. We adapt FPO into our online fine-tuning codebase for Robomimic. To ensure fair comparison under the same tasks and pretrained policies, most environment and optimizer settings are shared with RoboFFT. The main algorithmic differences are that FPO does not use our SDE explorative sampling strategy and ratio-temperature calibration adopted in RoboFFT, while following the original FPO convention of using

DRWR is a lightweight diffusion reward-weighted regression baseline following the implementation convention in DPPO

For all baselines, we match the Robomimic environment wrappers, observation preprocessing, action chunking, base-policy training data, and evaluation protocol whenever applicable. The hyperparameters of DPPO, ReinFlow, and DRWR follow their original implementations unless a task-specific adaptation is necessary. Since the released ReinFlow manipulation implementation focuses on pixel-input Robomimic tasks, for state-input tasks we adapt secondary settings such as optimizer and update-batch configurations while keeping the core ReinFlow design unchanged. For fair comparison, the number of inference steps and finetuning steps are tuned on each task, so that each baseline achieves its nearly best performance. Appendix C
Additional Analyses for the Robomimic Experiments
C.1
Performance Analysis
This subsection provides additional discussion for the main Robomimic comparison in Sec.
5.1
, where the comprehensive performance of RoboFFT-F, RoboFFT-D and the baseline methods are evaluated under both state-input and pixel-input settings.
Across the easier
Lift
and
Can
tasks, RoboFFT-D and RoboFFT-F reach final success rates comparable to reverse-process baselines such as DPPO and ReinFlow. Their convergence can be slightly slower in some early-stage curves, but the final policy quality remains competitive. This suggests that the forward-process surrogate ratio preserves enough policy-gradient signal for improving already competent pretrained policies, while avoiding explicit likelihood computation through the reverse denoising chain.
The advantage of RoboFFT becomes more pronounced on the harder tasks. On
Square
and
Transport
, especially with pixel observations, RoboFFT shows a more sustained improvement trend and stronger final performance. Reverse-process methods can suffer from instability or later performance recession, likely because optimizing through a long internal sampling chain introduces a more complicated credit-assignment path and a heavier computation graph, making the gradients and parameter updates instable. In comparison, RoboFFT directly applies forward noising to the final rollout action and optimizes a matching-loss-based surrogate ratio, which keeps the optimization path closer to imitation pretraining.
The forward-process baselines, DRWR and FPO, are generally less competitive in the Robomimic manipulation setting. DRWR uses reward-weighted regression and does not include a PPO-style trust region, making it more sensitive to high-variance reward weights in sparse-reward tasks. FPO uses a forward-process PPO-style ratio, but in our implementation it lacks the manipulation-oriented stabilization designs used in RoboFFT, including controlled SDE exploration and ratio-temperature calibration. These differences help explain why simply applying a forward matching loss is not sufficient for robust online fine-tuning on long-horizon manipulation tasks.

E.7
Interpretation of the t-SNE Visualization
The t-SNE visualization in Fig.
15
provides a complementary view of how RoboFFT reshapes the action distribution beyond a single rollout trajectory. Compared with the pretrained policy, whose sampled action chunks are more diffusely distributed and contain many low- or negative-advantage samples, the finetuned policy forms a more concentrated region with noticeably higher diagnostic advantages. In particular, after fine-tuning, a dense cluster of positive-advantage actions emerges in the embedding space, indicating that RoboFFT increases the probability mass around actions that are preferred by the diagnostic critic
Q
viz
Q_{\mathrm{viz}}
.
This observation is consistent with the rollout-timeline analysis in Fig.
7
. The timeline visualization shows that, at key decision stages such as grasping, transporting, and aligning the object, the finetuned policy improves the average action quality while reducing sample diversity. The t-SNE visualization further shows that this effect is not restricted to one selected trajectory: across a broader set of anchor states collected from successful and failed rollouts, the finetuned policy tends to move sampled action chunks toward higher-advantage regions. Together, these results suggest that RoboFFT improves the pretrained generative policy by concentrating its action distribution around more task-relevant and higher-quality action modes, rather than merely increasing random exploration. Note that the density of a t-SNE embedding is an intuitive signal of action mode concentration instead of a direct estimate of
policy likelihood or the number of behavioral modes. The observed concentration therefore does not by itself establish
either mode collapse or preservation of all useful modes.

Appendix H
Extended Related Work
H.1
Generative Models for Robot Manipulation
Generative models have become an increasingly important policy class for robot manipulation, as they provide expressive distributions over complex and potentially multimodal action sequences. Early approaches
[
58
,
27
]
formulate imitation learning with a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE). More recently, diffusion-based policies have demonstrated substantially greater expressiveness for continuous control. Diffusion Policy
[
12
,
19
]
models the conditional action distribution through an iterative denoising process, enabling stable learning of high-dimensional and multimodal action distributions and motivating a broad family of diffusion-based manipulation policies. Flow-matching models provide an alternative generative formulation by learning continuous transport from a simple noise distribution to the action distribution. Methods such as ManiFlow
[
53
]
further improve sampling efficiency and policy expressiveness through consistency-based flow training, demonstrating strong performance on diverse manipulation tasks. In parallel, vision-language-action (VLA) models have extended robot policies toward large-scale generalist control by leveraging pretrained vision-language representations and heterogeneous robot datasets. RT-2
[
6
]
and OpenVLA
[
22
]
generate discretized robot actions within large autoregressive vision-language models, while
π
0
\pi_{0}
[
4
]
and
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
[
18
]
combine a pretrained vision-language backbone with a flow-matching action expert for continuous action generation.
H.2
RL for Generative Robot Policy
Reinforcement learning has been increasingly explored to improve generative policies beyond behavior cloning. Early studies mainly focus on offline RL with fixed datasets. Diffusion Q Learning
[
49
]
parameterizes the actor as a diffusion model and combines diffusion regression with Q value maximization, while IDQL
[
14
]
uses an implicit Q-function to select actions sampled from a diffusion behavior policy. This idea has also been extended to flow-based policies. Flow Q Learning (FQL)
[
36
]
learns a flow matching behavior policy together with a one-step RL policy, avoiding recursive differentiation through iterative flow generation. Although these methods exploit the expressiveness of generative policies, their improvement is constrained by the coverage of the offline dataset and the accuracy of learned value functions.
More recent work considers online or offline-to-online adaptation of pretrained generative robot policies. One direction keeps the base policy frozen and learns a lightweight steering or residual component. DSRL
[
47
]
performs RL in the latent-noise space of a pretrained diffusion or flow policy without modifying its parameters, while residual RL methods learn corrective actions on top of a frozen behavior cloning policy
[
2
,
44
,
20
]
. These approaches preserve pretrained behaviors and reduce the complexity of online optimization, but restrict policy improvement to the residual or latent space exposed by the frozen policy.
In contrast, full policy finetuning directly updates the generative model parameters. DPPO
[
39
]
formulates diffusion denoising as a multi-step MDP and applies PPO over reverse denoising transitions. ReinFlow
[
57
]
extends likelihood-based online optimization to flow policies by injecting stochasticity into deterministic flow trajectories. Forward process methods such as FPO
[
34
]
and its extensions
[
54
]
instead construct policy-gradient objectives from flow matching losses, avoiding explicit marginal likelihood computation. Reinforced finetuning has also been extended to VLA policies, with
[
11
,
51
]
combining offline value learning and online policy optimization for real-world manipulation. RoboFFT belongs to the full policy finetuning family, but performs PPO-style optimization through the forward noising process, providing a unified framework for diffusion, flow, and VLA policies.

article.headline: 用前向加噪做PPO：生成式机器人策略在线微调
article.lede: 研究团队提出 RoboFFT，用前向加噪的匹配损失充当替代似然比，让扩散与流策略可直接做 PPO 在线微调。
article.problem: 扩散与流匹配策略擅长从示教中拟合多模态动作分布，但纯模仿学习受限于示教质量、协变量偏移和对部署状态的覆盖不足。想用强化学习继续提升时，这类策略的动作分布由迭代采样隐式给出，似然比无法直接计算，PPO 一类目标难以套用。现有的逆向过程方法把去噪链当作多步 MDP 来优化，计算与显存开销大，长链还容易带来梯度不稳定。
article.method: RoboFFT 改为在采完动作之后对动作施加前向加噪，复用预训练时的加权 score / flow matching 损失作为替代负对数似然，用 exp(L_old − L_θ) 构造替代策略比，再套上带裁剪的 PPO 目标。对确定性采样的流策略，作者向采样过程注入固定强度 η 的噪声，改成 Euler–Maruyama SDE 采样器以提供可控探索。实现上用蒙特卡洛多次估计匹配损失（新旧策略复用同一组噪声样本），并引入比例温度 α_ratio 校准替代比的数量级。
article.results: 在 Robomimic 的 Lift、Can、Square、Transport 四个稀疏奖励任务（状态与像素输入）上，RoboFFT 与逆向过程基线表现相当或更好，在 Square、Transport 上更稳定。训练耗时方面，RoboFFT-F 相对 ReinFlow 平均加速 1.53×，RoboFFT-D 在四个状态输入任务上相对 DPPO 平均加速 38.0×（即便如此仍使用 N_mc=16）。在 3.3B 参数的 VLA 模型 π0 上，LIBERO-Object 与 LIBERO-Spatial 两套任务均较预训练策略有提升，与 π_RL 基线相当。真机四个任务各 20 次试验，成功率分别为：Pick Eggplant 12/20→离线 18/20→在线 20/20，Peg Insertion 10/20→19/20→20/20，Pour 9/20→15/20→18/20，Cabinet Retrieval 5/20→14/20→17/20；Pick Eggplant 上 BC 聚合仅 14/20、DRWR 12/20。
article.why_it_matters: 它把生成式策略的 RL 微调拉回到与预训练同一条损失上，避开了对完整去噪链的反向传播，使扩散、流和 VLA 策略能用同一套 PPO 式流程做在线提升。对长程、稀疏奖励的机器人操作来说，这是把「示教初始化 + RL 后训练」做成低成本常规流程的一步。
article.limitations: 匹配损失只是真实动作对数似然的替代品，其数值尺度会随噪声调度、动作维度和策略结构变化，因此仍需比例温度等额外校准；作者自己的诊断显示，替代比与 ReinFlow 式参考比的 Spearman 秩相关仅约 0.2（虽然后期 90% 以上样本的相对误差降到 5% 以下），排序一致性有限。此外方法依赖 on-policy PPO，数据效率不高、无法充分复用历史轨迹，真机部署需借助离线到在线流程反复采数据与重训，实际耗时较长。
article.figure_caption_zh: RoboFFT 流程概览：先用遥操作数据以 score / flow matching 损失预训练基座策略，在线阶段用 SDE 采样器生成动作并从环境获得奖励，最后对动作前向加噪、复用匹配损失作为替代似然完成 PPO 式策略更新。

figure.caption: Overview of {RoboFFT}. We first collect the offline data leveraging teleoperation and pretrain the base policy with the score / flow matching loss. The pretrained policy then generates actions using an SDE sampler and receives reward feedback from the environment. Finally, we apply forward noising and reuse the matching loss as a surrogate likelihood for PPO-style policy update.

page_papers.title: DONIC: Generalist Dexterous Bimanual Tracking Control from Human Demonstrations
page_papers.abstract: Despite recent progress in dexterous reference tracking, existing models focus primarily on single-hand manipulation and a limited range of interactions, leaving the bimanual dexterous behaviors common in real life unaddressed. The scarcity of contact-rich bimanual manipulation data and the increased complexity of coordinating contacts make developing a generalist bimanual tracker particularly challenging. Therefore, we present 1) DONIC, the first generalist bimanual tracker jointly trained across operation categories and human-motion sources, together with 2) BiHOI, a multi-view dataset of 1,575 sequences spanning 229 objects and emphasizing sustained bimanual interaction, where reconstructed interactions are retargeted into robot references. DONIC combines proximal policy optimization with behavioral cloning in a feedback loop that recycles verified successful executions into training demonstrations. An object-centered per-hand reward maintains object-motion feedback while supervising each hand according to its reference contact role. Clip-Centered Advantages remove reference-dependent advantage offsets while preserving within-trajectory differences. Together, these designs enable one single policy to learn coordinated manipulation across heterogeneous references. Without finetuning, a single checkpoint achieves 86.79% success on unseen trajectories of training objects and 57.32% on held-out objects, surpassing the state-of-the-art bimanual tracking baselines by 77.36 and 45.73 percentage points.

1
Introduction
Dexterous manipulation supports household assistance, industrial assembly, and assistive care. Unlike gripper-based manipulation, it requires precise coordination of finger motions and changing hand–object contacts to grasp, reorient, and reposition objects
[
28
,
2
,
8

33
]
. Generalizing across objects and behaviors is challenging, especially when human demonstrations must be retargeted to robot hands with different kinematics
[
26
,
19
,
38

. Simulation-ready objects
[
4
,
5

6

[

40

[
19
,

1

, yet remain largely limited to single-hand tasks. Many everyday tasks instead require asymmetric bimanual coordination: one hand stabilizes an object while the other opens, rotates, or repositions it
[
9

. This motivates a generalist bimanual reference tracker that learns from diverse human motion to control different objects and tasks with one policy.
Developing such a tracker poses two challenges. First, public datasets include bimanual manipulation
[
9
,

,
10

, but fully tracked hand–object sequences with sustained two-hand contact remain scarce, limiting the available coordination patterns. Second, a shared policy must learn trajectories with changing hand roles and contact timing. Hand-pose accuracy alone does not ensure successful object manipulation, while requiring both hands to satisfy contact conditions can mask one hand’s progress. Unequal clip difficulty also creates advantage offsets that can weaken updates for useful actions in harder sequences. Shared training therefore needs feedback grounded in object motion and each hand’s reference contacts, alongside advantages that preserve differences among transitions within each clip.
We address these challenges with

, a generalist bimanual reference tracker, and BiHOI, a multi-view hand–object interaction dataset. BiHOI contains

32

We reconstruct both hands and the object, then retarget hand motion to robot references paired with the object trajectory. Combined with public references, BiHOI broadens the training objects and coordination patterns.
DONIC
learns one policy for both hands through proximal policy optimization (PPO)
[
31

and behavioral cloning (BC) on verified demonstrations. Trajectory-specific policies optimize screened references, while successful shared-policy executions are verified and reused. At inference, one checkpoint tracks new references without further training. Our
object-centered per-hand reward

77.36

45.73

•

•

From human references to executable manipulation.

[
15

[

29
]

Joint refinement against multi-view metric depth combines geometric alignment with reconstruction and temporal regularization, producing bimanual MANO parameters, a metric object mesh, and its 6-DoF trajectory in a common world frame.

.
Retargeting.
We map the reconstructed human motion to the Wuji robot hands through frame-wise kinematic fitting, following standard retargeting practice
[
11
,
27
,
19
]
.
After wrist-frame alignment, we fit hand keypoints to robot links under joint limits, initializing and regularizing each frame against the preceding solution. Smoothing occurs only before retargeting. The resulting wrist and finger references are paired with the object trajectory.

, a generalist bimanual tracker, and BiHOI, a multi-view bimanual interaction dataset. Object-centered per-hand rewards and CCA support iterative PPO+BC training, yielding one checkpoint that generalizes to unseen trajectories and objects without fine-tuning and substantially outperforms adapted baselines. Ablations support both learning signals and the benefit of additional BiHOI data.
However, our quantitative evaluation focuses on simulated single-object interactions and relies on reconstructed, retargeted motion references.
We aim to extend
DONIC
to longer-horizon and multi-object manipulation, evaluate on an independent benchmark, and investigate transfer to physical bimanual systems.

Appendix A
Additional Related Work
Executable human references and shared control.
Human demonstrations provide motion targets but do not directly specify robot actions: differences in hand kinematics and simulated contact can make a kinematically plausible reference physically difficult to execute. Reference-based trackers address this gap through closed-loop control. DexTrack
[
19
]
combines trajectory-specific demonstration generation with generalist learning; Dexplore
[
38
]
expands exploration around reference motions; and AdaDexTrack
[
1
]
combines specialist distillation with reference modulation. Our reference-conditioned action interface and iterative reinforcement–imitation learning loop build on this line of work. Our contributions within that loop are the object-centered per-hand reward and Clip-Centered Advantages (CCA), designed for shared bimanual tracking across heterogeneous references.
What generalization means here.
Generalization across grasped objects, manipulation skills, and complete reference trajectories imposes different requirements. UniDexGrasp++
[
33
]
studies generalizable dexterous grasping, while BiDexHD
[
43
]
learns trajectory-conditioned bimanual policies within operation categories. Our controller is jointly trained across operation categories and human-motion sources. We evaluate new trajectories of training objects and trajectories involving held-out objects with the same checkpoint. These two splits test reference and object generalization; they do not, by themselves, establish generalization to held-out operation categories or arbitrary manipulation goals.
Interaction capture and usable control data.
GRAB, GigaHands, OakInk2, TACO, and H2O provide complementary sources of hand–object interaction
[
32
,
10
,
41
,
20
,
13
]
. HOI4D and HO-Cap further broaden capture settings and annotation tools
[
21
,
34
]
. Our comparison distinguishes the inventory of a source dataset from the subset retained for robot training. A clip enters our bimanual pool only if the required hand and object tracks are available and both hands contact the object at some point. This allows sequential as well as simultaneous hand participation. BiHOI complements these sources with a higher measured proportion of simultaneous bimanual contact in the analyzed recordings.

Single-object representation.
For multi-object recordings, conversion retains one primary object: TACO keeps the tool rather than the target, and OakInk2 selects the main object from its hand-role program annotations. The controller represents the selected object by a fixed mesh and a rigid pose. Articulation and deformation are not modeled explicitly, even when the captured object belongs to those categories.
B.2
Multi-View Reconstruction and Annotation
The reconstruction pipeline uses learned image predictions to initialize geometry, then calibrated multi-view observations to recover physical scale and temporal consistency. Its five stages are mask/depth extraction, object reconstruction and tracking, participant-specific hand calibration, hand-motion reconstruction, and joint refinement. Figure
S1
summarizes the complete calibrated multi-view reconstruction and annotation pipeline.
Figure S1:
Reconstruction and annotation pipeline.
Synchronized multi-view RGB observations are processed to obtain SAM3 object masks and metric depth maps. The object branch performs metric reconstruction followed by robust multi-view 6D tracking, while the hand branch performs participant-specific hand calibration and multi-view hand-pose reconstruction. The two branches are finally refined jointly using depth-guided hand–object optimization.
Masks and metric depth.
We use SAM3
[
7
]
in two stages. The first frames from all cameras form an ordered cross-camera sequence: a single object prompt initializes consistent masks across views. Each camera video is then tracked temporally using its first-frame mask. At each synchronized time, Depth Anything 3
[
18
]
processes the views with calibrated intrinsics and world-to-camera extrinsics. Extrinsic-scale alignment anchors depth to metric camera translations. The resulting depth supports object-scale recovery and subsequent pose refinement.

article.headline: DONIC：一套策略完成双手灵巧跟踪
article.lede: DONIC 用单个 checkpoint 在未见轨迹上取得 86.79% 成功率，并发布 1,575 段双手交互数据集
article.problem: 现有灵巧参考跟踪模型大多只处理单手操作和有限的交互类型，日常生活中常见的不对称双手协调，即一只手固定物体、另一只手开合或旋转，仍未被覆盖。接触丰富的双手操作数据稀缺，而且两只手的角色分工与接触时机各不相同，使通用双手跟踪器更难训练。
article.method: DONIC 把 PPO 与行为克隆放进迭代闭环：轨迹专属策略产出可执行示范，通用策略验证成功的执行被回收进示范库。物体中心的逐手奖励在持续反馈物体位置、朝向与速度的同时，按参考指定的接触角色分别监督左右手，并允许两手异步接触。Clip-Centered Advantages 在 GAE 之后按参考 clip 减去均值优势，去掉 clip 相关的偏移，同时保留 clip 内的相对差异。
article.results: 不微调时，单个 checkpoint 在 unseen-traj（53 条未见轨迹）上成功率为 86.79%、Comp 为 67.62%，在 unseen-obj（164 段留出物体）上为 57.32% 和 54.69%，比最强基线 Dexplore-bi 分别高 77.36 和 45.73 个百分点。腕部平移误差从 21.88 cm 降到 3.96 cm（unseen-traj）、从 19.46 cm 降到 4.58 cm（unseen-obj）。消融显示，去掉 CCA 后成功率降至 81.13% 和 48.17%，去掉接触门控后降至 81.13% 和 48.78%；加入全部 1,575 段 BiHOI 后，训练池从 1,845 增至 3,420 段，成功率升至 88.68% 和 59.76%。
article.why_it_matters: 双手协调是家务、装配与辅助护理中的常态，而通用灵巧跟踪此前基本停留在单手；DONIC 说明一个策略可以跨操作类别与多个人类动作数据源联合训练，并在新参考上直接部署。它同时给出一个强调持续双手接触的多视角数据源，可缓解该领域的数据短缺。
article.limitations: 定量评估全部在模拟中进行，只覆盖单刚体物体交互，参考来自重建并重定向的人体动作，作者也承认尚未检验留出操作类别与无约束目标条件操作。接触监督依赖净力与表面距离的代理判据，重建流程没有显式接触或碰撞损失，也还没有真实双手机器人上的验证。
article.figure_caption_zh: BiHOI 的多视角记录经重建与重定向后，与公开数据参考一起组成训练池；共享双手策略在 PPO+BC 迭代闭环中学习，物体中心逐手奖励、Clip-Centered Advantages 与行为克隆提供互补的学习信号。

page_papers.title: Not Just a Subject: Capturing Adaptive Scene-Specific Variance for Visual Storytelling
page_papers.abstract: Recent advancements in diffusion models have significantly improved text-to-image generation, enabling their application to visual storytelling, where coherent image sequences are generated from narrative prompts. However, existing methods primarily focus on identity preservation and often fail to adapt to diverse scene variations, resulting in semantic misalignment and structural inflexibility. We propose EOS-Story, a training-free framework that harmonizes identity consistency with scene-specific adaptation across text and vision spaces. In the text space, we decouple the narrative into identity and scene sub-prompts to prevent information dilution, but this leaves the scene without access to appearance cues. To bridge this gap, we introduce Cross-Contextual Bridging, which softly injects a phrase-level appearance residual into the scene's <EOS> embedding. In the vision space, we find that scale mismatch between identity and scene subjects causes a few identity tokens to be repeatedly transferred, producing structural artifacts. We address this with Adaptive Identity Preservation, which anchors identity features at the scene-specific scale (Identity Anchoring) and integrates them via Identity-Aware Self-Attention. To evaluate performance under varied spatial compositions, we extend the Consistory+ benchmark with diverse framing scenarios (Consistory+_+). Extensive experiments show that EOS-Story achieves competitive or superior performance on both benchmarks.

Abstract
Recent advancements in diffusion models have significantly improved text-to-image generation, enabling their application to visual storytelling, where coherent image sequences are generated from narrative prompts. However, existing methods primarily focus on identity preservation and often fail to adapt to diverse scene variations, resulting in semantic misalignment and structural inflexibility. We propose EOS-Story, a training-free framework that harmonizes identity consistency with scene-specific adaptation across text and vision spaces.
In the text space, we decouple the narrative into identity and scene sub-prompts to prevent information dilution, but this leaves the scene without access to appearance cues.
To bridge this gap, we introduce Cross-Contextual Bridging, which softly injects a phrase-level appearance residual into the scene’s
⟨
\langle
EOS
⟩
\rangle
embedding. In the vision space, we find that scale mismatch between identity and scene subjects causes a few identity tokens to be repeatedly transferred, producing structural artifacts. We address this with Adaptive Identity Preservation, which anchors identity features at the scene-specific scale (Identity Anchoring) and integrates them via Identity-Aware Self-Attention. To evaluate performance under varied spatial compositions, we extend the Consistory+ benchmark with diverse framing scenarios (Consistory+_+). Extensive experiments show that EOS-Story achieves competitive or superior performance on both benchmarks.
Keywords:
Storytelling Text-to-Image Generation
1
Introduction
Diffusion models
[
26
,
23
]
have recently advanced the quality of text-to-image generation, enabling diverse applications in visual content creation.
Among these, the visual storytelling task, applicable to digital comics and character-driven animation
[
22
]
, is particularly challenging because it requires aligning with evolving narrative semantics while maintaining a coherent subject across scenes
[
30
]
.
Figure 1
:
Limitations in scene-level adaptation of previous methods.
Existing approaches often fail to account for
scene-specific variance
: (a)
semantic misalignment
in simple cases, (b)
loss of fine-grained prompt details
in complex scenarios, and (c) inability to adapt to
diverse viewpoints and scales
. These issues often lead to repetitive subject structures and weakened alignment with scene-specific prompts. In contrast, our method achieves better scene-level fidelity by adaptively harmonizing identity consistency with the unique context of each scene.
Recent approaches
[
40
,
17
,
30
]
explicitly design mechanisms to preserve subject identity by transferring subject-relevant features into each scene during generation.
While these methods effectively maintain identity consistency,
they often underrepresent
scene-specific variance
in both text and vision spaces—the diverse semantic and visual elements that vary across narrative contexts (
Fig.
1
).
First, at the semantic level, current methods
[
17
,
40
,
30
]
often treat narrative prompts as monolithic inputs, where various semantics (e.g., appearance and scene descriptions) are encoded into a unified embedding.
This can lead to
information dilution
, making it difficult for the model to uniformly attend to all details
[
14
]
.
As a result, even when a prompt contains rich details (e.g., specific actions or environmental changes), the model often fails to selectively extract scene-specific cues from the prompt.
This directly undermines narrative fidelity, producing scenes that ignore their intended semantics (
Fig.
1
a,b).
Second, at the visual level, existing approaches typically rely on spatially blind feature injection, where identity features are transferred without accounting for the spatial constraints or framing of each scene.
This oversight of structural scene variance (e.g., camera angles or subject scales) can lead to
subject inflexibility
, such as contextually mismatched poses or repetitive structural patterns across scenes (
Fig.
1
b,c).
Consequently, subjects are rendered with rigid structural patterns that ignore each scene’s intended layout, further weakening alignment with scene-specific prompts.
Therefore, achieving coherent storytelling requires scene-specific adaptation, where identity consistency is harmonized with the semantic and structural variance of each scene.
To address this issue, we propose
EOS-Story
, a framework designed to adaptively account for scene-specific variance via two complementary modules,
(1) Cross-Contextual Bridging:
We hypothesize that semantic misalignment arises when long and complex prompts are encoded holistically, causing scene-varying attributes to be diluted
[
16
,
14
]
.
Rather than encoding all information in a single prompt, we decouple the narrative into an identity prompt describing the subject and a scene prompt describing the scenario.
For instance, “a woman with blond hair reading a book.” is split into an identity prompt (“a woman with blond hair.”) and a scene prompt (“a woman reading a book.”).
However, this separation introduces a new challenge: since the scene prompt contains no appearance information, the subject generated within the scene has no way to reflect the actual target identity.
To bridge this semantic gap without reverting to monolithic encoding, we preserve the scene sub-prompt as a semantic anchor and softly inject appearance information at the embedding level.
Motivated by the strong generative influence and summarization ability of
⟨
\langle
EOS
⟩
\rangle
embeddings
[
20
,
37
]
,
we interpret it not merely as a terminal token, but as a
residual-based semantic control
point for scene-aware storytelling (
Sec.
3.1
).
Unlike prior EOS-based methods that substitute the
⟨
\langle
EOS
⟩
\rangle
embedding between prompts differing by a single word (e.g., an object class)
[
9
,

Notably, improvements from CCB are primarily reflected in text-related metrics, whereas Adaptive Identity Preservation contributes more prominently to identity-related scores such as CLIP-I.

Without size aligning, scale discrepancies between identity and scene representations often lead to misaligned identity transfer, resulting in distorted subject proportions.
In contrast, size-aware alignment ensures that identity features are referenced at an appropriate spatial scale, promoting more coherent subject integration.
5
Conclusion
In this work, we propose
EOS-Story
, a training-free framework that adaptively models scene-specific variance in visual storytelling across text and vision spaces. We introduce
Cross-Contextual Bridging
, which decouples the narrative into identity and scene sub-prompts and bridges the resulting semantic gap by injecting phrase-level appearance residuals into the scene’s
⟨
\langle
EOS
⟩
\rangle
embedding. To complement this with structural adaptation, we further propose
Adaptive Identity Preservation
, which anchors subject features at the scene-specific scale and refines integration through Identity-Aware Self-Attention. To evaluate scene adaptability, we extend Consistory+ with diverse framing variations (Consistory+_+).
Extensive experiments show that EOS-Story achieves competitive or superior performance in both prompt fidelity and structural adaptability.

Appendix 0.B
Consistory+_+ & Framing Evaluation Details
The ShotBench
[
15
]
includes a wide range of framing phrases across eight categories (
Tab.
7
).
To ensure a focused and rigorous evaluation of scene-specific structural variance, we intentionally restricted the scope to three primary categories, excluding the remaining five based on the following methodological criteria: (1) Prompt Redundancy: Shot Framing descriptors (e.g., “single”, “2 shot”) primarily specify the number of characters, which is already inherently defined by the subject phrases in the storyboard prompts; (2) Redundancy Mitigation: Lens Size phrases (e.g., “wide lens”) are largely redundant as they are semantically encompassed by the Shot Size category (“wide shot”); (3) Domain Incompatibility: Camera Movement is inherently applicable to temporal video sequences and is thus irrelevant to static image generation; and (4) Task Relevance: Lighting-related categories fall outside the scope of our work, as they primarily focus on stylistic or artistic variations rather than the structural and compositional elements that define scene-specific variance.
Framing Phrase Filtering.
Although SDXL generally produces textually well-aligned images, it sometimes struggles to accurately reflect specific framing phrases.
Before incorporating these phrases into our benchmark extension, we first evaluate how well they are captured by the base SDXL model using the ShotBench evaluation mechanism.
To quantitatively assess phrase reflection, we construct approximately 90 diverse scene prompts and append each framing phrase at the end (e.g., “A photo of a woman baking cookies, close-up shot”).
We generate images for 10 random seeds per phrase and compute the top-1 and top-3 accuracy, along with standard deviations, as shown in
Fig.
16
.
For example, in the “shot size” category with 7 phrase options, this results in a total of 6,300 images (90 scenes × 7 phrases × 10 seeds).
We filter out framing phrases whose top-1 accuracy is zero (e.g., “extreme wide shot”), as these are not reliably reflected in the generated outputs from SDXL.
Consistory+_+
With the remaining framing phrases, we extend the original Consistory+ benchmark using GPT-4o.
Since these phrases are visually meaningful primarily for animate subjects, we first guide GPT-4o to determine whether the subject in each prompt is animate.
Then, the model is instructed to append the most appropriate framing phrase for the given scene, resulting in Consistory+_+.
Framing Accuracy Evaluation.
Following the evaluation protocol in
[
15
]
, we provide the generated image along with the corresponding framing category (e.g., shot size) and prompt the model with a multiple-choice question.
For instance, for shot size evaluation, we prompt the model with a multiple-choice question such as
“What is the shot size of this shot?” and provide predefined options (e.g., wide shot, medium shot, close-up shot).
The predicted category is compared against the framing phrase specified in the text prompt, and accuracy is reported.

Layer Application Variation.
We apply Identity Anchoring (IA) and Identity-Aware Self-Attention (IASA) at different layers of the unet decoder in the diffusion model.
While prior works typically transfer identity-related features within the decoder (up-block) layers, we further investigate the impact of layer selection.
As shown in
Fig.
21
, we vary the application layers and plot the resulting CLIP-T and CLIP-I scores.
Interestingly, when IA and IASA are applied to configurations that include the up-block layers, the CLIP-I score notably improves (surpassing 0.880).
These results empirically highlight the importance of the decoder layers (up-blocks) in effectively conveying identity features and enhancing the image quality during generation.

SD3 Applicability.
We use the Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large weights with a CFG scale of 4.5 and 28 sampling steps.
In SDXL, identity information is incorporated via extended attention, where the subject key and value embeddings are concatenated with those of the scene. However, in DiT-based models, fixed positional encodings and sequence-length constraints make such direct concatenation non-trivial
[
3
,
18
]
.
To address this architectural difference, we compute attention along two parallel paths: (i) the original scene query–key–value path and (ii) a subject-referenced path using the scene query with subject key and value embeddings. The resulting attention outputs are then combined, enabling implicit identity referencing without modifying the positional encoding structure.
Despite the architectural adaptation, the core semantic control mechanism remains intact. As shown in
Fig.
25
and
Sec.
0.C.2
, our method consistently improves alignment, demonstrating its applicability to DiT-based diffusion models.

FLUX Applicability.
Although SD3 also adopts MM-DiT blocks, we further extend our method to FLUX, as many recent models are built upon it. Since FLUX relies solely on a T5 encoder—unlike the CLIP encoder used in the SD series—the ⟨EOS⟩ token acts merely as an end-of-sentence marker with negligible influence on generation. We therefore apply only the AIP module to FLUX, which is model-agnostic by design.

article.headline: 免训练故事生成：把外观残差注入场景的EOS嵌入
article.lede: 汉阳大学提出 EOS-Story，在文本与视觉两个空间同时处理「保身份」与「随场景变」，并扩展 Consistory+
article.problem: 现有的视觉故事生成方法大多只盯着主体身份保持，把整段叙事当作一个整体提示编码，长提示中场景相关的外观与动作细节容易被稀释，生成结果与场景语义对不齐。在视觉一侧，身份特征被空间无关地直接注入，当身份主体与场景主体的尺度不匹配时，只有少数身份 token 被反复搬运，导致跨场景出现重复的结构伪影、姿态僵硬、无法适应不同视角与景别。
article.method: 作者提出免训练的 EOS-Story，包含两个互补模块。Cross-Contextual Bridging 把叙事拆成「风格+主体」「风格+主体+外观」「风格+主体+场景」三个子提示，用身份提示与风格锚点之间的 ⟨EOS⟩ 嵌入差作为外观残差，加到场景提示的 ⟨EOS⟩ 上，从而在不加长场景描述的前提下补回外观线索。Adaptive Identity Preservation 则先用 Identity Anchoring 把身份特征缩放到每个场景中主体的实际尺度并做置信度过滤的匹配融合，再由 Identity-Aware Self-Attention 让场景 token 有选择地关注身份特征；在 U-Net 解码器上，第 9 步之前用锚定、之后切到注意力细化。
article.results: 在 Consistory+ 上，EOS-Story 的 CLIP-T 为 0.9042，高于 SDXL 基线的 0.8971、StoryDiffusion 的 0.8985 和 1P1S 的 0.8871；DreamSim 0.2005、Aesthetic 6.1764、ImageReward 1.1680 均为表中最好，但 CLIP-I 0.8850 低于 IP-Adapter 的 0.9398。在作者扩展的 Consistory+_+ 上，CLIP-T 0.8998、DreamSim 0.2146、Aesthetic 6.1791、ImageReward 1.3217，同样在 CLIP-T 与 ImageReward 上领先。20 名被试、40 个故事板的用户研究中，52.8% 的情形选择本方法；生成 5 个故事占用 47777 MB 显存、耗时 118.570 秒，显存略高于对比方法而延迟相当。
article.why_it_matters: 它提示了一个容易被忽略的点：故事生成中的「不协调」不只来自视觉特征注入，也来自文本编码阶段的信息稀释，而在 ⟨EOS⟩ 上做短语级残差注入是一个廉价、免训练、可插拔的控制点。同时它把「景别/机位多样性」纳入评测，暴露出仅靠身份相似度指标会掩盖结构僵化的问题。
article.limitations: 方法依赖 CLIP 的 ⟨EOS⟩ 上下文汇总特性，作者自己承认无法直接迁移到 T5 或 LLM 文本编码器的模型上（FLUX 上只能退化为仅用 AIP 模块）；此外主体掩码来自交叉注意力图，偶尔会圈错区域导致错位生成，遇到「faun」这类罕见概念时基座 SDXL 本身就会失败。评测方面，Consistory+_+ 的景别短语是先按 SDXL 能否生成来筛选的，且只对人物、动物等有生命主体添加取景标签，用户研究规模也仅 20 人。
article.figure_caption_zh: EOS-Story 的整体流程：文本一侧用 Cross-Contextual Bridging 将短语级外观残差注入场景提示的 ⟨EOS⟩ 嵌入，视觉一侧用 Identity Anchoring 做尺度对齐、再用 Identity-Aware Self-Attention 细化身份特征融合。

page_papers.title: Drift, Then Spread: Learning One-Step Generative Policies for Online Reinforcement Learning
page_papers.abstract: Generative policies offer expressive action distributions for online reinforcement learning (RL), but many diffusion- and flow-based policies require costly iterative sampling. We propose DriftSpread, a one-step generative policy based on Drifting for online maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL. To incorporate entropy without a tractable policy density, we build on an energy-based view of Drifting and derive critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from the negative MaxEnt objective. Our method learns these updates sequentially in the same actor, using action regression for value improvement and distribution matching to capture the effect of entropy. The actor updates require neither direct samples from the critic-defined Boltzmann target nor policy-density or score estimation. Under exact fitting with a fixed critic, we prove convergence to the Boltzmann target in the small-step limit followed by the long-time limit. On MuJoCo, DriftSpread achieves the highest aggregate normalized return among all evaluated methods, while outperforming the diffusion- and flow-based baselines in both training and inference efficiency.

Drift, Then Spread: Learning One-Step Generative Policies for Online Reinforcement Learning
Chunyu Luo
Hongyu Zhao
Guangyi Ni
Yue Song
Lingkai Kong
The University of Hong Kong  Beihang University
Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen  Independent Researcher  Tsinghua University
Correspondence to:
lingkaikong@hku.hk
.
Abstract
Generative policies offer expressive action distributions
for online reinforcement learning (RL), but many diffusion-
and flow-based policies require costly iterative sampling.
We propose
DriftSpread
, a one-step generative policy based on
Drifting for online maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL.
To incorporate entropy without a tractable policy density,
we build on an energy-based view of Drifting and derive
critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from the
negative MaxEnt objective.
Our method learns these updates sequentially in the same
actor, using action regression for value improvement and
distribution matching to capture the effect of entropy.
The actor updates require neither direct samples from
the critic-defined Boltzmann target nor policy-density
or score estimation.
Under exact fitting with a fixed critic, we prove
convergence to the Boltzmann target in the small-step
limit followed by the long-time limit.
On MuJoCo,
DriftSpread
achieves the highest aggregate
normalized return among all evaluated methods,
while outperforming the diffusion- and flow-based
baselines in both training and inference efficiency.
