Generative policies offer expressive action distributions
for online reinforcement learning (RL).
Diffusion- and flow-based policies can capture multimodal
distributions that are difficult to represent with a single
Gaussian
(
Dong et al., 2025
;
Celik et al., 2025
)
.
However, many of these approaches generate actions through
iterative sampling, requiring repeated network evaluations
during training and inference.
Recent MeanFlow-based methods reduce this cost through
few-step or one-step action generation
(
Dong et al., 2026
;
Chen et al., 2025
;
Kim et al., 2026
)
.
Drifting offers a different way to train one-step
generators
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
.
At each training iteration, it uses target data to
move generated samples toward the desired distribution,
then trains the generator to reproduce the moved
samples from the same inputs.
Through these repeated updates, the generator learns
to produce samples from the target distribution in
a single forward pass at inference.
This approach has shown better performance than
MeanFlow variants in one-step image generation on
ImageNet
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
.
These results motivate exploring Drifting for online
RL, where its use remains less studied.
We consider the maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL objective,
which balances expected return with policy entropy
to encourage exploration
(
Haarnoja et al., 2018
)
.
The critic defines a Boltzmann target distribution
for policy improvement, but does not directly provide
samples from it
(
Li et al., 2026
)
.
We therefore adopt an energy-based view of Drifting
(
Gretton et al., 2026
;
Han et al., 2026
)
,
using the negative MaxEnt policy-improvement objective
as the energy.
This energy guides updates to actions generated by
the current policy.
For the value term, critic gradients tell us how to
move actions toward higher values.
The entropy term is harder to use: an implicit actor
generates actions but does not provide a tractable
density for computing their distribution’s entropy.
We therefore need training targets that capture
the effect of entropy without explicitly computing it.
We propose
DriftSpread
, a one-step generative policy in the
Drifting model family for online MaxEnt RL.
Our key idea is to derive two updates from this energy
and fit them sequentially to the same actor through
repeated Drift–Spread cycles.
In each cycle, Drift uses critic gradients to move
generated actions toward higher values.
The actor then learns to reproduce these updated
actions from the same inputs through regression.
Spread captures the entropy contribution through
diffusion of the action distribution.
We approximate this diffusion by adding appropriately
scaled independent noise to actions from the updated
actor, then train the actor to match the resulting
distribution.
This allows the actor to learn the effect of entropy
without explicitly computing it.
For a fixed critic, we prove
that the learned policy converges to the Boltzmann
target distribution in the small-step, long-time limit.
Our main contributions are:
(1) We introduce
DriftSpread
, a Drifting model for online
MaxEnt RL with expressive policies and one-step action
generation.
(2) We develop sequential Drift–Spread training through
critic-guided regression and entropy regularization to
address the challenge of entropy computation for implicit
policies.
(3) On MuJoCo,
DriftSpread
outperforms 13 baselines
in aggregate normalized return, with lower training
costs than the diffusion, flow, and MeanFlow baselines
(Figure
1
).
2
Related Work
Generative policies for online RL.
Diffusion and flow models provide expressive action
distributions for online RL.
One line of work optimizes policies by backpropagating
critic gradients through diffusion or flow sampling
(
Wang et al., 2024
;
Lyu et al., 2025
)
.
DIME also differentiates through diffusion sampling
while optimizing a variational lower bound on the
MaxEnt objective
(
Celik et al., 2025
)
.
Another line of work constructs training targets
for learning critic-defined Boltzmann distributions.
DQS uses weighted averages of critic gradients
to construct score targets
(
Jain et al., 2025
)
.
SDAC and MaxEntDP instead use critic values to weight
denoising supervision and noise estimates, respectively
(
Ma et al., 2025
;
Dong et al., 2025
)
.
Reverse flow matching unifies these gradient-expectation
and noise-expectation formulations through posterior-mean
estimation
(
Li et al., 2026
)
.
These approaches use iterative action sampling,
motivating few-step and one-step policies for online RL.
MeanFlow was introduced for one-step generative modeling
and learns average velocities
(
Geng et al., 2025
)
.
Recent online RL methods use this formulation
to learn policies with fewer generation steps.
FPMD trains rectified-flow and MeanFlow policies
through policy mirror descent, with both variants
supporting one-step inference
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
.
MFPO trains few-step MeanFlow policies using velocity
estimates for critic-defined Boltzmann targets
(
Dong et al., 2026
)
, while SOM constructs velocity
targets from critic-based score estimates to train
one-step MeanFlow policies
(
Kim et al., 2026
)
.
Drifting models and policy learning.
Drifting learns one-step generators by repeatedly
moving generated samples and training the generator
to reproduce their updated positions.
This approach has achieved state-of-the-art performance
in one-step image generation on ImageNet
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
.
Subsequent work relates specific Drifting fields
to Wasserstein gradient flows
(
Gretton et al., 2026
)
and uses
optimal-transport couplings to construct sample
updates
(
He et al., 2026
)
.
W-Flow derives sample movements from an objective
over distributions and trains a one-step generator
on the resulting samples
(
Han et al., 2026
)
.
Drifting has also been applied to policy learning.
For offline RL, DriftQL combines critic-guided
policy improvement with a Drifting regularizer
based on the behavior distribution
(
Houssaini et al., 2026
)
.
For offline-to-online RL, Drifting Field Policy
derives a KL-regularized policy update through
Wasserstein gradient flow and constructs training
targets from actions ranked by the critic
(
Koo et al., 2026
)
.
Our work focuses on online MaxEnt RL from scratch.

Conclusion and Limitations
We introduced
DriftSpread
, a Drifting-based approach to
learning expressive one-step policies for online RL.
Building on an energy-based view of Drifting, we derive
critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from
the MaxEnt objective.
The two updates are learned sequentially by the same
actor: Drift moves actions toward higher values,
while Spread matches a broader distribution constructed
from the updated actor.
This design incorporates the effect of entropy without
estimating policy densities or scores, while allowing
each action sample to be generated in one forward pass.
Under exact fitting, our analysis establishes convergence
to the fixed-critic Boltzmann target in the small-step,
long-time limit.
MuJoCo experiments show that
DriftSpread
combines strong
control performance with efficient training and inference,
supporting Drifting as a practical approach to
generative policy learning.
Our work leaves two directions for future research.
First, our evaluation is limited to simulation
environments.
Testing on real-world control tasks would help
assess robustness to observation noise and changes
in system dynamics.
Second, we use a fixed spreading-noise distribution
and scale during training.
Adapting the spreading strength as learning progresses
may better balance exploration and value improvement.

article.headline: 先漂移后扩散：在线强化学习的单步生成策略
article.lede: 从最大熵目标拆出 critic 引导的漂移与熵诱导的扩散，顺序训练同一 actor，推理只需一次前向。
article.problem: 扩散与流策略能表达多峰动作分布，但需要迭代采样，训练和推理开销都高。最大熵目标里的熵项对隐式策略没有可计算的密度，而 critic 定义的 Boltzmann 目标又不直接提供样本。
article.method: 作者把负最大熵目标当作能量，由 Wasserstein 梯度流导出速度场，并分解为 critic 引导的漂移项和熵诱导的扩散项。actor 先用 critic 梯度构造目标做动作回归，再用特征函数下的 MMD 分布匹配学习加噪后的扩散分布。两步在同一 actor 上顺序执行，推理时单次前向即出动作。
article.results: 在五个 MuJoCo 任务上，DriftSpread 在 13 个对比方法中取得最高聚合归一化回报，推理时间为 0.15 ms/action，对比 DIME 的 1.24 ms 和两步 MeanFlow 方法 MFPO 的 0.36 ms；HalfCheetah-v3 与 Walker2d-v3 上后期平均回报最高。二维高斯玩具例中顺序拟合最终 KL 为 0.000422，而调过权重的联合拟合为 0.512165。
article.why_it_matters: 它说明 Drifting 这类一步生成器可以接入在线最大熵 RL，在不估计策略密度或分数的前提下保留熵带来的探索。推理成本接近普通高斯策略，为生成式策略的实际部署降低了门槛。
article.limitations: 收敛到 Boltzmann 目标的证明依赖精确拟合与固定 critic，且只在小步长后接长时间的双重极限下成立。实验全部在 MuJoCo 仿真中进行，扩散噪声的分布与尺度在训练中固定、不随学习进程调整，真机鲁棒性尚未验证。
article.figure_caption_zh: DriftSpread 总览：(a) critic 学习与顺序的 Drift–Spread actor 更新交替进行，Drift 用动作回归、Spread 用分布匹配；(b) 负最大熵目标示意，Drift 把动作推向更高 critic 值，Spread 随后加宽分布以体现熵的作用。

The maps $f_ $ represent the same actor at different training stages, each generating an action sample from reference noise in one forward pass. (b) The surface schematically represents the negative MaxEnt objective over policy distributions. The samples below illustrate how Drift moves actions toward higher critic values and Spread then broadens the post-Drift distribution to capture the effect of entropy.

page_papers.title: CineMem: Attention-Aligned Fine-grained Memory Retrieval for Multi-Shot Long Video Generation
page_papers.abstract: Autoregressive video generation relies on memory retrieval to model long-range dependencies. This capability becomes particularly critical for multi-shot generation, where models must reconcile substantial visual changes across shot transitions with persistent semantic continuity. Existing methods tend to perform memory retrieval at the frame level and share the same historical context across all query tokens, overlooking the heterogeneous information needs and leading to redundant retrieval and inefficient use of historical memory. To bridge this gap, we introduce CineMem, an attention-aligned fine-grained memory retrieval framework that combines online memory organization with query-adaptive retrieval for autoregressive multi-shot video generation. Specifically, guided by intrinsic memory-access patterns revealed through attention analysis, we propose an online-clustered KV cache as a memory organization strategy over all historical tokens, enabling semantic-aware memory grouping and more precise retrieval. In addition, we introduce a query-level retrieval mechanism that provides broader access to historical information under a fixed retrieval budget, thereby improving long-term memory utilization. Together, these designs enable the multi-shot video generator to preserve long-range consistency across shot transitions, particularly in revisitation scenarios, while approximating full-memory access under a constrained memory budget. To facilitate evaluation, we further introduce a suite of task-specific, VLM-assisted metrics for faithful inter-shot consistency assessment. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.

CineMem: Attention-Aligned Fine-grained Memory Retrieval for Multi-Shot Long Video Generation
Xiaoxue Wu

Abstract
Autoregressive video generation relies on memory retrieval to model long-range dependencies. This capability becomes particularly critical for multi-shot generation, where models must reconcile substantial visual changes across shot transitions with persistent semantic continuity.
Existing methods tend to perform memory retrieval at the frame level and share the same historical context across all query tokens, overlooking the heterogeneous information needs and leading to redundant retrieval and inefficient use of historical memory.
To bridge this gap, we introduce CineMem, an attention-aligned fine-grained memory retrieval framework that combines online memory organization with query-adaptive retrieval for autoregressive multi-shot video generation.
Specifically, guided by intrinsic memory-access patterns revealed through attention analysis, we propose an online-clustered KV cache as a memory organization strategy over all historical tokens, enabling semantic-aware memory grouping and more precise retrieval.
In addition, we introduce a query-level retrieval mechanism that provides broader access to historical information under a fixed retrieval budget, thereby improving long-term memory utilization. Together, these designs enable the multi-shot video generator to preserve long-range consistency across shot transitions, particularly in revisitation scenarios, while approximating full-memory access under a constrained memory budget.
To facilitate evaluation, we further introduce a suite of task-specific, VLM-assisted metrics for faithful inter-shot consistency assessment. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.
Figure 1:
15-second multi-shot videos autoregressively generated by
CineMem
. By combining clustered memory with fine-grained query-adaptive retrieval, CineMem maintains coherent semantic flow across shot transitions, particularly in revisitation scenarios. Project page:
https://uknowsth.github.io/CineMem/
†
†
footnotetext:
*
Work done during an internship at Shanghai AI Laboratory.
†
Corresponding authors.
1
Introduction
Building on bidirectional architectures and extensive pre-training, recent diffusion models
(
Blattmann et al., 2023
;
Ho et al., 2020
;
Rombach et al., 2022
;
Song et al., 2020
)
deliver impressive visual quality, but at substantial computational cost for long-duration generation.
Autoregressive generation offers a natural alternative for streaming video synthesis, typically combining a sliding-window mechanism with memory routing to maintain long-range consistency and stable generation
(
Huang et al., 2026
;
Yin et al., 2025
)
. This capability is particularly important for multi-shot video generation
(
Guo et al., 2025b
;
Luo et al., 2026
)
, which aims to synthesize coherent, film-like narratives through frequent shot transitions accompanied by substantial viewpoint changes. Maintaining a continuous and coherent narrative flow across discrete shot boundaries naturally calls for a well-designed memory retrieval strategy, especially
when previously observed subjects, scenes, or viewpoints reappear after intervening shots.
Existing memory mechanisms for causal video generation remain generally coarse-grained. Basic sliding-window strategies are widely adopted in single-shot causal models
(
Huang et al., 2026
;
Yang et al., 2025
)
, inevitably discarding distant information as autoregressive rollout proceeds. In multi-shot scenarios, some methods preserve temporally predefined anchors as persistent memory
(
Chen et al., 2026b
)
, such as the first frames of individual shots.
These designs follow fixed routing patterns determined by temporal structures rather than the model’s intrinsic memory-access patterns, limiting their ability to fully exploit historical information.
More recent studies introduce retrieval-based memory strategies
(
Meng et al., 2026a
;
Luo et al., 2026
)
, which typically augment fixed sinks and adjacent context with frame-level routing.
The resulting routing decision is shared across all query tokens.
Although such designs allow content-aware access to historical cues, they still rely on coarse temporal grouping and overlook heterogeneous memory requirements across queries.
Consequently, long-horizon autoregressive generation remains constrained by frame-level historical conditioning, leaving much of the available memory underutilized.
In this work, we explore how an autoregressive multi-shot video model can retrieve long-term historical information under a constrained memory budget by leveraging its intrinsic memory-access patterns.
Rather than merely preserving adjacent-frame information for pixel-level continuity, memory in multi-shot scenarios should support the recovery of previously observed visual content after multiple shot transitions, a setting we refer to as revisitation.
To this end, we propose CineMem, an attention-aligned fine-grained memory retrieval framework that combines online memory organization with query-adaptive retrieval for autoregressive multi-shot video generation.
By adapting memory organization and retrieval granularity to attention-based selection patterns, CineMem enables more effective access to long-term history and improves long-range consistency across shot transitions, particularly in revisitation scenarios, as illustrated in Figure
1
.
To investigate the intrinsic memory-access patterns of autoregressive diffusion models,
we first develop a training framework that converts a bidirectional video model into a long-duration autoregressive multi-shot generator operating in a chunk-by-chunk manner, while allowing each current chunk to attend to the full generation history.
To stabilize long-horizon rollout, we further incorporate an error accumulation mitigation strategy during adaptation.
We then analyze the attention distributions between query tokens in the current chunk and all historical memory tokens. We observe a clear clustering structure among historical memory tokens and substantial variation in retrieval preferences across query tokens and attention heads.
These observations motivate our designs for online memory organization and query-adaptive retrieval.
Specifically, our framework comprises two complementary designs, as illustrated in Figure
2
. First, we apply online clustering to the KV cache to organize historical memory throughout autoregressive rollout. As generation proceeds, historical tokens are grouped according to their semantic similarity, with each cluster serving as a retrieval unit.
In contrast to conventional frame-level schemes that partition tokens by fixed frame membership regardless of content, our design forms content-aware groups, which alleviates the redundancy introduced by retrieving entire frames, while avoiding the high computational cost of treating every historical token as an individual memory unit.
Second, we introduce query-adaptive memory access in a query-wise and head-wise manner. Given their heterogeneous retrieval preferences, each query-head pair selects its most relevant clusters from memory.
Under a fixed per-query memory budget, this individualized retrieval provides broader access to the generation history, yielding a larger effective attention receptive field without increasing the retrieval cost.
Together, these designs better match intrinsic memory-access patterns while balancing
retrieval granularity, historical coverage, and computational efficiency, enabling CineMem to maintain long-range consistency across frequent shot transitions.
For evaluation, we adopt a comprehensive protocol covering video-level quality, intra-shot consistency, and inter-shot consistency. Since conventional similarity-based metrics can assign deceptively high inter-shot consistency scores to videos that fail to perform the intended shot transition, we further introduce a VLM-assisted evaluation protocol that jointly considers transition execution and semantic preservation. This provides a more faithful assessment of inter-shot consistency in multi-shot generation. Experimental results show that CineMem achieves superior consistency compared with existing autoregressive baselines while remaining competitive with large-scale bidirectional models.
Moreover, our attention-aligned retrieval designs are effective in a plug-in setting without additional fine-tuning, demonstrating their ability to better exploit historical information during autoregressive rollout.
Overall, our work highlights the importance of fine-grained memory organization and retrieval for coherent long-horizon autoregressive multi-shot video generation.
Figure 2:
Overview of CineMem.
Existing autoregressive video generation methods tend to perform memory retrieval at the frame level, which may result in redundant retrieval, inefficient memory utilization, and overlooked heterogeneous information needs across query tokens. CineMem combines an online-clustered KV cache with query-adaptive retrieval to enable a finer-grained memory retrieval strategy. As illustrated by the attention receptive fields, CineMem provides broader (2/3 vs. 12/12) access to historical information under the same retrieval budget.
2
Related Work
Autoregressive Video Generation and Memory.
Diffusion-based autoregressive video generation enables streaming synthesis by progressively generating frames or chunks through autoregressive rollout
(
Gao et al., 2024
;
Chen et al., 2024
;
Liu et al., 2026b
;
Bruce et al., 2024
;
Liu et al., 2026a
;
Guo et al., 2025a
)
.
Recent methods adapt pretrained bidirectional video models through post-training or distillation
(
Zhu et al., 2026
;
Huang et al., 2026
;
Yin et al., 2025
;
Cui et al., 2026
)
, relying on fixed anchors, sliding windows, or coarse-grained memory retrieval to maintain long-range consistency
(
Ji et al., 2025
;
Hu et al., 2026
)
. OminiMem
(
Zhao et al., 2026
)
further introduces a fine-grained head-adaptive retrieval framework, but primarily focuses on single-shot video generation.
Meanwhile, fine-grained KV-cache organization has been explored in LLMs
(
Liu et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2026c
;
Zhu et al., 2025
)
mainly for inference acceleration in the text domain.
In contrast, our work investigates fine-grained retrieval over visual memory with the primary goal of preserving long-range consistency, which we study in the more demanding setting of autoregressive multi-shot video generation.
Multi-Shot Video Generation.
Multi-shot video generation aims to synthesize sequences with discrete shot transitions while preserving narrative, subject, and scene consistency. Most existing approaches are built upon bidirectional video models and can be broadly categorized into two paradigms: generating individual shots separately and subsequently composing them
(
He et al., 2023
;
Xie et al., 2024
;
Zheng et al., 2024
;
Long et al., 2024
)
, or directly modeling multi-shot sequences in an end-to-end manner
(
Guo et al., 2025b
;
Qi et al., 2025
;
Wu et al., 2026b
;
Wu et al., 2026a
;
Meng et al., 2026b
;
Wang et al., 2026
;
Jia et al., 2026
)
. In autoregressive video generation, several methods enable dynamic content control by updating prompts during streaming synthesis, but primarily focus on single-shot generation
(
Yang et al., 2025
;
Ji et al., 2025
)
. More recently, autoregressive approaches have begun to explore multi-shot generation. ShotStream
(
Luo et al., 2026
)
reformulates the problem as next-shot generation, while CausalCine introduces content-aware memory routing for accessing historical information
(
Meng et al., 2026a
)
. Nevertheless, their memory retrieval remains relatively coarse-grained, limiting the effective use of long-term historical information.
3
Method
In this section, we present the methodology and insights of CineMem. After introducing the preliminaries in Section
3.1
, we describe our autoregressive adaptation framework in Section
3.2
, which enables the analysis of intrinsic memory-access patterns in Section
3.3
. Guided by these insights, Sections
3.4
and
3.5

3

3.3
Memory Selection in Attention Module
Based on the full-memory model, we analyze memory-access patterns during autoregressive rollout to guide the design of a fine-grained retrieval mechanism that best matches the model’s intrinsic selection behavior under full-memory attention. While conventional retrieval schemes typically define the retrieval unit at the chunk-to-frame level, we revisit the fundamental token-to-token memory selection process inherent in attention, which motivates our fine-grained retrieval design. For each generated chunk, memory selection is essentially the process by which current tokens, serving as queries, select relevant historical memory tokens through their keys and values.
For a query, highly attended keys receive higher attention probabilities, which mathematically correspond to larger normalized dot-product similarities. We therefore use this signal to study token-wise selection relationships and reveal the underlying memory-selection patterns.
Memory structure.
Efficient retrieval requires grouping, since treating each token as a separate group reduces retrieval to full-memory attention. Frame-level retrieval instead treats each frame as a group, implicitly assuming stronger correlations among tokens within the same frame. However, this assumption may not always hold, especially when a frame contains diverse content. To investigate this, we cluster the full-memory tokens and visualize the results in Figure
4(a)
. Clear clustering patterns emerge: highly similar tokens tend to form cross-frame clusters, while tokens within each cluster exhibit semantic consistency to some extent. We also observe stronger correlations among tokens from the first frame than among those from other frames, consistent with prior findings on the importance of the first latent sink
(
Chen et al., 2026a
)
. These observations motivate grouping memory by token similarity rather than frame membership.
This is because frame-based grouping may introduce redundant information, as retrieving a group due to a few highly relevant tokens also includes many weakly related ones. Moreover, using a single centroid to represent semantically diverse tokens from the same frames can weaken their semantics and reduce retrieval precision.
Heterogeneous memory selection.
Turning to the query side, each query in attention independently computes its similarity to all keys, naturally motivating query-level retrieval.
In practice, different queries and attention heads attend to distinct memory tokens.
We visualize these selection patterns in Figure
4(b)
and observe clear heterogeneity across queries and heads. Even when each query-head pair selects only the top 30% most relevant memory tokens, their overall memory receptive field covers nearly the full memory, which indicates the necessity of query-wise and head-wise retrieval.
(a)
Clustering of full-memory tokens and representative patterns of selected clusters.
(b)
Heatmap of query-head memory preferences and memory coverage.
Figure 4:
Intrinsic memory-selection patterns under the full-memory setting.
Memory tokens exhibit semantically meaningful clustering structures, while different query-head pairs show distinct preferences over memory tokens. Although each query-head pair selects a subset of the most relevant tokens, their union covers nearly the entire memory. See Appendix
A
for more details.
3.4
Online Clustered KV Cache
To enable fine-grained memory grouping, we introduce an online cluster KV cache. During autoregressive rollout, memory tokens are dynamically grouped according to their cosine similarity, such that semantically related tokens are assigned to the same cluster.
This design leverages the semantic coherence within each cluster: tokens relevant to the same query are likely to share similar semantic information, reducing redundant retrieval while improving retrieval effectiveness.
To support fine-grained query-level retrieval, clustering is performed independently for each attention head.
We retain the first and latest chunks as memory anchors.
As rollout proceeds, expired adjacent chunks are progressively incorporated into retrieval candidates through online clustering. Specifically, newly introduced tokens are assigned to existing clusters based on centroid similarity, followed by cluster refinement.

Query-level Retrieval
Considering the heterogeneous memory selection patterns discussed in Section
3.3
, we design a query-level retrieval mechanism, specifically query-wise and head-wise retrieval, for fine-grained memory access.
Conventional retrieval shares a single historical memory subset across all queries, which cannot capture diverse query and head preferences, causing redundant retrieval of irrelevant tokens and missing relevant historical information.
This motivates a more fine-grained retrieval unit. Instead of sharing, we allow each query-head pair to independently select relevant memory from the full history. Combined with the clustered KV cache in Section
3.4
, this design enables query-specific access to relevant memory clusters while maintaining the same retrieval budget, substantially expanding effective memory access and approximating full-memory attention under a constrained memory budget.

4.2
Evaluation and Results

Implementation of PTCS.

Metrics.
To comprehensively evaluate streaming multi-shot video generation, we construct an evaluation set of 100 prompts and establish an evaluation protocol covering video-level, intra-shot-level, and inter-shot-level metrics. Video-level metrics assess fundamental properties of generated videos, including visual aesthetics
(
LAION-AI, 2022
)
, transition control
(
Soucek and Lokoc, 2024
)
, and text alignment
(
Wang et al., 2023
)
, while intra-shot metrics
(
Oquab et al., 2024
;
Fu et al., 2023
)
evaluate consistency within individual shots. More importantly, inter-shot evaluation measures semantic consistency across shot transitions.
However, existing similarity-based inter-shot metrics suffer from an inherent ambiguity: a high similarity score may indicate either strong transition consistency or simply the absence of a meaningful transition. Consequently, models with weak transition control may receive deceptively high consistency scores.
To address this issue, we introduce a VLM-based metric
(
Achiam et al., 2023
)
, the Prompt-conditioned Transition-Consistency Score (PTCS), as illustrated in Figure
6
. PTCS rewards transitions only when they are successfully executed while preserving the required semantic consistency.
PTCS consists of two complementary components: Prompt-conditioned Continuity Preservation (PCP) and Prompt-conditioned Transition Alignment (PTA). Given a hierarchical prompt, we first construct a semantic state graph to identify the semantic elements that should remain unchanged and those expected to change across the transition. PCP measures whether the required elements are consistently preserved before and after the transition, whereas PTA evaluates whether the intended changes, such as modifications in focal subjects or camera configurations, are correctly realized. For each transition, PTCS is computed as the geometric mean of PCP and PTA and then averaged over the evaluation set. By jointly evaluating unchanged elements and intended changes, PTCS provides a more direct and faithful assessment of inter-shot consistency.

Figure
5

(
Yesiltepe et al., 2026
;
Ji et al., 2025
;
Huang et al., 2026

(

(

Notably, we do not include CausalCine

Strong bidirectional baselines
(

Meng et al., 2026b

In contrast, CineMem generates stable multi-shot videos in an autoregressive setting while faithfully following the prescribed transitions and maintaining cross-shot consistency, including challenging revisitation scenarios.
Quantitative Results.
Table
2
reports the quantitative comparison on our evaluation set. CineMem achieves strong performance across video-level quality and intra-shot consistency metrics, demonstrating its ability to generate high-quality videos while maintaining stable shot-level content. For inter-shot evaluation, CineMem achieves the best performance on PTCS, which jointly considers unchanged elements and intended changes during shot transitions. Notably, models with high similarity-based inter-shot scores or PCP values often exhibit limited transition control, while models specifically designed for multi-shot generation may still receive relatively low scores on these metrics. This indicates that similarity-based or preservation-only metrics can overestimate inter-shot consistency when the intended transition is not properly realized. By explicitly considering both preserved and changing elements specified in the prompt, PTCS provides a more faithful evaluation of transition quality. Finally, CineMem achieves superior PTCS performance and even surpasses larger bidirectional models with substantially more parameters.
4.3
Ablation Study
To validate the effectiveness of different design choices in CineMem, we conduct ablation studies from three perspectives, with results summarized in Table
3
.
Training Strategy.
In Section
3.2
, we introduce resampled history context to simulate autoregressive error accumulation during training. Compared with the standard teacher-forcing strategy, resampling context training provides more consistent training conditions with autoregressive inference and achieves superior performance across different metrics, especially in long-horizon consistency.
Retrieval Strategy.
We analyze different retrieval strategies introduced in Sections
3.4
and
3.5
under a plug-in setting. Specifically, we compare our clustered KV cache and query-wise retrieval with frame-level grouping and shared retrieval. To isolate the effect of retrieval design, we directly apply different strategies to the adapted base model without additional training. As shown, query-wise retrieval consistently improves performance under both frame-level and clustered memory organization, demonstrating the importance of fine-grained memory access. Moreover, clustered KV cache further improves transition quality and inter-shot consistency over frame-level grouping, validating the effectiveness of semantic-based memory organization. Notably, without additional training, our retrieval strategy achieves comparable performance to full-memory attention while obtaining higher inter-shot consistency, demonstrating its effectiveness under a constrained memory budget.
Query-level Retrieval Variant.
We investigate a query grouping variant of our retrieval mechanism. Instead of performing independent retrieval for each query, this variant recursively partitions queries into groups according to their spatial and semantic similarity using an adaptive tree structure and shares retrieved memory within each group.
Although query grouping provides an effective approximation by exploiting query similarity, it remains slightly inferior to fully query-wise retrieval, further validating the importance of fine-grained query retrieval.
5
Conclusion
In this paper, we introduce CineMem, a fine-grained memory retrieval framework for autoregressive multi-shot video generation. Combining an online clustered KV cache with query-adaptive retrieval, CineMem enables broader historical access and improves long-range consistency in revisitation scenarios. We develop an autoregressive adaptation framework with resampled context to analyze intrinsic memory-access patterns, revealing semantic clustering among memory tokens and heterogeneous query-head preferences that motivate our design. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.
Our results highlight the importance of fine-grained memory modeling for autoregressive video generation. Rather than relying only on recent frames, autoregressive models should exploit information throughout history. Advances in memory organization and retrieval will enable scalable long-horizon video generation.

A.2
Pre-RoPE Clustering vs. Post-RoPE Clustering
Figure 10:
Visualization of token clustering before and after RoPE.
Compared with Pre-RoPE representations, Post-RoPE similarities exhibit stronger positional dependency and weaker semantic clustering structures.
In Section
3.4
, we introduce an online clustering mechanism to organize memory tokens into semantic groups rather than predefined frame-based partitions. In practice, before entering each transformer block, token representations are augmented with positional encoding. Our clustering and retrieval operations are therefore performed before RoPE (Pre-RoPE). This design choice is motivated by the observation that positional encoding introduces strong absolute position information into token representations, which can obscure semantic similarity and weaken semantic clustering structures.
In fact, the visualization in Figure
4(a)
is obtained using token representations before positional encoding. To further investigate this effect, Figure
10
presents representative clustering results before and after applying RoPE. We observe that RoPE-transformed tokens exhibit stronger position-dependent similarity patterns, while the semantic grouping structure becomes less apparent. Therefore, performing clustering and retrieval after positional encoding may bias memory organization toward positional grouping and degrade into a behavior similar to frame-level partitioning, limiting the benefits of semantic-aware memory organization. These observations support our choice of conducting clustering and retrieval in the Pre-RoPE space.

Appendix C
Analysis of Efficiency
In this section, we analyze the efficiency of CineMem and compare it
with two representative memory access strategies. Full-history attention is
considered as an upper bound in terms of memory availability, as it provides
access to the complete historical context without retrieval constraints.
Meanwhile, frame-group retrieval serves as an efficient coarse-grained
baseline by selecting a fixed number of historical frames with shared routing.
In contrast, CineMem performs fine-grained query-head-wise retrieval over
online-clustered memory, aiming to achieve a better balance between retrieval
granularity and computational cost.
We evaluate these strategies from both theoretical and practical perspectives.

overhead, while the practical evaluation measures actual inference efficiency.

D.2
The effectiveness of Prompt-conditioned Transition-Consistency Score
As discussed in Section
4.2
, conventional similarity-based inter-shot consistency metrics evaluate transitions by measuring feature similarity between frames from different shots. However, such metrics inherently favor cases where adjacent shots exhibit limited visual changes, assigning high consistency scores even when the intended transition is not successfully realized. This limitation explains why some methods can achieve high inter-shot consistency scores while exhibiting poor transition control. These observations motivate our design of PTCS, which explicitly considers both semantic preservation and prompt-specified transition changes. Given that PTCS serves as a key metric for evaluating the effectiveness of CineMem, we further analyze its validity in this section.
We visualize several multi-shot examples with PTCS evaluations in Figure
13
. Qualitatively, PCP successfully reflects transitions where semantic consistency is violated, while PTA captures both missing transitions, where the intended shot change is not realized, and unexpected changes introduced during transitions, including inconsistencies in style, character identity, spatial relationships, or even subtle local details. By jointly considering these two complementary aspects, PTCS provides scores that better align with the desired properties of shot transitions. In contrast, similarity-based inter-shot consistency metrics may produce misleading evaluations: when the visual composition remains similar, they can assign high scores despite missing or incorrect transitions, while failing to distinguish valid and invalid transitions under substantial compositional changes.
Figure 13:
Qualitative comparison between PTCS and similarity-based inter-shot consistency metrics.
The examples illustrate cases where PTCS better reflects transition correctness by jointly considering semantic preservation and prompt-specified changes.
To complement the quantitative evaluation, we conduct a user study to investigate whether PTCS aligns with human perception of inter-shot consistency. Specifically, we select 30 prompts for evaluation, and participants rate each generated video on a scale from 1 to 5 from three perspectives: overall video quality, intra-shot consistency, and inter-shot consistency. The mean opinion scores (MOS) are summarized in Table
4
.
As shown, the human evaluation results are consistent with the trends observed in PTCS. Methods with higher PTCS scores generally receive higher inter-shot consistency ratings from human participants, while models that achieve high similarity-based consistency scores but fail to perform the intended transitions receive substantially lower human scores. This agreement indicates that PTCS better captures human-perceived transition consistency by jointly considering semantic preservation and prompt-specified changes. Furthermore, CineMem achieves the highest MOS in inter-shot consistency and competitive overall video quality, demonstrating its ability to generate coherent multi-shot videos with controllable transitions.

. CineMem achieves the highest PTCS across all shot-count groups, while also consistently obtaining the strongest transition control and intra-shot consistency. Notably, its advantage is preserved for prompts containing six to seven shots, where autoregressive error accumulation and long-range dependency modeling become more challenging. This result indicates that our memory retrieval mechanism remains effective as the generation horizon increases.
Revisit distance.
Finally, Table
7
analyzes performance with respect to revisit distance, which directly reflects the temporal range over which previously generated content needs to be recalled.
CineMem maintains strong performance across all distance ranges and achieves the highest PTCS for the longest revisit range of 13-18 chunks.
It also consistently achieves the best transition control and intra-shot consistency across different revisit distances. These results further support the effectiveness of our fine-grained memory retrieval in preserving long-range historical information and maintaining consistency when previously observed content reappears after a long temporal interval.

Longer Video Generation

Figure 17:
Cases of longer video generated by CineMem.
To further investigate the long-horizon generation capability of CineMem, we provide additional qualitative results on 30-second videos. As shown in Figure
17
, CineMem can continuously extend autoregressive generation while maintaining coherent visual content and long-range consistency across multiple shot transitions. These results highlight the potential of fine-grained memory retrieval for enabling more scalable autoregressive video generation over extended durations.
Appendix F
Limitation and Failure Case
Limitations.
Due to limited computational resources, our experiments are conducted on a relatively small-scale autoregressive backbone with a limited amount of training data for adapting a bidirectional model into a long-horizon autoregressive generator. Consequently, the visual quality of generated videos may lag behind that of large-scale state-of-the-art diffusion models with substantially larger model capacity and training data. Nevertheless, our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed memory retrieval framework and reveal meaningful insights into memory utilization in autoregressive diffusion models. We expect that the proposed approach can further benefit from larger-scale models and datasets.
Figure 18:
A failure case in complex multi-entity scenarios.
Although the generated video preserves revisitation consistency across shots, inconsistencies such as character disappearance and detail changes occur during the transition from Shot 1 to Shot 2. This example highlights the difficulty of handling multi-entity reasoning and spatial relationship preservation in autoregressive video generation.
Failure Cases.
Our memory retrieval mechanism aims to approximate the intrinsic full-memory access pattern under a constrained memory budget by enabling more effective historical information retrieval. However, it still struggles in scenarios requiring complex multi-entity reasoning, as illustrated in Figure
18
. In the presented example, the generated video exhibits issues such as missing characters and inconsistent details across shot transitions.
Such failures are particularly challenging for autoregressive generation. In this case, an early chunk introduces four characters through its prompt, while a later chunk requires only three characters. The model must therefore generate a valid transition by adjusting the camera viewpoint while preserving the spatial relationships and identities established in previous shots. However, the earlier chunks are generated without knowledge of future shot requirements, making such coordinated transitions inherently difficult, especially when the initial composition does not provide sufficient flexibility.
Therefore, multi-entity scenarios with complex shot transitions remain challenging even for full-memory autoregressive generation or bidirectional models, as they require reasoning beyond historical information retrieval. While our proposed memory mechanism improves access to relevant historical content and achieves promising results on certain multi-entity scenarios (see supplementary project page), handling complex entity interactions remains an important direction for future work.
Appendix G
Future Work
Beyond the proposed online clustered KV cache and query-adaptive retrieval framework, several directions remain open for future exploration. For memory organization, more effective clustering strategies could further improve retrieval quality. Meanwhile, exploiting the shared retrieval patterns among queries may provide more efficient alternatives to fully query-wise and head-wise retrieval, as explored by the query-group variant in Section
4.3
. These directions may enable more scalable and efficient memory mechanisms for autoregressive video generation.
From the perspective of autoregressive video generation, integrating entity-aware or structure-aware memory retrieval could help address challenging multi-entity scenarios discussed in Section
F
. Furthermore, extending autoregressive generation to substantially longer horizons remains a promising direction toward more scalable long-form video synthesis.

article.headline: 更细粒度的记忆检索让自回归多镜头视频更连贯
article.lede: 上海AI实验室提出 CineMem：用在线聚类 KV 缓存与逐查询检索替代帧级路由，1.3B 模型 PTCS 达 0.8
article.problem: 自回归视频生成要靠记忆检索维持长程依赖，多镜头场景尤其如此：镜头切换带来大幅视觉变化，却仍要求主体、场景和风格在切换后保持连续，重访此前看过的内容时最难。现有方法大多在帧级别检索，且所有 query token 共享同一份历史上下文，既忽略了不同 query 与注意力头各异的信息需求，也造成大量冗余检索，使历史记忆远未被用满。
article.method: 作者先把 Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B 双向模型适配成分块自回归多镜头生成器，并用重采样真值帧构造历史来缓解误差累积，再利用全记忆注意力分析其内在选择模式：历史 token 呈现跨帧的语义聚类结构，而不同 query-head 组合的记忆偏好差异明显。据此提出按注意力头在线聚类的 KV 缓存（目标簇大小 1024、最大 1200 token，超限拆分、过小合并，并加入负载惩罚与分配一致性项），以及每个 query-head 独立检索 28 个簇的查询级检索；每个 query 还固定访问首块与最新块作为锚点。评测方面提出 PTCS，由 VLM 同时判断该保留的语义是否保留、该执行的转场是否真的发生，取两者几何平均。
article.results: 在自建的 100 条 prompt 评测集上，CineMem 的 PTCS 为 0.8242，高于双向模型 MultiShotMaster 的 0.7984 和 14B 的 HoloCine 的 0.7385，远高于因果基线 ShotStream 的 0.6917；转场控制得分 0.9960 为全表最高。30 人规模用户研究中，其镜头间一致性均分 4.37±0.31 为最高，整体画质 4.15±0.47 略低于 MultiShotMaster 的 4.18±0.42。理论算力上，自注意力加检索共 638.82 TFLOPs，低于全历史注意力的 932.56 和帧级检索的 650.02，但聚类带来的检索开销为 15.018 TFLOPs，而帧级检索仅 0.0453。模型在 16 张 H200 上训练，检索部分训练 3K 步。
article.why_it_matters: 这项工作说明，自回归多镜头生成的瓶颈不只是窗口长度，更是记忆的组织粒度与检索粒度是否与注意力本身的选择模式对齐；同一思路在无需额外微调的即插即用设置下也有效。它同时给出了一个能识别“根本没转场却被相似度打高分”的评测指标，对后续多镜头生成评测有直接参考价值。
article.limitations: 受算力限制，实验只用了 1.3B 骨干和 45K 训练视频，作者承认生成画质可能落后于更大规模扩散模型；复杂多实体转场仍会失败，例如人物消失、细节前后不一致。消融中聚类检索的检索开销比帧级检索高出约两个数量级，且即插即用设置下 PTCS 为 0.8007，低于完整训练后的 0.8242，收益有相当部分依赖额外训练。
article.figure_caption_zh: CineMem 的记忆检索框架：推理时每个 query-head 分别从首块、相邻块和按头在线聚类的候选簇中读取记忆，相邻块经带拆分合并平衡的在线聚类逐步并入候选，训练时则用重采样真值帧构造记忆输入以缓解误差累积。

figure.caption: {Our memory retrieval framework.} Through multi-stage initial adaptation, we convert a bidirectional model into an autoregressive multi-shot model with memory retrieval. During inference, queries access memory from the first chunk, adjacent chunk, and retrieved candidates via token-wise and head-wise retrieval. Previous adjacent chunks are progressively integrated into retrieval candidates through online KV-cache clustering with cluster balancing. During training, resampling ground truth frames provides memory inputs to alleviate error accumulation.

Abstract
Multi-turn image editing aims to modify an image according to a sequence of instructions, enabling more effective interactive visual content creation for users. However, existing methods often exhibit noticeable drift after only a few editing turns, manifesting in two aspects: 1)
unstable
visual quality, with accumulating artifacts and degraded details; and 2)
inconsistent
image content, with unintended changes to preserved regions and prior edits.
To address these challenges, we propose
MT Forcing
, a novel training paradigm for multi-turn image editing with unified multimodal models (UMMs) based on autoregressive diffusion.
Specifically, we propose
Single-Turn
D
istribution
M
atching
D
istillation (
Single-Turn DMD
), which supervises student self-rollouts with a teacher that applies cumulative edits to the source image in a single turn, providing visual-quality guidance without recursive error accumulation.
Additionally, we introduce
Teacher-Forcing Guidance
, which supervises history-dependent transitions on reference trajectories during warmup and as a regularizer during distillation, encouraging cross-turn content consistency beyond what per-turn distribution matching alone can ensure.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the multi-turn image editing capabilities of UMMs, yielding more stable visual quality and stronger cross-turn consistency.

Since each edit builds on the results of prior turns, multi-turn image editing is inherently causal

Such a design enables later edits to draw on the accumulated interaction history while responding to new user instructions.
However, existing methods often exhibit drift after only a few editing turns (see Fig.

unstable

During training, the model typically conditions on reference histories, whereas inference requires recursively conditioning on its own imperfect histories.
To overcome these challenges, we propose
MT Forcing
, a training paradigm for UMMs based on AR diffusion that enables stable and consistent multi-turn image editing. First, we introduce Single-Turn

istribution
M

D
istillation (
Single-Turn DMD
) to counteract visual-quality drift across editing turns.
Our design follows two observations: 1) a single editing turn typically introduces limited degradation
[
72
]
; and 2) editing models can execute multiple actions in one turn
[
73
]
(see Fig.
4
).
These observations motivate using single-turn editing quality as the reference for every turn of a multi-turn student.
Specifically, we reorganize all instructions up to the current turn into a
bundled prompt
that expresses their cumulative editing intent as a single edit to the source image.
Conditioned on this prompt and the source image, the teacher executes the accumulated edits in one turn, providing a quality reference without cross-turn error accumulation.
The student performs autoregressive self-rollouts during training
[
29
,
1
]
, conditioning each edit on its own imperfect outputs.
At each turn, a DMD loss

,
94

16
,
44
]
aligns the student’s rollout output distribution with the teacher’s single-turn output distribution for the same cumulative editing intent.
This trains the student to maintain visual quality under the histories encountered during inference, mitigating exposure bias and progressive visual degradation.
However, the bundled prompt specifies cumulative editing intent without fixing the visual details established in preceding student outputs (see Fig.
4
), so per-turn distribution matching alone does not guarantee cross-turn consistency.
To improve cross-turn consistency, we introduce

, which trains the student with teacher forcing on consistent reference trajectories

,

,

]
.
We apply this teacher-forced supervision in two stages.
1)
Teacher-Forcing Warmup
: before Single-Turn DMD training, we perform supervised fine-tuning to teach the model to produce consistent edits conditioned on coherent reference histories.
2)
Teacher-Forcing Regularization
: during Single-Turn DMD training, we retain this supervision with a lower weight as a regularizer to preserve history-dependent behavior and cross-turn consistency during distillation
[
97
,
78
,
8
]
.
Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that MT Forcing achieves more stable visual quality, greater content consistency, and better instruction following across successive editing turns.
To evaluate multi-turn image editing comprehensively, we build on MTEdit-Bench’s
[
6
]
assessment of instruction following, content consistency, and visual quality.
We additionally introduce
Pixel
\mathrm{Pixel}
, a metric based on image matching
[
24
]
that measures geometric alignment between successive editing outputs.
MT Forcing also achieves better alignment under this metric, providing additional evidence of improved content preservation across turns.
In summary, we 1) propose Single-Turn DMD to stabilize visual quality across editing turns by aligning student rollouts with a single-turn teacher;
2) introduce Teacher-Forcing Guidance to preserve cross-turn content consistency through teacher-forced training on consistent reference trajectories; and 3) combine these complementary objectives into MT Forcing, which achieves more stable visual quality, greater content consistency, and better instruction following in extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments.

5  Conclusion
We presented MT Forcing, which combines learning on self-generated histories with reference supervision for stable and consistent multi-turn image editing with autoregressive UMMs.
Single-Turn DMD transfers single-turn editing quality to student rollouts using a teacher that realizes cumulative editing intent directly from the source image, avoiding recursive error accumulation in its supervision.
Teacher-Forcing Guidance complements marginal distribution matching with reference-conditioned supervision during warmup and distillation, encouraging the history–output dependencies needed for content preservation.
Experiments on SenseNova-U1 and SenseNova-U1.5 demonstrate improved instruction following, content consistency, and drift robustness on the eight-turn step-wise sub-bench of MTEdit-Bench, with increasingly pronounced benefits at later turns.

article.headline: MT Forcing：稳定多轮图像编辑
article.lede: 提出 MT Forcing，用单轮分布匹配蒸馏加教师强制引导，缓解自回归扩散多轮图像编辑的漂移。
article.problem: 多轮图像编辑中，模型常在几轮后出现视觉质量不稳定和内容不一致；作者将其归因于训练时使用参考历史、推理时却递归使用自生成历史所导致的暴露偏差。现有方法难以同时抑制伪影累积和保持前序编辑内容。
article.method: MT Forcing 包含两个组件：Single-Turn DMD 将截至当前轮的全部指令重组为单轮“捆绑提示”，用单轮教师对齐学生自 rollout 的每轮输出分布；Teacher-Forcing Guidance 在参考轨迹上以 flow matching 监督历史相关转移，先用于 warmup，再作为蒸馏阶段的正则项。两者结合，在自生成历史上做分布匹配，同时用参考轨迹约束跨轮一致性。
article.results: 在 MTEdit-Bench 八轮子集上，第 8 轮 IF/CC 分别提升 7.45/6.82（SenseNova-U1）和 4.65/4.46（SenseNova-U1.5）；SenseNova-U1.5 的 DRS 全程保持 4.20–4.35，基线从 4.09 降至 3.03；其八轮平均 Pixel 从 6.34 降至 0.74，降幅 88.4%。消融中完整方法取得 9.66 IF、8.40 CC、4.30 DRS 和 0.74 Pixel。
article.why_it_matters: 它把自回归扩散的 rollout 训练与单轮教师蒸馏结合，为多轮交互式图像编辑提供了一种可复用的稳定化训练思路。
article.limitations: 实验仅覆盖 MTEdit-Bench 的 100 个会话、8 轮设定和两个 SenseNova-U1 系列模型；论文未给出推理开销或失败率的具体数字，跨模型与更长轮次的泛化仍待验证。
article.figure_caption_zh: MT Forcing 总览：单轮 DMD 对齐学生 rollout 与单轮教师分布，教师强制引导在参考轨迹上监督历史相关转移，整体训练先 warmup 后蒸馏并加正则。

figure.caption: {Overview of MT Forcing.} (a)~Single-Turn DMD matches student rollout marginals to single-turn teacher distributions. (b)~Teacher-Forcing Guidance supervises history-dependent transitions on reference trajectories via flow matching to encourage cross-turn consistency. (c)~Overall training: teacher-forcing warmup followed by DMD with teacher-forcing regularization.

Abstract
Deep learning (DL) methods have substantially improved predictive performance across a wide range of downstream prediction tasks, enabling new discoveries in multiple domains. However, principled DL methods for non-Euclidean random objects remain relatively scarce, despite the growing importance of modern biomedical outcomes taking the form of probability distributions, random graphs, functions, and other random objects in metric spaces. Motivated by a new generation of digital and clinical biomarkers, we propose a deep learning framework for regression with random objects in metric spaces. Our approach operates directly on the metric structure of the response space, avoiding restrictive manifold or Euclidean embedding assumptions imposed by many existing methods. At the same time, it retains modern statistical guarantees under the stated statistical assumptions. We establish statistical consistency and convergence rates for the proposed estimator, and characterize conditions under which it can mitigate the curse of dimensionality for hierarchically compositional regression functions. Extensive simulation studies demonstrate competitive predictive performance, with gains over several competing approaches in multiple Euclidean and non-Euclidean configurations. Finally, we demonstrate the practical utility of the proposed framework in two digital health case studies with distribution-valued outcomes in Wasserstein spaces, using high-resolution accelerometry and continuous glucose monitoring data. Embedding-based deep-learning methods may be less suitable when no informative low-dimensional representation exists or when the learned embedding does not adequately preserve the intrinsic geometry of the response space.
Keywords: metric spaces; deep learning; curse of dimensionality; digital health.
1

Introduction
Technological advances in biomedicine are generating increasingly dense and nearly continuous measurements of human physiology, behavior, and environment
[
8
]
. Digital health data offer new opportunities to characterize human health at an unprecedented resolution and to develop novel personalized medicine strategies
[
23
]
. At the same time, they pose new analytical challenges that are not naturally addressed by conventional multivariate statistical methods. In many modern biomedical applications, the outcome of interest is not adequately represented by a scalar or a finite-dimensional vector, but instead takes the form of a random object belonging to a metric space
(
𝒴
,
d

(\mathcal{Y},d)

[
33
]

A prominent example arises in continuous glucose monitoring (CGM). Rather than characterizing an individual’s glucose profile exclusively through summary measures such as mean glucose, glucose variability, or time spent within prespecified glycemic ranges, the entire collection of glucose measurements can be represented through a
glucodensity

[

27

Similar distributional representations have been proposed for other high-resolution digital-health measurements, including accelerometer-derived physical activity, where the distribution of activity intensities provides an individualized representation without relying on prespecified physical activity thresholds

29

article.headline: 面向度量空间随机对象的深度学习回归框架
article.lede: 新框架直接在响应空间的度量结构上做回归，给出统计一致性证明，并用血糖与加速度计数据做验证。
article.problem: 生物医学与数字健康产生的结局越来越多是概率分布、随机图、函数等取值于度量空间的随机对象，而不是标量或有限维向量。现有深度学习方法大多依赖流形或欧氏嵌入假设，针对非欧氏随机对象的、带统计保证的回归方法仍然稀缺。论文要解决的就是：在不预设嵌入的前提下，如何对度量空间取值的响应做深度学习回归。
article.method: 作者提出一个直接利用响应空间度量结构（Fréchet 均值意义下）的深度学习回归框架，从而绕开限制性的流形或欧氏嵌入假设，同时保留现代统计保证。理论上给出估计量的相合性与收敛速率，并刻画了在分层复合回归函数下缓解维数灾难的条件。数值上做了多组模拟，对比深度Fréchet回归（DFR）、全局Fréchet回归（GFR）、KNN与随机森林（RF），并在两个分布型结局的数字健康案例（高分辨率加速度计、连续血糖监测）中演示。
article.results: 模拟设定为 p∈{5,10,15,20}、训练样本量 n∈{200,300,400,500}、独立测试集 n_test=2000，每组重复100次蒙特卡洛；神经网络方法统一用3个隐藏层、每层50个ReLU单元、训练1000个epoch、Adam 学习率0.005、小批量32。在 2-Wasserstein 分布型响应、q=1 的情景中，所提方法在20种配置里有14种取得最低平均 W2 误差；在 q=4 的产品交互高斯分布情景中，KNN 在20种配置中的14种误差最低，所提方法只在其余6种最好，且在 p=20 时较有竞争力。血糖案例的20名测试参与者上，随机森林的中位 Wasserstein 误差最小，所提方法与GFR中位表现相近，DFR略大，KNN最大，各方法四分位区间明显重叠。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「分布本身就是结局」的数字生物标志物（如 glucodensity、活动强度分布）纳入有理论保证的深度学习回归框架，为高分辨率生理数据的个性化建模提供了不必先降维成少数汇总指标的路径。
article.limitations: 两个分布型案例中没有任何单一方法全面最优：血糖数据上随机森林中位数误差最小，所提方法在不同受试者间误差波动很大，对个体异质性比随机森林更敏感；作者也指出，当不存在有信息的低维表示、或学到的嵌入不能充分保持响应空间内在几何时，基于嵌入的深度学习可能并不合适。

Does Steering Break Your Model? A Multi-Dimensional Evaluation Suite for LLM Steering Methods
Haotian Yang

Abstract
Activation steering provides a lightweight and flexible way to control large
language model (LLM) behavior. However, effective steering requires more than inducing the intended behavior:
it should also limit unintended changes and remain robust across inputs and training data.
Existing evaluations cover these dimensions only in fragments. As a result, the trade-offs between efficacy and side effects have not been systematically characterized.
We introduce
SteerScope
, a two-axis,
multi-dimensional evaluation suite that jointly characterizes
steering
outcomes
and
method properties
through 15 metrics. We score
target efficacy and side effects on language quality, task capabilities,
and safety and reliability, and further assess generalization and data
dependence through steering-specific metrics for sample efficiency and sample
sensitivity.
Rather than comparing methods at a single operating point, we characterize their efficacy–side-effect trade-offs.
Under matched models, tasks, and evaluation protocols, we benchmark 23 methods spanning 4 families, including prompting, LoRA, and SFT as
baseline methods, and release the suite as an extensible codebase.
We find that current activation steering methods do not yet surpass the Prompt Steering baseline in their overall balance between steering efficacy and side effects:
across both model scales, no evaluated activation steering method achieves higher efficacy without incurring greater composite side effects.
We further uncover a
consistent coupling between steering efficacy and side effects. Under OOD
prompts, target efficacy is often preserved, whereas side effects tend to become
more pronounced, particularly through declines in instruction relevance and
fluency. Methods also exhibit sharply different sample-efficiency profiles.
1
1

2

Corresponding author:
liangmingpan@pku.edu.cn
.
https://github.com/yht0511/steerscope
1
Introduction
As large language models (LLMs) are deployed across diverse tasks and
applications, fine-grained control over their behavior has become increasingly
important
(
Ouyang et al., 2022
)
. Prompting and fine-tuning are widely used
for this purpose. However, prompting lacks an explicit mechanism for continuously
adjusting the strength of a desired behavior, while fine-tuning requires
additional training and parameter updates
(
Wu et al., 2025a
)
. Recently,
activation steering
has emerged as a promising approach to behavioral control. It intervenes in internal
representations, such as the residual stream, to induce or suppress specific
concepts, styles, and safety-related behaviors
(
Turner et al., 2023
;
Zou et al., 2023
;
Rimsky et al., 2024
)
. By keeping
the backbone parameters frozen and allowing intervention strength to be adjusted,
activation steering is more lightweight and adjustable.
However, the effects of steering are not always confined to the intended target.
Prior work has reported multi-dimensional side effects across language quality,
task capabilities, safety, and reliability. These include degraded generation
quality and task performance, as well as changes in bias, refusal, and jailbreak
susceptibility
(
Stickland et al., 2024
;
Bhalla et al., 2024
;
Sprejer et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2026d
)
. Existing evidence suggests that
these side effects may arise from concept entanglement, whereby concepts
are not behaviorally independent and steering one can unintentionally alter
others
(
Durmus et al., 2024
;
Siu et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2026d
)
. Beyond these side effects, steering outcomes may vary across
input distributions. They may also depend on the amount and composition of the
data used to construct the intervention
(
Tan et al., 2024
;
Braun et al., 2025
;
Ding et al., 2026
)
. Together, these challenges motivate a
comprehensive evaluation framework organized around two questions:
what steering
changes
and
when those changes hold
.
Recent work has begun to establish benchmarks for evaluating LLM steering, such as
AxBench
(
Wu et al., 2025a
)
,
SteeringSafety
(
Siu et al., 2026
)
,
FaithSteer-BENCH
(
Ding et al., 2026
)
, and
CLaS-Bench
(

To bridge this gap, we introduce
SteerScope
, a comprehensive, multi-dimensional evaluation suite for LLM steering.
1.
Systematic evaluation taxonomy.
SteerScope organizes 15 metrics into a hierarchical taxonomy with two complementary axes (Fig.
1
, left).
Steering Outcomes
examines what steering changes, covering target efficacy and side effects on language quality, task capabilities, and safety and reliability.
Method Properties
examines when steering effects hold, covering generalization under cross-lingual prompt shifts and dependence on training data.
2.
Broad method coverage.
We evaluate 23 methods spanning 4 families on 2 models.
These include diverse activation steering methods alongside prompting, LoRA, and SFT baselines.
3.
Efficacy–side-effect trade-off characterization.
We characterize each adjustable method through its efficacy–side-effect trade-offs, revealing how unintended effects change alongside target efficacy.
Our central finding is that
current activation steering methods do not outperform the Prompt Steering baseline in the efficacy–side-effect trade-off on either evaluated model
.
Although some activation steering methods outperform this baseline on existing benchmarks, none achieves higher target efficacy without greater composite side effects under our default aggregation.
On Gemma-2-9B-it, for example, A-PSR improves the Concept Expression score by 1.30 points but incurs an average normalized degradation of 0.12.
Consistent with this, steering efficacy and side effects generally increase together as intervention strength grows.
Nevertheless, activation steering remains useful because its adjustable intervention strength provides access to high-efficacy operating points.
Among activation steering approaches, methods with learned interventions tend to achieve more favorable trade-offs than optimization-free methods.
We further find that target efficacy is often preserved under out-of-distribution prompts. In contrast, side effects tend to become more pronounced, particularly through declines in instruction relevance and fluency.
Finally, sample efficiency varies substantially across methods, reflecting
different levels of dependence on training-data size.
2
Related Work
Representation-Based Activation Steering.
Representation-based activation steering controls model behavior by intervening on
internal activations at inference time. Early methods often modeled target concepts
with linear directions, motivated in part by the linear representation hypothesis
(
Bolukbasi et al., 2016
;
Elhage et al., 2022
;
Park et al., 2024
;
Nanda et al., 2023
)
. Existing methods span
contrastive directions, subspaces, latent representations,
geometric transformations, hypernetworks, and nonlinear interventions
(
Turner et al., 2023
;
Zou et al., 2023
;
Marks & Tegmark, 2024
;
Wu et al., 2024
;
Pham et al., 2026
;
Sun et al., 2025
;
Wu et al., 2025b
;
Jin et al., 2026
;
You et al., 2026
;
Zhao et al., 2026
)
. We organize the methods evaluated in this
work by their underlying mechanisms in Section
4
.
Benchmarks for Activation Steering.
Existing benchmarks have begun to standardize the evaluation of activation steering, but each covers only a subset of the relevant evaluation dimensions. AxBench
(
Wu et al., 2025a
)
evaluates 500 steering targets across activation steering, prompting, and fine-tuning methods, but its off-target evaluation is limited to instruction following and fluency. SteeringSafety
(
Siu et al., 2026
)
studies behavioral entanglement across nine predefined safety perspectives within a curated safety concept set. FaithSteer-BENCH
(
Ding et al., 2026
)
focuses on deployment-time reliability, evaluating clean controllability, capability preservation, and robustness under changing conditions at a single calibrated operating point. SteerEval
(
Xu et al., 2026
)
broadens evaluation across behavioral domains and concept granularities, while CLaS-Bench
(
Gurgurov et al., 2026
)
extends steering evaluation to 32 languages and cross-lingual transfer.
Complementary studies have identified specific steering side effects, including degradation in generation coherence
(
Bhalla et al., 2024
)
, capability–behavior trade-offs
(
Sprejer et al., 2026
)
, and sensitivity to individual samples and prompt conditions
(
Tan et al., 2024
)
.
Overall, existing evaluations cover safety entanglement, deployment reliability, cross-lingual control, and other aspects, but remain fragmented across evaluation dimensions and steering methods.

4
Steering Methods
We evaluate 23 representative methods and baselines, plus a Random control. The methods span diverse steering mechanisms while avoiding redundant variants and enabling both method- and mechanism-level analysis. A broader catalogue is provided in Appendix
B
.
4.1
Optimization-Free Steering Methods
Concept Directions.
These methods construct steering directions from activation patterns associated
with a target concept.
DiffMean
adds the difference between positive
and negative mean representations to model activations at inference
time
(
Marks & Tegmark, 2024
)
;
PCA
extracts the first principal component
from positive-example activations
(
Wu et al., 2025a
)
, while
LAT
applies PCA to contrastive activation
differences
(
Zou et al., 2023
)
. As a control,
Random
applies
DiffMean after randomly partitioning the training examples, removing
concept-specific label alignment.
Structured Interventions.
These methods introduce geometric, latent-space, or unit-level interventions.
Spherical Steering
performs norm-preserving geodesic rotation toward a target direction, aiming to better respect the geometry of the model’s representation space
(
You et al., 2026
)
.
HiDRA
performs steering in a higher-dimensional feature space, where discriminative structure can be captured
(
Pham et al., 2026
)
.
AUSteer
steers in discriminative LLM components and assigns adaptive strengths
(
Feng et al., 2026
)
.
SAE-Based Methods.
SAE-based methods use decoder directions from a sparse-autoencoder dictionary
(
Huben et al., 2024
)
.
SAE
uses a concept-associated feature, while
SAE-A
selects the feature with highest target-discriminative AUROC
(
Wu et al., 2025a
)
.
4.2
Directly Optimized Steering Methods
Learned Steering Directions.
Several methods learn interventions using supervised training.
Linear Probe
trains a linear discriminator between positive and negative representations and uses the learned weight vector as the steering direction
(
Alain & Bengio, 2017
;
Wu et al., 2025a
)
.
SSV
optimizes an additive vector using a language-modeling loss on training responses
(
Wu et al., 2025a
)
, and
ReFT-r1
similarly learns a rank-one representation intervention, jointly optimizing concept detection and generation-time steering objectives
(
Wu et al., 2025a
)
.
Learned Subspace and Adaptive Interventions.
LoReFT
learns a low-rank intervention subspace over hidden representations
(
Wu et al., 2024
)
.
PSR
combines a learned steering direction with an activation-dependent gate, allowing intervention strength to vary across tokens
(
Heyman & Vandeputte, 2026
)
. We evaluate its all-layer variant (
A-PSR
) and single-layer variant (
S-PSR
).
RePS
learns an intervention through preference optimization
(
Wu et al., 2025b
)
.
ODESteer
constructs a vector field from the gradient of a learned nonlinear barrier function and applies multi-step integration
(
Zhao et al., 2026
)
;
StepODESteer
uses the same construction with a single update step.
4.3
Hypernetwork-Based Steering Methods
These methods use shared auxiliary networks to generate steering interventions conditioned on natural-language targets.
HyperSteer
trains a transformer-based hypernetwork that maps a natural-language steering target and the model’s internal activations to a dynamically generated steering vector
(
Sun et al., 2025
)
.
FLAS
instead trains a transformer-style FlowBlock to parameterize a concept-conditioned velocity field over activation space
(
Jin et al., 2026
)
.
4.4
Non-Representation-based Steering Methods
Four baseline methods that do not operate directly on model representations are included: two prompting baselines and two parameter-update baselines.
Prompt Steering
uses an LLM to convert each target concept into a short steering context, whereas
Simple Prompt Steering
uses a fixed concept-conditioned instruction; both prepend the resulting context to the original instruction. The prompt templates are provided in Appendix
C.5
. We further evaluate
Supervised Fine-Tuning
(SFT)
(
Ouyang et al., 2022
)
and
Low-Rank Adaptation
(LoRA)
(
Hu et al., 2022
)
as the two parameter-update baselines.

Reducing side effects remains a key challenge for steering methods.
Across both model scales, methods with an explicit steering factor generally incur
larger composite side effects as target efficacy increases. At its Overall-selected
method-level steering factor, A-PSR improves Concept Expression by 1.20 and 1.30 points on
Gemma-2-2B-it and Gemma-2-9B-it, respectively, while incurring composite side
effects of 0.11 and 0.12. Recent methods such as
A-PSR outperform Prompt Steering on AxBench’s Overall and Concept Expression
metrics. Figure
3
further shows that individual
methods can locally surpass Prompt Steering on particular capability metrics.
Yet when a broader range of side effects is considered, no activation steering
method dominates the Prompt Steering baseline on the efficacy–side-effect
trade-off. We examine the robustness of this aggregate
comparison to alternative metric weightings in
Appendix
D.1.1
. These results suggest that future work on steering should focus on reducing unintended effects.
Optimization-free methods generally exhibit worse efficacy–side-effect trade-offs.
Compared with prompting and methods with learned interventions, optimization-free methods generally exhibit less favorable efficacy–side-effect trade-offs. One possible explanation is that prompting leverages existing instruction-following capabilities, while methods with learned interventions incorporate task-specific feedback through gradient-based training. In contrast, directions extracted from representation statistics or pretrained features do not directly constrain the resulting behavioral changes.
Low-strength steering can improve off-target metrics.
Some low-strength interventions improve off-target performance relative to the
unsteered model. Reversing the steering direction removes or reverses these
gains, suggesting direction-dependent conceptual entanglement rather than a
generic effect of weak perturbations
(Appendix
D.3
).
Beyond the aggregate score, method rankings vary across individual side-effect
metrics, underscoring the need for multi-dimensional evaluation. Ranking
agreement is generally stronger on Gemma-2-9B-it than on Gemma-2-2B-it
(Appendix
D.2
).

5.3
Generalization
Taken together across both model scales, activation steering methods tend to
exhibit lower Cross-Lingual Retention than Prompt Steering, although retention varies
substantially across methods and models.
Target efficacy transfers more readily than behavioral quality.
For most methods, base-relative Concept Gain changes only modestly from ID to
OOD prompts, and several methods achieve comparable or higher gains OOD.
In contrast, steering-induced Instruction Degradation is larger under OOD
prompts for 11 of the 13 methods shown in Table
1
,
while Fluency Degradation is larger for 9 of 13. These results suggest that
cross-lingual prompt shifts often preserve the intended steering effect while amplifying certain steering-induced side effects. Complete results for all methods and both model scales are reported in Appendix
D.9
.

Conclusion
We introduced
SteerScope
, a comprehensive evaluation suite for LLM steering organized around two axes:
Steering Outcomes
and
Method Properties
. Our
taxonomy organizes steering evaluation into target efficacy, side effects on
language quality, task capabilities, and safety and reliability, and method
properties under distribution and training-data changes. We further provide a
systematic taxonomy of steering methods and conduct controlled comparisons across
optimization-free, directly optimized, and hypernetwork-based approaches, alongside
prompting, LoRA, and SFT baselines. By comparing strength-dependent
efficacy–side-effect curves across methods and model scales, SteerScope provides
a broader view than comparisons based on selected operating points.
Our evaluation reveals that performance on existing benchmarks does not fully
reflect steering quality. Activation steering methods that outperform the Prompt Steering
baseline on existing benchmarks do not necessarily maintain this advantage
when broader side effects are considered, and stronger steering efficacy is generally
accompanied by larger unintended effects. Activation steering nevertheless remains
valuable for its adjustable access to high-efficacy operating points. Among
activation steering approaches, methods with learned interventions tend to achieve more
favorable trade-offs than optimization-free methods. Improvements at weak
intervention strengths suggest that side effects can reflect conceptual entanglement
rather than uniform degradation. We further find that under out-of-distribution
prompts, target efficacy is often preserved, whereas side effects tend to be
more pronounced. Methods also exhibit substantially different sample-efficiency profiles.
Use of Generative AI
We used generative AI in the experimental workflow. DeepSeek-V3.2-Instruct generated concept-conditioned positive and negative responses for the contrastive training data, as well as concept-specific instructions for Prompt Steering, A-PSR, and S-PSR. GPT-4o-mini was used to score concept expression, instruction relevance, and fluency; Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct was used to evaluate JailbreakBench responses. The corresponding prompts, scoring criteria, and settings are reported in the experimental details and appendix. We also used generative AI to polish the manuscript. The authors take responsibility for the LLM-generated materials and LLM-based judgments used in this work.

Definition
Contrastive Data
Uses contrastive positive and negative examples of a target concept to derive a steering vector.
Scaling
Multiplies selected activation components, directions, or subspaces rather than adding a vector.
Linear Change
Locates a dominant linear direction that best represents a target concept and steers by linear addition.
Subspace Change
Locates a dominant multi-dimensional subspace that best represents a target concept and steers in that subspace.
Geodesic
Steers by geodesic rotation or norm-preserving.
Latent Space
Steers in a transformed representation space, such as SAE, random-feature, kernel, or invertible latent spaces.
Adaptive Strength
Adapts the steering strength based on the input prompt or current activations at inference time or gated.
Multi-Step Dynamics
Applies steering through multiple sequential updates.
SAE-Based
Uses a sparse autoencoder to select or construct steering directions.
Shared Module
Creates a reusable learned steering tool across multiple concepts.
