Appendix C
Experimental Details
C.1
Models and Shared Setup
We evaluate all methods on instruction-tuned Gemma-2 models at 2 scales,
google/gemma-2-2b-it
and
google/gemma-2-9b-it
. For methods
defined at a single intervention site, we intervene on the residual stream at
layer 20 in both models, matching the intervention site used during both
training and evaluation of HyperSteer
(
Sun et al., 2025
)
,
FLAS
(
Jin et al., 2026
)
, and S-PSR
(
Heyman & Vandeputte, 2026
)
. Layer 20 corresponds
to approximately 77% and 48% of the
26- and 42-layer model stacks, respectively. The
training data for each concept contain 72 contrastive
response pairs generated by DeepSeek-V3.2-Instruct, giving 144 labeled examples. Unless
otherwise specified, training uses bfloat16 precision and a base random seed of
42, from which method- and concept-specific seeds are derived. Gradient-based
methods use AdamW with a linear learning-rate schedule and no warmup, except for
FLAS as specified below. All methods use the complete CONCEPT500 setting, except
SFT, which is trained and evaluated on 20 concepts.

C.6
Prior Human Validation of AxBench-Style Judges
Our Concept Expression, Instruction Relevance, and Fluency evaluators follow
the AxBench prompts and ternary scoring scheme and use the same judge model,
GPT-4o-mini
(
Wu et al., 2025a
)
. AxBench evaluated these judges against human
ratings using five participants, each of whom scored 30 steered generations
spanning six methods on Gemma-2-9B at layer 20. The reported Pearson correlation
was
0.57
0.57
among human raters and
0.58
0.58
between the LLM judge and human raters,
indicating that, in the AxBench setting, LLM–human agreement was comparable to
inter-human agreement.
The comparable LLM–human and inter-human agreement supports the use of these
AxBench-style evaluators in SteerScope. We further complement the three
LLM-based scores with established task-specific benchmarks and deterministic
evaluators wherever available.

D.2
Ranking Agreement Across Side-Effect Metrics
To examine whether the aggregate score masks metric-specific differences, we
rank methods by their degradation on each side-effect metric at their
Overall-selected method-level steering factors. We then compute Spearman correlations between the
metric-specific rankings.
Figure 8:
Spearman correlations between method rankings produced by different
side-effect metrics on Gemma-2-2B-it (left) and Gemma-2-9B-it (right) at
layer 20. Each method is evaluated at its Overall-selected method-level steering factor.
The metrics do not produce fully consistent method rankings, supporting the
need for multi-dimensional side-effect evaluation.
Ranking agreement is mixed on Gemma-2-2B-it but generally stronger on
Gemma-2-9B-it. JailbreakBench false refusal is a notable exception, showing
weak or negative correlations with most other metrics.
We hypothesize that this difference may reflect the range of evaluation examples each
model can solve. The 9B model may solve more difficult examples whose successful
completion depends on multiple overlapping capabilities; steering-induced
disruption of these shared capabilities may therefore manifest across several
metrics simultaneously. In contrast, floor effects on the 2B model may obscure
such shared degradation.

interventions disappear or become degradations when their steering directions are

article.headline: 23种激活引导方法评测：无一全面胜过提示引导
article.lede: SteerScope用15项指标、23种方法在 Gemma-2 两个规模上系统评测激活引导，发现激活引导方法在效能与副作
article.problem: 激活引导只需冻结主干、在推理时干预内部表示，就能诱导或抑制目标概念，但已有评测往往只覆盖局部维度：AxBench 的副作用只测指令遵循与流畅度，SteeringSafety 聚焦安全纠缠，FaithSteer-BENCH 只在单一标定工作点评估且不覆盖语言质量与安全副作用。因此，「引导改变了什么」与「这些改变在分布偏移和训练数据变化下是否成立」这两个问题一直缺乏统一刻画。
article.method: 作者提出 SteerScope，把15项指标组织成两条轴：Steering Outcomes 轴测量目标效能（Concept Expression）以及语言质量、任务能力、安全与可靠性三类共11项副作用，并按干预强度扫描得到效能–副作用权衡曲线；Method Properties 轴在固定方法级因子下测量跨语言泛化（英语为ID，中、韩、意、西为OOD）与数据依赖（样本效率、样本敏感性）。实验在 Gemma-2-2B-it 与 Gemma-2-9B-it 的残差流第20层上，以相同概念、任务与评测协议对比了横跨4个方法族的23种方法，外加 prompting、LoRA、SFT 基线与随机对照。
article.results: 在各自按 Overall 选定的方法级因子上，A-PSR 使 Concept Expression 在 Gemma-2-2B-it 和 Gemma-2-9B-it 上分别提升1.20与1.30分，同时带来0.11与0.12的复合副作用（11项指标归一化退化的等权平均）；在两个模型尺度上，没有任何激活引导方法能在不增加复合副作用的前提下取得高于 Prompt Steering 的效能。对11项副作用指标做100万次 Dirichlet 权重重采样后，Prompt Steering 在 Gemma-2-2B-it 上于99.83%（Dirichlet(1)）的抽样中不被支配，Gemma-2-9B-it 上为99.92%。跨语言方面，表1中13种方法里有11种在OOD提示下指令退化变大、9种流畅度退化变大；Gemma-2-2B-it 上 Prompt Steering 的保留率为1.0026，A-PSR 为0.9157，FLAS 仅0.4256。样本效率实验中，训练集规模取每个概念6、12、36、72行，全量为N=144，HyperSteer 与 DiffMean 在小数据预算下保留了较大比例的全量效果，而 A-PSR、FLAS、LoRA、ReFT-r1 需要更多数据。
article.why_it_matters: 它说明在 AxBench 式指标上胜出的激活引导方法，一旦把语言质量、任务能力与安全可靠性一起纳入，优势就会消失，这提示后续工作应把重心放在压低非预期副作用而非单纯拉高目标效能。公开的可扩展代码库也让不同引导方法能在统一协议下被横向比较。
article.limitations: 评测只覆盖 Gemma-2 的2B与9B两个规模和残差流第20层这一单点干预位置，跨语言泛化仅涉及中、韩、意、西四种语言，SFT 基线因算力限制只在20个概念上训练与评测；方法级因子是在完整ID评测集上挑选后固定使用，作者自己也承认这会给工作点标定带来一定乐观偏差。此外效能与部分副作用依赖 GPT-4o-mini 与 Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct 作为裁判，评分噪声未被纳入置信区间。

IQuest-Q1: Advancing Foundation Capabilities
for Agentic CLI Systems
IQuest Research
Abstract
We present IQuest-Q1, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) agentic foundation model with 320B total parameters (15B activated).
IQuest-Q1 is developed through a three-stage process:
(1)
stable and efficient pre-training
, combining Stable SplitNorm, Muon, and
μ
\mu
P with a two-stage curriculum whose second stage increases the coding-data mixture, preserving a wide stability margin between safe and optimal learning rates;
(2)
fine-grained mid-training
, expanding the data mixture across domains and formats and progressively extending the context;
and
(3)
multi-scaffold with multi-version post-training
, combining SFT, domain-specialized RL, and MOPD across various scaffolds to integrate complementary training signals and strengthen agentic coding capabilities.
Furthermore, model merging combines different experts and checkpoints from different stages while mitigating conflicts among their parameter updates.
The resulting IQuest-Q1 demonstrates capabilities in both coding and general tasks.
We release IQuest-Q1 as an open-source model to support community research and development.
Figure 1
:
IQuest-Q1 performance across benchmarks. DeepSeek-V4-Flash/Pro refer to the official 0731/0813 releases, respectively. Humanity’s Last Exam is reported without tools. IQuest-CLIBench is our proprietary built-in benchmark for evaluating human-agent collaboration and user experience (see Section
5
for details).
1
Introduction
LLM-based agents allow language models
[
47
,
5
,
12
,
90
,
61
,
80
,
84
]
to perform tasks through iterative reasoning, action, and interaction with external environments, rather than merely generating responses
[
46
,
4
,
78
]
. Among these environments, command-line interfaces (CLIs) have become one of the most general ways for language models to interact with external systems, use tools, access files, and execute code.
As a result, building more capable agentic models requires stronger CLI capabilities.
In this work, we release IQuest-Q1, an open-source agentic foundation model with broad CLI capabilities across a wide range of general and coding tasks, with strengths in software engineering, general-purpose task execution, long-horizon reasoning and execution, and cybersecurity.
We also optimize IQuest-Q1 for real-world CLI use, with reliable tool use and robust performance across different agent harnesses.
Methods.
IQuest-Q1 is trained through a multi-stage pipeline (see
Figure 2
) to progressively develop general knowledge, long-context capabilities, and agentic CLI capabilities.
General pre-training combines Stable SplitNorm
[
94
,
68
]
, Muon
[
35
]
, and
μ
\mu
P parameterization
[
75
]
with a two-stage curriculum that increases the coding-data mixture in the second stage. This design improves scaling efficiency while maintaining a wide stability margin between safe and optimal learning rates.
Mid-training then expands the data mixture across domains and formats while progressively extending the context.
Post-training (shown in
Figure 6
) builds diverse CLI
[
46
,
36
]
capabilities through synthesized tasks executed in production environments.
Specifically, SFT establishes basic CLI interaction, while RL enhances capabilities through task-level feedback and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) consolidates complementary model capabilities from diverse frozen experts into a unified model.
Model merging further combines complementary capabilities from expert models trained for different CLIs, while mitigating conflicts among their parameter updates.
Results.
Figure 1
shows the results of IQuest-Q1 on 8 agentic and reasoning benchmarks, highlighting three aspects of its capabilities:
(1)
Advancing coding capability.
IQuest-Q1 demonstrates coding capabilities across benchmarks, including DeepSWE v1.1, CyberGym, and NL2Repo.
(2)
Broad general agentic and reasoning capability.
Beyond coding, IQuest-Q1 demonstrates capabilities on general agentic and reasoning benchmarks, including JobBench, Agents’ Last Exam, and Humanity’s Last Exam.
(3)
Optimized CLI interaction experience.
On our internal IQuest-CLIBench, IQuest-Q1 manifests user-facing CLI interaction capabilities on interactive task.
Beyond benchmark performance, IQuest-Q1 participates in an iterative model-development process built on our internal infrastructure, contributing to the development of its own successors under human supervision.
This human-on-the-loop process provides a practical pathway towards recursive self-improvement, allowing model-generated improvements to accelerate subsequent model iterations.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
•
IQuest-Q1: an open-weight agentic model optimized for CLI capability.
IQuest-Q1 is a sparse MoE model with 320B total parameters, of which 15B are activated per token, combining substantial general-purpose, coding-agent, and CLI interaction capabilities.
We release its model weights to support further research and development in the community.
•
CLI-centric training pipeline.
We build the training pipeline around CLI-based agentic interaction. Pre-training progressively develops the capabilities required for downstream interaction through staged data mixtures. Post-training specializes these capabilities through task and environment synthesis, multi-scaffold RL, and MOPD to consolidate multiple models into a unified model.
•
Model development with human-on-the-loop RSI.
We incorporate IQuest-Q1 into our iterative model-development process, allowing it to evaluate its capabilities and suggest potential improvements through a unified infrastructure interface under human supervision.
This process enables continuous model improvement while shortening the overall development cycle.
Figure 2
:
Training pipeline of IQuest-Q1.
2
Model Architecture
2.1
Overall Architecture
IQuest-Q1 builds on the Transformer architecture
[
66
]
with sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers
[
17
]
and hybrid sliding-window attention (see
Figure 3
). The attention stack interleaves Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)
[
3
]
and Sliding Window Attention (SWA)
[
26
]
. Within each attention module, a query-aware sink token
[
1
]
provides an adaptive destination for excess attention mass. Query–key normalization (QKNorm) stabilizes attention by controlling query and key scales
[
21
]
, and QKNorm Clip is additionally applied to prevent excessively large affine parameters. Partial RoPE applies rotary position embeddings
[
57
]
to only a subset of the dimensions in each attention head. On the feed-forward side, the first Transformer layer replaces sparse MoE routing with a dense MLP to mitigate expert load imbalance in the earliest layer of the model.
To improve scaling effectiveness, IQuest-Q1 adopts Stable SplitNorm to increase effective depth
[
10
,
52
]
. For efficient and stable scaling, we combine the Muon optimizer
[
35
]
with
μ
\mu
P parameterization
[
75
]
, supporting efficient optimization and learning-rate transfer across model sizes.
Stable SplitNorm.
Traditional Pre-Norm
[
72
]
may underutilize the depth of the model. As the unnormalized residual stream accumulates across layers, its variance can grow with depth, reducing the relative contribution of later residual updates
[
58
]

[
94
,
68
]
. We refer to this design as
SplitNorm
, which splits the normalization strategy across Transformer sublayers: the residual stream entering the attention sublayer is normalized, whereas the residual stream entering the feed-forward network (FFN) is kept unnormalized. This design combines the stability benefits of Pre-Norm with the stronger depth utilization associated with Post-Norm, mitigating the underutilization of deeper layers in Pre-Norm architectures. Recursive Multi-token Prediction.
To improve backbone learning through additional future-token supervision, we incorporate two multi-token prediction (MTP)
[

,

[

Scaling Efficiency and Stability
Scaling efficiency.
To evaluate scaling efficiency, we conduct a controlled comparison between IQuest-Q1 and a representative Qwen3-MoE-style design

As shown in

Infrastructure
Data Packing.
Sequence packing reduces padding overhead in language-model training
[
29

. To improve effective token throughput at a fixed sequence length and global batch size, we apply best-fit packing to the globally shuffled data stream using a bounded look-ahead window. The window contains up to
2
​

​

2BS

B
B

S

Long-context training amplifies compute imbalance arising from document-length variation. Packed sequences are therefore reordered across data-parallel replicas to balance computation at micro-batch granularity.
Sink Attention and Context Parallelism.
Context parallelism uses ring-based K/V exchange for full attention
[
34
]
, while sliding-window attention exchanges only the required halo and overlaps these exchanges with computation in both the forward and backward passes. During halo exchange, each rank computes attention over its local K/V, producing outputs for interior queries and partial outputs with associated Log-Sum-Exp (LSE) statistics for boundary queries. Once the halo arrives, the rank computes the complementary contributions for boundary queries and combines the local and halo partial outputs through LSE-based renormalization. This allows boundary queries to make progress before remote K/V becomes available while preserving sliding-window attention semantics. We illustrate the halo exchange schedule and partial output merging
in
Figure 10
in the appendix. Both full and sliding-window attention execution paths fuse learnable sink contributions into attention computation to reduce memory traffic.
Correctness Validation.
To reduce silent errors introduced by model and training changes during RSI, the agent mines semantic invariants from the model’s training setup. These invariants are converted into checks that run during distributed training to detect deviations from single-machine semantics and violations of predefined correctness constraints.

3.3
Mid-Training and Long-Context Extension
3.3.1
Training Curriculum
Mid-training bridges broad pre-training and specialized agent post-training through a curriculum that combines a diverse data mixture, selective token-level supervision, and progressive context extension.
Data Organization.
The mid-training mixture comprises three principal categories: high-quality natural corpora, QA pairs, and agentic trajectories. We organize training data using a chat template adapted for mid-training, retaining a selected subset of special tokens, including those associated with reasoning and tool calls.
Token-Level Loss Masking.
We specify loss masks directly for individual tokens, independently of the role-specific special tokens used to determine supervision in a typical post-training setup. This decouples data formatting from loss computation and allows supervision to be tailored to selected spans within each training example, with finer control than masking entire conversational roles.
Progressive Context Extension.
We extend the maximum training context lengths through 32K, 128K, and 512K tokens, using variable-length sequence packing throughout. The global-attention RoPE base increases from
500,000
500,000

1,000,000
1,000,000

remain fixed.
Optimization across Phases.
The mid-training learning rate follows a single cosine decay across all three context-length phases, with no additional warmup. At phase transitions, we transfer model weights and reinitialize the optimizer state while preserving the learning-rate schedule’s progress.
3.3.2
Agentic Data Construction Guided by Trajectories
Agentic mid-training requires large and diverse trajectory corpora, but suitable trajectories are scarce and concentrated in a limited set of tasks and environments. To expand coverage while preserving realistic interaction patterns, we use selected trajectories as behavioral anchors and pre-training documents to broaden technical and task coverage.
Using these sources, we construct executable, containerized instances from compatible code repositories, following prior work on tasks derived from repositories and trajectory generation at scale
[
85
,
71
]

3.4
Evaluation
We evaluate pre-training and mid-training using two complementary types of evaluations. First, we compute
bits-per-byte (BPB) on held-out agent trajectories
. Lower BPB indicates that the model assigns higher likelihood to behaviors observed in competent agent trajectories, providing a generation-free measure of how well the model captures the trajectory distribution. This metric can provide a fine-grained training signal that complements downstream task-level evaluations.
We further decompose long-horizon agent behavior into
atomic abilities
and evaluate how reliably the model performs each ability. This fine-grained evaluation helps identify specific capability gaps and informs data selection and curriculum design. Together, these two evaluation paradigms provide complementary signals for tracking and improving agentic capabilities during pre-training and mid-training.

4.2
Environment Integrity and Reward Hacking Mitigation
Agentic training environments are vulnerable to reward hacking, where models exploit leaked solutions or weaknesses in task verifiers instead of solving the intended tasks. Such behavior can contaminate SFT data and introduce misleading reward signals during RL. To prevent this, we apply three layers of protection: environment preparation, execution-time checks, and trajectory auditing.
Environment Preparation.
Before collecting trajectories, we prepare task environments to prevent solution leakage. Depending on the task, we clean Git history, remove files that could reveal existing solutions, or create fresh environments containing only the required materials. We also isolate task environments to prevent unintended access to hidden evaluation data or resources from other tasks.
Execution-Time Checks.
During rollouts, we restrict access to external resources and sensitive task files. Depending on the environment, we enforce network restrictions or intercept tool calls before execution. We develop blocking rules from observed hacking behaviors to prevent agents from retrieving existing solutions, upstream code, or hidden evaluation materials. These checks preserve access to legitimate dependencies and task resources. Blocked operations return explicit feedback, allowing agents to continue without the prohibited access.
Trajectory Auditing.
We further audit collected trajectories using rule-based checks and rubric-guided LLM judgments. The audits examine executed commands, tool outputs, and submitted solutions to identify behaviors such as retrieving leaked fixes, accessing hidden tests, or modifying evaluation scripts. Confirmed hacking trajectories are excluded from training, while suspicious cases can be flagged for further review. We also use detected cases to refine our environment restrictions and blocking rules.
Task-Specific Safeguards.
We adapt these safeguards to the needs of each task. For SWE-like tasks, we keep only the Git history up to the base commit and use hooks in Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode to block attempts to retrieve existing solutions. For Terminal-Bench, we remove Git history when it is not needed and check commands before execution when it must be preserved. ProgramBench takes a different approach, building fresh containers with only the compiled oracle and task documentation, without exposing the original repository.

Multi-harness, Multi-version Episodes.
To improve the model’s performance across different agent harnesses and versions, we train a shared policy on trajectories collected from diverse harness configurations, including Claude Code, Codex, and their different versions.
Each episode specifies a task domain, harness and its version, environment, and evaluator.
During training, the policy interacts with different harnesses, observing public instructions, tools, and execution feedback while reference solutions and hidden checks remain isolated.

Rewards and Failure Attribution.
Independent verifiers determine terminal correctness. For long trajectories, auxiliary segment-level rewards are restricted to measurable progress, while penalties address unnecessary computation, constraint violations, and reward hacking. Model-generated diagnoses require evidence from execution records before contributing to these signals. Failures are attributed before optimization: policy-caused errors supply learning signals, environment or harness faults unrelated to policy behavior are masked, and evaluator faults block sample consumption. Token-level updates use recorded rollout probabilities through the existing Token-In, Token-Out (TITO) pipeline. The resulting specialized policies can subsequently be consolidated through MOPD.

4.7
Post-Training Infrastructure
Multi-harness and Multi-version Agent Runtime.
A single policy can be trained on trajectories from multiple harnesses and versions within one run.
Each training instance specifies its scaffold, task environment, and verifier. The runtime executes the corresponding configuration and verifies the task in an isolated sandbox while preserving tool orchestration, context management, and interaction flow. We map different API protocols to a unified policy interface to reduce the difficulty of downstream integrations.
Rollout-training Consistency.
We implement an end-to-end TITO path at the model-serving boundary. Specifically, we apply a session-level prefix tree to retain token histories shared across turns and branches.
A request then combines its environment observations with a recorded token prefix. The corresponding response is returned in the structured format expected by the scaffold. Finally, we retain trajectories paired with rewards and token-level masks from the tree at the end of the sequence.
Asynchronous Distillation and Teacher Execution.
We implement MOPD in a fully asynchronous training system. We apply periodic synchronization of student parameters and explicit control of sample staleness, limiting the policy lag introduced by asynchronous execution. We execute teacher forward passes with the training engine on trajectories generated online by the student, producing token-level teacher log probabilities.
We use the same execution path for teacher evaluation and student log-probability computation to reduce discrepancies caused by the training engine.
This framework supports independently configured teachers through a common scheduling interface. Teachers reuse the same execution resources through weight switching. We store teacher weights in distributed storage and load them on demand, with only the shards required by the active teacher placed in GPU memory.
Weights of the next teacher are prefetched during the current forward pass with overlapping computation. This design supports additional teachers without a proportional increase in resident GPU replicas.

5.4
Results
Table 2
shows the results under the reported evaluation configurations. We highlight representative results and remaining gaps below.
Coding and Software Engineering.
IQuest-Q1 demonstrates a broad range of repository-level coding capabilities, including bug fixing and feature addition, achieving scores of 57.5 on SWE-Bench Pro and 64.6 on DeepSWE v1.1.
It also handles repository generation from natural language across NL2Repo-Bench (63.0) and PaperBench (86.0), covering general programming and research code reproduction.
Terminal-Bench and SkillsBench further evaluate long-horizon terminal workflows and skill-driven coding. On our internal IQuest-CLIBench, IQuest-Q1 further demonstrates practical CLI interaction capabilities.
General Capabilities.
IQuest-Q1 scores 75.0 on Toolathlon-Verified, 52.7 on AutomationBench, and 77.1 on Claw-Eval, reflecting its capabilities in tool use and multi-step task execution. On BrowseComp and WideSearch, it reaches 85.5 and 81.8, respectively, demonstrating information-seeking capabilities across the two search settings. It also records 55.7 on JobBench and 50.9 on APEX-Agents 1.1, covering task execution in professional workflows. Beyond agentic interaction, scores of 93.3 on GPQA Diamond and 93.0 on IMOAnswerBench-Verified reflect its scientific and mathematical reasoning capabilities. Expert-level reasoning remains challenging: HLE scores of 39.2 without tools and 55.7 with tools indicate room for improvement in both settings.
6
Capabilities with CLI Agents
Figure 7
:
Representative interactive frontend applications generated by IQuest-Q1 from natural-language specifications, covering game worlds, scene editing, and scientific exploration.
6.1
Interactive Frontend Generation
IQuest-Q1 generates diverse interactive frontend applications from user queries, combining visual design, scene construction, and interaction logic in browser-runnable HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. These tasks showcase its CLI coding capabilities by turning implementations into interactive artifacts.
We provide examples (see
Figure 7
) from domains including games, creative tools, and scientific visualization. For example, the underwater sandbox combines an explorable world with building and mining, while the sunset racing game couples vehicle control with camera movement and race-state feedback. The garden editor links flower parameters and planting actions to a 3D scene. Together, they suggest how IQuest-Q1 coordinates rendering, user input, and application state to create interactive web experiences with distinct visual styles.
6.2
Iterative Development under Human Supervision
We illustrate a model development iteration in which an agent built on IQuest-Q1 identifies a capability gap, implements a solution, and evaluates the model under human supervision and intervention.
The iteration targets adaptation to different scaffolds and tool-call schemas. While the model handles familiar schemas well, it can fail on unfamiliar ones, producing 35 tool-call errors in one long-horizon task due to mismatched tool names and parameters.
Trace Tool-call Failures and Identify Data Inconsistencies.
The agent traces the failures across 6,054 tool calls and finds that the training data is heavily biased toward a single tool-call schema, with some records containing mismatches between tool definitions and call parameters due to preprocessing. It proposes cleaning these inconsistent records and augmenting the training data with diverse tool-call schemas.
Human experts review the diagnosis and proposed intervention before approving the training run.
Implement Mixed-schema Data Augmentation and Model Training.
The agent implements the data cleaning and augmentation pipeline and prepares the experiment configuration. The training run uses 2.35B tokens and 938.7 GPU hours. The resulting model checkpoint is evaluated on held-out schemas and familiar schemas, while checking for performance regressions.
This iteration demonstrates the potential of iterative model development with IQuest-Q1, while also highlighting the importance of human supervision.
The agent drives failure analysis, intervention design, implementation, and evaluation, with human experts reviewing key decisions and controlling costly experiments and changes carried forward to subsequent iterations.
6.3
Cyber Security
Beyond general software engineering tasks, we further evaluate IQuest-Q1 on defensive cybersecurity tasks, where understanding and validating vulnerabilities are essential for improving software security. IQuest-Q1 achieves a score of 84.5 on CyberGym
[
67
]
, a benchmark that evaluates the ability to reproduce and validate real-world vulnerabilities in large open-source codebases, providing evidence to support vulnerability diagnosis and remediation.
We further assess the practical utility of these capabilities in real-world security workflows. During a three-day deployment, human cyber security experts, assisted by IQuest-Q1, produced 30 vulnerability reports. All reports were independently validated by fellow security experts, and findings affecting open-source projects were responsibly disclosed to their respective maintainers.
The participating experts reported that IQuest-Q1 provided substantial support for their defensive security work, particularly in understanding and validating security issues.
Limitations
•
Text-only input. IQuest-Q1 has no native image, audio, or video input capability.
•
Output reliability. Generated explanations and code may be incorrect. Code changes should be reviewed or verified with task-appropriate tests.
•
Tool integration. Tool calls use the IQuest-specific format in the chat template. Structured tool execution and reasoning extraction require compatible serving parsers and an agent harness.
•
Challenges in Real-World CLI Tasks. Real-world CLI tasks often require iterative debugging and verification. IQuest-Q1 may overlook constraints, repeat failed attempts, or leave issues unresolved, necessitating human review and supervision.
•
Ongoing development. IQuest-Q1 still has limitations in its capabilities and reliability, and we will continue to advance its capabilities. Furthermore, we release the model weights, deployment configurations, and agent-integration instructions to facilitate further research and continued development in the community.
Conclusion
We present IQuest-Q1, an open-source agentic foundation model with broad CLI capabilities. We train IQuest-Q1 through a multi-stage pipeline to progressively develop general knowledge, long-context capabilities, and agentic CLI capabilities. IQuest-Q1 demonstrates capabilities on coding, general agentic tasks, and reasoning-heavy tasks.
Furthermore, IQuest-Q1 participates in our internal iterative model-development loop,
providing a foundation for continuing model development.

article.headline: IQuest-Q1：面向CLI的开源MoE代理模型
article.lede: IQuest研究发布320B总参数、15B激活的稀疏MoE模型IQuest-Q1，面向命令行代理任务并开源权重。
article.problem: LLM代理通过迭代推理、行动与环境交互执行任务，而命令行界面（CLI）是模型使用工具、访问文件与执行代码的通用入口。要让代理在真实软件工程、长程任务与网络安全等场景中可靠工作，需要更强的CLI能力。但面向CLI的代理基础模型仍缺少系统化的训练与开源方案。
article.method: IQuest-Q1采用三阶段训练流程。预训练结合Stable SplitNorm、Muon与μP，并用两阶段课程在第二阶段提高代码数据比例；中训练扩展数据混合并逐步将上下文扩展到512K token。后训练以SFT、领域专用RL和多教师同策略蒸馏（MOPD）整合多脚手架信号，再做模型合并。
article.results: 模型为320B总参数、15B激活的稀疏MoE，预训练与中训练共使用29T tokens；在相同训练数据下，其缩放效率为Qwen3-MoE式设计的1.93倍。评测中SWE-Bench Pro 57.5、DeepSWE v1.1 64.6、Terminal-Bench 2.1 83.2、CyberGym 84.5、HLE无工具39.2与带工具55.7、GPQA Diamond 93.3，内部IQuest-CLIBench为53.7；外推临界模型规模约为572B激活参数/12T总参数。
article.why_it_matters: 开源权重与面向CLI的代理训练流程可降低社区构建命令行代理的门槛，并支持软件工程、长程任务与防御性网络安全等应用研究。
article.limitations: 局限包括仅支持文本输入、工具调用依赖IQuest专用格式与兼容解析器，真实CLI任务仍可能忽略约束或重复失败，需要人工复核。此外IQuest-CLIBench为内部专有基准且部分基线分数来自自测，跨模型比较需谨慎。

Semantically Steerable Image Tokenization
Danilo de Goede
Affiliation:
QUVA Lab, University of Amsterdam
Affiliation:
VIS Lab, University of Amsterdam
Mohammad Mahdi Derakhshani
Affiliation:
VIS Lab, University of Amsterdam
Yuki M. Asano
Affiliation:
Fundamental AI Lab, University of Technology Nuremberg
{d.degoede,m.m.derakhshani,c.g.m.snoek}@uva.nl, yuki.asano@utn.de
Cees G. M. Snoek
Affiliation:
QUVA Lab, University of Amsterdam
Affiliation:
VIS Lab, University of Amsterdam
Abstract
Adaptive image tokenizers compress an image into a variable number of tokens matched to its complexity, and recent work makes this allocation controllable: conditioned on a target reconstruction error, the tokenizer itself decides how many tokens an image needs.
However, the fidelity measure guiding this allocation shapes which aspects of the image are preserved under compression.
The pixel-wise error used in prior work is blind to the spatial structure that carries an image’s meaning, and under heavy compression such tokenizers are prone to abruptly discarding tokens that encode essential content.
We introduce GIST (
G
uided
I
mage
S
emantic
T
okenizer), an adaptive tokenizer that can be steered toward a requested
semantic
fidelity.
Its token allocation is jointly controlled by pixel-level and semantic target errors, with semantic error measured in the feature space of a frozen DINOv3 encoder.
This joint control enables
semantic protection
: with the semantic target fixed at zero, the reconstruction target can be relaxed to discard pixel detail while preserving what the image depicts.
In a controlled comparison on ImageNet-100, GIST outperforms its pixel-controlled counterpart KARL at every token count, with up to
30
%
30\%
lower LPIPS and
37
%
37\%
lower DreamSim.
On average, lowering its semantic target reduces LPIPS
2
×
2\times
faster per token than lowering the reconstruction target, and up to
5
×
5\times
in the low-token regime.
Semantic fidelity is thus an effective control signal for adaptive tokenization: it lets a tokenizer see, and so preserve, what an image depicts.
“Humans can recognize the gist of a novel image in a single glance,
independent of its complexity.”
—
Oliva and Torralba (2006)
1
Introduction
The visual world is inherently heterogeneous: some scenes depict a single object against a plain background, while others capture complex environments dense with detail.
Yet the image tokenizers underpinning modern generative models
(
Esser et al., 2021
;
Rombach et al., 2022
;
Chang et al., 2022
)
are blind to this difference — they allocate the same number of tokens to every image, regardless of its content.
This allocation is wasteful: tokenizers exist to compress images into compact latent sequences over which generative modeling becomes tractable, and the length of this sequence directly governs training and inference cost.
A growing line of work therefore makes the token count adaptive
(
Duggal et al., 2025b
;
Yan et al., 2025
;
Miwa et al., 2025
;
Bachmann et al., 2025
)
.
These tokenizers can encode an image into a variable number of tokens, but leave the choice of token count to a trial-and-error search at inference.
Ideally, the user would instead specify how faithful the encoding should be and let the tokenizer itself determine the token count.
KARL by
Duggal et al. (2025a)
realizes exactly this: conditioned on the image and a target reconstruction error, it predicts the required token count in a single forward pass and halts the remaining tokens.
However, what the tokenizer prioritizes preserving depends on how fidelity is measured.
KARL measures fidelity with a pixel-wise reconstruction error that treats pixels independently and is blind to the spatial structure and co-dependence that carry an image’s meaning.
An encoding can therefore meet the pixel target yet fail to preserve what the image depicts.
For example, a small bird against an open sky can become an unrecognizable blob of similar colors yet contribute little to the overall pixel error.
Indeed, we experimentally observe that under heavy token compression, KARL is prone to abruptly halting tokens that encode essential image content.
We introduce GIST (
G
uided
I
mage
S
emantic
T
okenizer), an adaptive image tokenizer that can be steered toward a requested
semantic
fidelity.
Its token allocation is jointly controlled by a reconstruction target error
ϵ
rec
\epsilon_{\mathrm{rec}}
and a semantic target error
ϵ
sem
\epsilon_{\mathrm{sem}}
, with semantic error measured in the feature space of a frozen DINOv3 encoder
(
Siméoni et al., 2026
)
.
These targets allow pixel-level and semantic fidelity to be specified independently: lowering
ϵ
rec
\epsilon_{\mathrm{rec}}
demands tokens that reproduce the image’s exact pixels, while lowering
ϵ
sem
\epsilon_{\mathrm{sem}}
demands tokens that preserve what the image depicts.
As illustrated in
Figure
1
, this two-dimensional control unlocks a new capability we call
semantic protection
: fixing the semantic target error at zero turns it into a guardrail under which the reconstruction target can be relaxed far more aggressively.
The encoder then discards tokens encoding redundant pixel detail while retaining those needed to preserve the image’s semantic content, as captured in DINOv3 feature space.
Figure 1:
Semantic control unlocks semantic protection.
(
Left
) GIST can be steered toward a requested semantic fidelity in DINOv3 feature space, as illustrated here with a red circle (top) and a hummingbird (bottom).
Raising the requested fidelity steers the encoding from little more than the image’s color distribution to a reconstruction that preserves what the image depicts.
(
Right
) Requesting full semantic fidelity turns this control into a guardrail: without it, compression into fewer tokens disintegrates the butterfly; with it, the subject remains recognizable down to 16 tokens.
We validate GIST on ImageNet-100 against KARL, with all models trained from scratch under identical conditions.
GIST Pareto-improves reconstruction quality at every number of active tokens, with up to
30
%
30\%
lower LPIPS and
37
%
37\%
lower DreamSim.
We further find that lowering the semantic target is more token-efficient than lowering the reconstruction target.
Per token, it reduces LPIPS
2
×
2\times
faster on average, and up to
5
×
5\times
in the low-token regime.
We find that these gains do not come from DINOv3 conditioning alone.
A variant with just the semantic target merely matches the baseline on reconstruction, yet its tokens are the most semantically informative of all models we train.
This suggests a division of labor.
Conditioning on DINOv3 feature error structures the latent space so that token complexity reflects the
meaning
of an image rather than only its pixel-level appearance.
Semantic protection converts this structure into reconstruction gains.
The takeaway is simple: an adaptive tokenizer can only preserve what its fidelity measure can see, and a semantic measure lets it see what the image depicts.
2
Related Work
Image Tokenization.
Image tokenizers compress images into compact latent representations over which generative models can be efficiently trained.
Modeling a distribution directly in pixel space is difficult due to its high dimensionality, much of which encodes perceptually irrelevant detail.
Tokenizers address this by mapping images to a lower-dimensional latent space that retains only the information necessary for faithful reconstruction.
Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
(
Kingma and Welling, 2014
)
learn such representations as continuous latents and form the basis of latent diffusion models
(
Rombach et al., 2022
)
.
VQ-VAE
(
van den Oord et al., 2017
;
Razavi et al., 2019
)
and VQGAN
(
Esser et al., 2021
)
instead apply vector quantization to produce discrete-valued tokens and have become the de facto tokenizers for masked
(
Chang et al., 2022
)
and autoregressive
(
Esser et al., 2021
;
Tian et al., 2024
;
Sun et al., 2024
)
image generation.
All of these tokenizers, however, share one structural constraint: the latent is a 2D grid whose size is fixed by the image resolution.
1D and Adaptive Tokenization.
TiTok
(
Yu et al., 2024
)
departs from the 2D grid: a ViT encoder distills the image into a short 1D sequence of register tokens
(
Darcet et al., 2024
)
.
The sequence length, however, is still fixed at training time, independent of image content.
Subsequent work makes the length adaptive: ALIT
(
Duggal et al., 2025b
)
recurrently grows the 1D sequence, while ElasticTok
(
Yan et al., 2025
)
, One-D-Piece
(
Miwa et al., 2025
)
, FlexTok
(
Bachmann et al., 2025
)
, and SMAP
(
Li et al., 2026
)
train with tail-token dropout
(
Rippel et al., 2014
)
so that any prefix of the ordered, coarse-to-fine token sequence remains decodable.
These methods make variable-length representations possible, but leave the choice of length to a search at inference: the user or the method itself must encode the image at several budgets and keep the shortest that suffices.
CAT
(
Shen et al., 2025
)
sidesteps this search by scoring image complexity with an LLM and routing each image to one of three grid resolutions, yet the budget is set by an external predictor, at coarse granularity, and cannot be conditioned on a requested fidelity.
KARL
(
Duggal et al., 2025a
)
instead makes the tokenizer itself decide: conditioned on the image and a target reconstruction quality, it predicts the required token count in a single forward pass and halts the remaining tokens.
GIST inherits KARL’s single-pass, quality-conditioned design but extends the notion of quality itself: where KARL targets pixel-space reconstruction error alone, GIST adds a second, semantic target, which we find improves token efficiency in the low-token regime.
Semantic Alignment of Tokenizers.
A separate line of work distills the semantic knowledge of pretrained vision encoders into tokenizers.
An influential precursor is REPA
(
Yu et al., 2025
)
, which aligns intermediate features of a diffusion transformer with DINOv2
(
Oquab et al., 2024
)
features and accelerates convergence by more than an order of magnitude.
VA-VAE
(
Yao et al., 2025
)
moves the alignment from the generator into the tokenizer: a foundation-model alignment loss structures the VAE’s latent space during training, which preserves reconstruction quality while making the latents far easier for diffusion transformers to model
(
Qu et al., 2026
, see also)
.
VFMTok
(
Zheng et al., 2025
)
and RAE
(
Zheng et al., 2026
)
take this idea further by building the tokenizer directly on frozen foundation model features.
Adaptive-length tokenizers have adopted this alignment only in the decoder: FlexTok and Semanticist
(
Wen et al., 2025
)
train their diffusion decoders with a REPA loss, and ReTok
(
Fu et al., 2026
)
decays a decoder-side alignment loss along its ordered token sequence.
In all of these methods, however, semantic alignment is a fixed training-time bias: it shapes what the model encodes and improves output quality at a given token count, but plays no role in deciding how many tokens an image receives.
GIST instead makes semantics an explicit control signal: the tokenizer is conditioned on a target quality in DINOv3
(
Siméoni et al., 2026
)
feature space, so the token count is steered by the requested semantic fidelity rather than by pixel fidelity alone.
DINOv3 thus serves purely to
measure
semantic fidelity for this conditioning — its features never supervise the tokens themselves, unlike the alignment approaches above.
3
Method
GIST builds on KARL
(
Duggal et al., 2025a
)
, a single-pass adaptive 1D tokenizer that allocates a variable number of tokens per image based on a single reconstruction target error.
We introduce a second conditioning signal: a semantic target error, measured in the feature space of a frozen DINOv3 encoder
(
Siméoni et al., 2026

.
This expands KARL’s one-dimensional fidelity control into a two-dimensional space in which pixel-level and semantic fidelity can be targeted independently.

Experiments
In this section, we explore how modeling an image tokenizer’s complexity along a semantic axis affects tokenizer behavior and performance.
We evaluate GIST against KARL in terms of reconstruction quality, and visually compare how the reconstruction and semantic targets affect the image reconstructions for both methods.
Subsequently, we study the role of the semantic control in GIST.
4.1
Setup
Model Variants.
We consider two variants of our method:
1.
GIST, which is conditioned on both a reconstruction and a semantic target error, and
2.

only

GIST decomposes complexity into two complementary axes and lets us control each independently, whereas GIST-1 replaces the reconstruction target with the semantic one and lets us isolate their individual behavior.

We evaluate GIST against KARL as our primary baseline.
We note a slight performance discrepancy between the authors’ published checkpoint and the model produced by their released training code.
To ensure a controlled comparison that isolates the effect of our contributions, all evaluated models are trained from scratch under identical conditions using the official, unmodified KARL training script.

5
Conclusion
We have presented GIST, an adaptive image tokenizer that can be steered toward a requested
semantic
fidelity.
Its token allocation is jointly controlled by a pixel-wise reconstruction target and a semantic target in DINOv3 feature space, allowing pixel-level and semantic fidelity to be specified independently.
Our experiments point to a division of labor between the two roles the semantic target plays.
During training, the DINOv3 target structures the latent space so that token complexity reflects the meaning of an image rather than only its pixel-level appearance.
At inference, it acts as a guardrail: with
ϵ
sem
\epsilon_{\mathrm{sem}}
fixed at zero, the reconstruction target can be relaxed freely while the encoder protects the tokens indispensable to the image’s semantic identity.
Under this guardrail, GIST Pareto-improves reconstruction quality over KARL
†
at every token count, and its tokens themselves become more semantically informative.
Our work also has its limitations.
First, our evaluation is deliberately controlled rather than competitive: all models are trained from scratch on ImageNet-100 over a pretrained VQGAN base.
Accordingly, we claim no state of the art.
The evidence supports the narrower point that semantic fidelity is an effective control signal for adaptive tokenization.
Second, the same principle that motivates GIST also bounds it: a tokenizer can only preserve what its fidelity measure can see, and we instantiate that measure with a single global feature, the DINOv3 CLS token.
For images whose meaning is distributed across many regions, such as a document page or a busy scene in which several objects matter equally, one global summary may under-specify what to protect.
Patch-level semantic targets are a natural extension.
More broadly, we see the DINOv3 target as one instance of a general recipe: any measure of what matters can serve as a conditioning target.
Because the measure only conditions the tokenizer and is never differentiated through, it need not even be differentiable.
A different vision encoder, a text encoder, or a task-specific score such as detection or OCR accuracy could take its place.
In this way, GIST can be tailored to the kind of information its tokens should preserve.
The tokens themselves also point beyond reconstruction.
Semantic alignment is known to ease generative training
(
Yu et al., 2025
;
Yao et al., 2025
)
, and we suspect GIST’s tokens offer a favorable interface for generative models trained on top of them.
Whether semantic steerability carries over to generation is a question we leave open for future work.
Humans recognize the gist of a novel image in a single glance, independent of its complexity; we hope GIST is a step toward tokenizers that see images the same way.

Two-Stage Training
We train GIST in two sequential training stages that share the overall objective, but differ in the space in which
ℒ
rec

•
Stage 1 – Latent Distillation Pre-Training:
We distill a pretrained, frozen VQGAN

The GIST decoder predicts a VQGAN codebook distribution at every 2D grid position.
Subsequently,

This avoids the costly pixel decoding during this pre-training stage.
•
Stage 2 – Pixel-Space Finetuning:
We finetune GIST jointly with the VQGAN to reconstruct high-fidelity images in pixel space.
To achieve this, we pass the output of the GIST decoder into the VQGAN decoder to reconstruct the original image in pixel space.

The discrepancy can originate on either

the

training side

We interpret these results as follows.
All three models share the same architecture, the same VQGAN base, and the same training recipe; they differ only in the target errors that condition the encoder.
Varying
T
T

What semantic conditioning changes is how the tokenizer models token complexity.
KARL
†
models complexity along a single reconstructive axis: it uses a pixel-wise error target to decide how many tokens to halt and which ones.
GIST-1 replaces this axis with a semantic one, and GIST models complexity along both.
These axes determine how a model halts tokens as its targets are relaxed.
Under a purely reconstructive axis, tokens are halted by pixel-level redundancy alone, which is blind to the spatial structure that carries an image’s meaning.
Under both axes, the semantic target can instead act as a guardrail that protects the image’s semantic identity as
ϵ
rec
\epsilon_{\mathrm{rec}}
is relaxed (

The gains of GIST under varying targets therefore stem from how conditioning on these targets organizes the latent space along complementary axes of complexity, rather than from base tokenizer capacity.

Appendix I
kNN Classification under Mean and Max Pooling
We measure the semantic informativeness of the latent tokens with a kNN classifier (
k
=
20
k{=}20
) on ImageNet-100, using the training set as gallery and the validation set as queries.
Since the number of active tokens varies per image, we pool the active register tokens of each image into a single vector.
In the main paper, we use mean pooling (
Figure
6(a)
).
In this appendix, we additionally report max pooling.
The two poolings summarize the tokens differently.
Mean pooling averages over all active tokens, so every token contributes equally to the representation.
Tokens that carry semantic information add to the class signal, whereas tokens that carry little semantic information dilute it.
Max pooling instead retains, for each feature dimension, the largest activation across the active tokens.
A token thus affects the representation only in the dimensions where it exceeds all other tokens.
Max pooling is therefore less sensitive than mean pooling to the addition of tokens that carry little semantic information.
A higher accuracy under max pooling than under mean pooling hence suggests that some tokens dilute the semantic information carried by the others.
In

Figure

We make two observations.
First, the ordering of the three methods is unchanged under max pooling.
GIST-1 performs best, followed by GIST and KARL
†
, at any number of active tokens.
The conclusions of the main paper therefore do not depend on the choice of pooling.
Second, the relation between the two poolings differs across methods.
For GIST-1, mean pooling yields a higher accuracy than max pooling, and accuracy increases approximately linearly with the number of active tokens.
For GIST and KARL
†
, we observe the opposite.
Max pooling yields a slightly higher accuracy than mean pooling, and accuracy remains approximately constant as the number of active tokens increases.
This difference corresponds to the target varied for each method.

article.headline: 自适应分词器学会按语义保真度分配 token
article.lede: GIST 在像素重建目标之外加入 DINOv3 特征空间的语义目标，让分词器按请求的语义保真度自行决定 token 数量
article.problem: 此前的自适应分词器 KARL 以像素级 L1 重建误差作为唯一控制信号，用户给定目标误差，它单次前向就预测所需 token 数并停掉其余 token。但像素误差逐像素独立计算，对承载图像含义的空间结构与像素间依赖不敏感：一片开阔天空下的小鸟可以被压成同色模糊块，却几乎不增加像素误差。作者观察到，在重度压缩下，KARL 容易突然停掉编码关键内容的 token。
article.method: GIST 沿用 KARL 的单次前向、按质量条件化的设计，但把一维保真度控制扩成二维：除重建目标误差 ε_rec 外，再加入一个语义目标误差 ε_sem，后者定义为输入图像与其重建在冻结 DINOv3-L/16 的 post-LayerNorm CLS 特征之间的均方误差。两个连续目标被映射到最近的上界 bin，再经可学习字典变成目标嵌入，与 patch 嵌入、register token 一起送入编码器，由 halting MLP 预测每个 token 的停止概率。训练沿用双前向流程：第一遍以随机预算 T∼U(16,256) 追求完美重建，并测出实际达到的 (ε_rec*, ε_sem*)；第二遍以该误差为条件并多给 ΔT 个 token，用 halting 损失教模型停掉冗余 token。语义目标只作为条件信号，梯度不穿过 DINOv3。
article.results: 在 ImageNet-100 上，所有模型都用官方未修改的 KARL 训练脚本从零训练、条件一致；GIST 在每一个 token 数量上都优于对照基线 KARL†，LPIPS 最多低 30%，DreamSim 最多低 37%。在 ε_rec 为 0.05/0.10/0.16 时，GIST 分别用 242/141/67 个 token，对应 LPIPS 0.15/0.22/0.29，而 KARL† 用 236/124/42 个 token，LPIPS 为 0.16/0.30/0.44。降低语义目标比降低重建目标更省 token：平均每增加一个 token 降低 LPIPS 的速度快 2 倍，在低 token 区间最多快 5 倍。kNN 分类（k=20）在 64/128/192 token 时，KARL† 为 21.9/23.3/24.2，GIST 为 28.0/28.4/28.6，仅用语义条件的 GIST-1 最高，为 33.9/37.0/39.0。用 ImageNet-100 检查点零样本迁移到 MS COCO，LPIPS 最多低 27%、DreamSim 最多低 28%。完整训练约需 470 H100 GPU 小时。
article.why_it_matters: 这项工作给出的判断很直接：自适应分词器只能保住它的保真度度量能看见的东西，把语义度量显式作为条件，token 预算就花在图像“画的是什么”上，而不是冗余像素细节上。由于该度量只参与条件化、不参与求导，任何衡量“什么重要”的指标（其他视觉编码器、文本编码器、检测或 OCR 精度）原则上都能替换进来。
article.limitations: 作者明确说明这是受控比较，而非与最先进方法竞争：模型全部在 ImageNet-100 上从零训练，基于预训练 VQGAN，因此不主张达到 SOTA；而且在固定输入 token 预算、只变预算不变目标时，GIST、GIST-1 与 KARL† 表现持平，说明增益来自目标如何组织潜空间，而非分词器基础容量。语义度量只用单个全局 DINOv3 CLS token，对含义分散在多个区域的图像（如文档页或多个同等重要物体的拥挤场景）可能欠指定；语义可控性是否能迁移到生成模型，作者留作未解问题。
article.figure_caption_zh: 左：KARL 只用像素级 L1 重建目标 ε_rec 控制分词器，编码像素忠实但对语义“失明”；右：GIST 保留该目标并加入 DINOv3 CLS 特征误差目标 ε_sem，迫使 token 保住图像所描绘的内容，从而可丢弃冗余像素细节。

, that uses a simple supervised learning objective with advantage conditioning while outperforming prior RL methods through effective conditional training and contrastive diffusion guidance during sampling.
Left:

Reinforcement Learning via Advantage Guidance
Zhiyuan Zhou
Sergey Levine
Affiliation:
UC Berkeley
Abstract
Reinforcement learning (RL) holds the promise of learning a policy that can outperform what is shown in the data. However, in practice, such systems suffer from instability and hyperparameter sensitivity. In contrast, supervised learning provides a stable and scalable training objective, but is fundamentally limited by the quality of the demonstrated behavior. In this paper, we ask whether we can perform policy optimization with something as simple and stable as supervised learning but as performant as RL. Unfortunately, naïvely training the policy with supervised learning and conditioning on future rewards or advantages typically underperform dedicated RL methods. We introduce a new policy extraction method,
Advantage Guidance
, that retains the simple supervised learning structure with advantage conditioning while outperforming prior RL methods through effective conditional training and contrastive diffusion guidance during sampling. We show that Advantage Guidance can significantly improve a model’s ability to respond to conditional advantage signals, and the contrastive guidance during sampling can use the learned advantage-conditioned policy to target the KL-regularized optimal policy. Empirically, we find that Advantage Guidance significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art RL methods on 26 long-horizon, sparse reward tasks across datasets with varying degrees of optimality.
Code:
github.com/zhouzypaul/advantage-guidance
1
Introduction
Reinforcement learning (RL) holds the promise of improving policy performance beyond what is shown in the data, and can in theory outperform imitation learning under suitable conditions
[
46
,
30
]
.
However, RL algorithms suffer from lots of instability and hyperparameter sensitivity issues in practice
[
49
,
17
,
22
]
, especially over off-policy or offline data.
Imitation learning, on the other hand, has been shown to be stable and scalable for policy training with modern generative modeling techniques like diffusion and flow matching.
This raises the question:
can we perform policy training with something as simple and stable as imitation learning, but as performant as RL?
To achieve the stability of imitation learning, one might be tempted to directly apply the supervised-learning loss function, training the policy to maximize the likelihood of actions seen in the data.
Previous works have explored accomplishing this with conditional, filtered, or weighted supervised learning
[
13
]
.
One set of methods, which we will refer to as
advantage-conditioned methods
[
28
,
2
,
18
,
42
]
, resorts to training a policy conditioned on advantage values, which estimate how “good” actions are.
During inference, the policy is queried with a high advantage to generate “good” actions.
Unfortunately, such naïve advantage-conditioned policies typically underperform dedicated RL methods (see
Figure
1
).
This is in part because advantage-conditioning does not generally result in a policy that always favors actions with higher advantages as RL policies do: the resulting policy is restricted to the queried advantage level, and this restricts the degree of policy improvement.
Moreover, we find it difficult to train a policy to respond to advantage conditioning in the first place: the policy often cannot match the requested advantage (see
Figure
1
), and can ignore the conditioning altogether and revert to unconditional imitation.
In this work, our goal is to train a policy with the simple and stable supervised learning objective conditional on continuous advantage estimates, while enabling the policy to generate actions that maximize advantage.
To accomplish this, we first derive a diffusion guidance formulation we call
contrastive guidance
for sampling at test time, which can target actions that maximize the advantage under a KL behavior constraint.
Then, to effectively train a flow-matching conditional policy that responds to the conditional values, we re-parameterize the conditional policy as a residual flow on top of a reference unconditional flow field.
We also propose an
action imagination
scheme: we use “imagined actions” sampled from the unconditional policy, and their advantage estimates, to train the advantage-conditioned policy under a broader action distribution for each state.
The resulting algorithm,
Advantage Guidance
, significantly improves the policy’s ability to respond to advantage inputs, and can target the KL-regularized optimal policy during sampling. Across
26
26
long-horizon, sparse reward tasks with both play-style and demonstration datasets in the offline RL setting, Advantage Guidance outperforms prior strong RL algorithms.
2
Related Work
Offline RL and policy extraction.
Offline RL aims to learn policies that outperform the behavior represented in a fixed dataset.
Prior works focus on learning value functions that mitigate erroneous extrapolation
[
3
,
19
,
27
,
29
,
54
]
, as well as policy extraction from that value function
[
5
,
16
,
20
,
34
,
39
,
47
,
53
]
.
However, many prior policy extraction methods can be difficult to apply in practice due to instability and hyperparameter sensitivity.
Another line of work, which closely relates to ours, circumvents this instability by converting the policy training objective to an imitation learning loss via advantage, reward, or return conditioning
[
28
,
6
,
13
,
45
]
, data filtering
[
6
,
52
,
9
]
, and loss weighting
[
39
,
41
,
35
]
.
We specifically study advantage conditioning, which avoids instability of loss-weighting, uses the full dataset for generalization, and has lower variance than return conditioning.
Existing advantage conditioning methods condition on continuous values
[
28
,
18
,
42
]
or binarized labels
[
2
,
48
]
, and during inference query with a fixed high advantage value, which may fall outside the training distribution, or learn an extra model to choose a high in-support query
[
28
,
18
]
.
In contrast, our method uses a form of contrastive diffusion guidance to maximize advantage without risking out-of-support advantage queries or needing additional models.
In addition, we find that previous methods struggle to respond to advantage inputs, and we introduce residual parameterization and action imagination training schemes to improve the policy’s responsiveness to advantages.
Flow and diffusion policies for RL.
Diffusion and flow matching have been widely studied for parameterizing the policy in RL
[
43
,
11

Using these iterative denoising methods is challenging because leveraging the action gradient requires backpropagating through a multi-step denoising process
[
51
,
21
,
12
,
57
,
50
,
33

[
58
,
38

.
Previous works avoid this unstable backpropagation process by treating each denoising step as an action in the environment
[
4
,
43

[
38
,
7
,
24

Another line of work avoids backpropagation entirely, instead directly guiding the iterative sampling process using critic gradient

or classifier-free guidance (CFG)

Like the latter, our approach avoids critic gradients, which are difficult to estimate for high-dimensional or partially noised actions.
Most similar to our work is CFGRL

15

Our approach instead trains on the entire dataset conditioned on continuous advantage values, and uses a form of contrastive guidance during sampling.
Empirically, we find that CFGRL usually underperforms in practice because its binary filtering criterion discards information on action quality.

Experiments
We conduct experiments to analyze the empirical effectiveness of Advantage Guidance on a range of long-horizon, sparse reward manipulation tasks.
Concretely, we study the following research questions:
(1)
How well does Advantage Guidance perform compared to prior RL methods on datasets with varying degrees of optimality?
(2)
Do residual parameterization and action imagination improve advantage alignment and policy performance?
(3)
Does contrastive guidance improve policy performance compared to CFG or no guidance?
Additionally, we conduct further ablation experiments in
Section
A.2
. All detailed results are documented in
Section
A.10
.

We evaluate all methods in the offline RL setting with

OGBench offers a suite of long-horizon challenging manipulation tasks, and OCBench is a recently proposed extension of OGBench that provides a more realistic action distribution meant to emulate the statistical properties of real-world human demonstrations.
In particular, the two benchmarks differ substantially in their offline dataset composition.
OGBench is a standard offline RL benchmark with
play-style
datasets generated by scripted behaviors pursuing random goals, often yielding highly suboptimal trajectories for the task objective.
OCBench offers
demonstration-based
datasets, consisting of trajectories generated by near-expert policies with high success rates on the task objective.
Compared to play-style datasets, these demonstrations cover narrower states and predominantly near-optimal actions, making it more challenging for offline RL because extrapolation errors are harder to avoid.
However, such data more closely resembles real-world robotics datasets, and OCBench’s design to emulate human demonstration statistics makes it particularly relevant.

8
Discussions
We demonstrated in this paper that Advantage Guidance can outperform more complex RL methods with a simple supervised learning objective with advantage conditioning and contrastive diffusion guidance during inference. Our work serves as a step towards simple, stable, yet performant off-policy RL algorithms. There are several promising directions for future research. First, our implementation uses a straightforward advantage estimate. While we find this to be empirically effective, a natural next step is to explore whether more intricate advantage estimates improve policy performance, and how policy extraction can be robust in case of noisy advantage estimates. Second, our approach uses contrastive guidance to maximize advantage during inference time, but too large a guidance weight usually lead to a decline in performance. Developing techniques to stably utilize larger guidance weights can further improve the performance of Advantage Guidance. Finally, it would be interesting to explore Advantage Guidance in (offline-to-)online RL settings.

A.4
Does A More Expressive Architecture Help with Advantage Alignment?
In this section, we investigate whether we can improve advantage alignment, and in turn policy performance, of naïve advantage conditioning by using a more expressive conditional policy architecture.
Specifically, we experiment with using a transformer architecture to ingest the conditional advantage.
We compare RCP-A, which uses a FiLM-like architecture that uses the advantage input to modulate the hidden states at every layer of the policy network, to a variant that instead uses a transformer to handle conditional inputs.
We represent each action position in the
H
=
5
H=5
action chunk with a separate token. These action tokens, together with an advantage token, an observation token, and a flow-time token, are processed jointly through self-attention. Each contextualized action token is then projected directly to the velocity vector for its corresponding action position. We use four transformer blocks with model width 256, eight attention heads (32 dimensions per head), and feed-forward width 1024. The FiLM RCP-A actor has approximately
1.39
1.39
M parameters, while the transformer actor has approximately
3.23
3.23
M parameters.
We tune the learning rate smaller (
1
​
e
−
4
1e-4
) for the transformer version to prevent overfitting.
We plot the performance comparison between RCP-A and its transformer variant, as well as Advantage Guidance, in
Figure
14
.
Figure
14
(left) shows that using a transformer is not significantly better in terms of advantage alignment: while the transformer policy output varies more when advantage input is changed, the policy gradient is still invariant to advantage inputs. In comparison, Advantage Guidance is much more responsive to different advantage inputs.
Figure
14
(right) plots the policy performance on OGBench. Overall, using a transformer does not affect policy performance much, and even slightly underperforms the original RCP-A agent.
This shows that there is no free lunch: we cannot expect to improve advantage alignment by simply swapping in a transformer policy backBFNe, and the residual parameterization and action imagination training schemes are critical.

article.headline: 优势引导：用监督学习目标做出超越RL的策略
article.lede: 伯克利提出 Advantage Guidance：把策略提取变成优势条件的流匹配监督学习，采样时用对比引导逼近KL正则最
article.problem: 直接在监督学习损失上以未来回报或优势值作为条件，训练出的「朴素优势条件策略」往往对条件输入不敏感：作者把这一现象命名为「优势对齐问题」，即生成动作的实际优势与请求值不匹配，高优势查询时常给出低于请求值的动作。诊断显示，以真优势标签和随机优势标签计算出的策略损失梯度余弦相似度接近 1，说明损失几乎不随优势标签变化；改变优势输入对动作的影响还不到初始噪声影响的一半。在 RCP-A 这类实现上，用不同优势值查询，20 个 OGBench 任务上的性能基本没有差别。
article.method: 作者把条件策略参数化为一个无条件的参考流场之上的残差流，让参考策略承担与优势无关的建模、残差专注于条件信号；并提出「动作想象」，即对数据集中每个状态额外用参考策略采样 K 个动作（K=7）连同其优势一起训练，以补足反事实监督，同时对优势做逐状态归一化。采样阶段推导出「对比引导」：在指数族条件似然（实用中取高斯）下，用一对对比标签 y+、y− 的分数差做扩散引导，可精确匹配 π̂(a|s)exp(A/β) 的分数，从而最大化优势而不是匹配某个固定值。
article.results: 在 20 个 OGBench 与 6 个 OCBench 长程稀疏奖励任务、10 个随机种子上评测。puzzle-3x3 平均成功率 AG 为 79.3，EDP 为 63.8、QGF 为 63.3、FQL 为 46.3；OCBench 上 block-double 为 91.4 对 EDP 84.0，chamber-easy 为 73.3 对 CFGRL 61.8，block-single 为 95.9 对 QGF 81.8。并非全面领先：cube-single 上 EDP 为 99.0、AG 为 94.9；与 best-of-N 采样的比较中，AG 在小 N 时优于 BFN，但 OGBench 上 N 足够大时略逊于 BFN，OCBench 上则始终更好。消融显示 K=3 会掉点、K 超过约 7 后收益饱和；对比引导在 OGBench 上与 CFG、纯条件采样相近，在 OCBench 上显著更好。
article.why_it_matters: 它说明一个稳定的监督学习目标加上采样期引导，就能在长程稀疏奖励任务上追平甚至超过刻意设计的 actor-critic 与扩散引导方法，为摆脱 RL 的不稳定性和超参敏感提供了一条务实的路径。
article.limitations: 引导权重过大时性能会下降，作者将其列为待解决问题；在 OGBench 上允许大 N 的 best-of-N 采样仍略优于本方法，说明测试期算力充足时优势并不绝对。此外全部实验基于 IQL 给出的优势估计、限于离线设定，未验证在线或离线到在线的场景，也未分析优势估计噪声带来的影响。
article.figure_caption_zh: 朴素优势条件策略受困于「优势对齐问题」：按指定优势值查询时，生成动作的实际优势分布很散，且常常低于请求值（每个域 5 个任务）。

Sensorimotor Alignment:
A Platonic Proxy for Embodied Policy Success
Yunfei Xie
Affiliation:
Rice University
Howard H. Qian
Affiliation:
Rice University
Shiyi Lan
Affiliation:
NVIDIA
Kaiyu Hang
Affiliation:
Rice University
Chen Wei
Abstract
Robotic foundation models are typically evaluated through costly closed-loop rollouts, which motivates cheap offline proxies for model capability.
The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH)
[
20
]
suggests that as representations improve, different modalities such as vision and language converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. We ask whether motion trajectories form another such modality: as embodied models become more capable, should their sensory representations converge toward the structure of physical motion?
To examine this, we propose
Sensorimotor Alignment
(
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
), a training-free offline metric that measures how well a model’s sensory representation aligns with the geometry of physical motion.
We find that
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
correlates positively with downstream robot task success across embodied model families, making it a low-cost offline proxy for prioritizing models before closed-loop evaluation.
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
can also identify promising vision-language model (VLM) backbones even
before
costly fine-tuning into vision-language-action models (VLAs).
Beyond this correlation,
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
offers representation-level explanations for phenomena observed in VLAs and world action models (WAMs).
With
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
, we extend PRH to embodied models and make sensorimotor alignment empirically measurable, offering insight into why an embodied model succeeds beyond its closed-loop success rate.
†
†

1
Introduction
Robotic foundation models increasingly build on large pretrained vision-language models
[
4
,
3
]
, video models
[
48
]
, and world action models
[
14
,
27
,
5
]
. Yet selecting and evaluating these models remains expensive: the most reliable test is still closed-loop rollout in simulation
[
29
,
32
]
or the real world
[
1
]
, where evaluation is slow, noisy, and benchmark-dependent. This expense motivates low-cost offline proxies for robotic capability.
A natural approach is to use existing perception-side proxies, such as visual question answering scores for VLMs
[
30
,
55
]
or pixel-level video quality for world models
[
17
,
50
,
22
]
. However, these metrics measure passive perception or generation quality, not whether a representation is organized for action
[
57
,
23
,
45
,
34
]
. Two scenes may look visually different but require similar robot motions; conversely, two visually similar scenes may demand different trajectories. For robot task success, a model must produce motions of different tasks even for scenes alike. This requires aligning the visual representation with the motor representation.
This perspective connects robotics to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH)
[
20
]
, which argues that as models of different modalities scale and solve diverse tasks, they are converging to a shared statistical model of reality in each of their own representation spaces.
For example, images and text are both projections of a common underlying reality.
As vision and language models scale,
they increasingly agree on the relative distances between data points.
We bring PRH to robotics and ask: can physical motion be viewed as another projection of the world, such that scaled embodied models better align vision and language representations with the structure of robot trajectories?
We test this prediction of PRH: the more capable an embodied model is, the more closely its sensory representations align with its motor representation. In other words, episodes nearby in sensory representation space should also be nearby in motor representation space.
We formalize this as
Sensorimotor Alignment
(
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
), a training-free metric, illustrated in
Figure
1
. For each episode in a robot dataset, a model’s image and text features form its sensory representation, and the recorded end-effector trajectory forms its motor representation. We measure alignment by comparing each episode’s nearest neighbors in sensory and motor spaces. More overlap between the two neighbor sets means stronger sensorimotor alignment.
In
Section
3
, we show that
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
correlates positively with downstream robot task success across model families, in simulated and real-world settings. The correlation is strong for Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) in closed-loop manipulation, indicating that models with higher sensorimotor alignment tend to perform better.
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
computed on raw Vision-Language Models (VLMs) also correlates with the success of the VLAs later fine-tuned from them, more strongly than their general visual question answering (VQA) scores do. For World Action Models (WAMs),
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
is likewise a better indicator of success than video quality metrics such as FID
[
17
]
, SSIM
[
50
]
, and PSNR
[
18
]
, and for real-robot policies,
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
computed offline correlates with physical-robot success under consistent conditions. These results suggest sensorimotor alignment reflects embodied performance better than passive perception or pixel quality.
Prior work has observed several phenomena in VLAs and WAMs only through closed-loop results, without explaining them at the representation level. We use
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
to supply that explanation, as shown in
Section
4
. For example, fine-tuned VLAs often ignore the language instruction and act mainly on what they see; we find that their task success correlates with the
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
of their vision features, not their text features.
Our contributions are threefold:
•
Inspired by the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, we propose a new view of embodiment: stronger embodied models should align their sensory representations more closely with their motor representation. To test this, we introduce
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
, a training-free offline metric that measures alignment between sensory and motor representations.
•
Across model families, in simulation and on real robots, higher
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
goes with higher task success, making
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
a low-cost offline proxy for choosing models before closed-loop evaluation.
•
We further find that
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
explains, at the representation level, phenomena that prior work observed only through closed-loop results, making it a diagnostic tool for understanding how design choices shape embodied models.
We make sensorimotor alignment measurable, offering a cheap, representation-level account of embodied model success that closed-loop success rates alone cannot reveal.

5
Related Work
Representation learning in robotics.
Many robotics studies pretrain visual representations to improve task performance
[
33
,
38
,
31
]
. However, there remains limited understanding of which representational properties lead to downstream task success. A few studies ask what makes a pretrained vision encoder useful for robot learning.
Hu et al. [19]
evaluate 14 frozen vision encoders and find that the correlation between vision encoder and downstream task success rate is not stable across policy-learning methods.
Burns et al. [8]
find that emergent segmentation predicts manipulation success under visual distribution shifts, but only for Vision Transformers. Theia
[
41
]
hypothesizes that higher feature-norm entropy improves robot learning, but reports the supporting correlations only within separate groups of encoders. These studies examine only vision encoders rather than a broader range of embodied models, and none of them accounts for the trajectories the robot executes when measuring the representation. By contrast,
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
compares
k
k
-nearest-neighbor sets in sensory and motor spaces, grounding the evaluation in robot behavior. The same
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
measure correlates with success across VLAs, raw VLMs, WAMs, and the encoders that
Hu et al. [19]
evaluate.
Platonic Representation Hypothesis.
Recent work has applied the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH)
[
20
]
to several new domains. In image generation, REPA
[
52
]
aligns diffusion-transformer features with self-supervised vision encoders, improving training speed and quality. CREPA
[
21
]
extends this recipe to video diffusion. In multimodal understanding, VIRAL
[
51
]
re-aligns multimodal large language models (LLMs) with their vision encoders, recovering visual detail lost in multimodal training. For cross-modal alignment,
Schnaus et al. [40]
match independently trained vision and language encoders through their shared geometry, without paired data. PRH has not yet been brought into robotics; we extend it to robotics by treating robot trajectories as another projection of the world, and find that more capable embodied models align their sensory representations more closely with it.
6
Conclusion
We introduce Sensorimotor Alignment (
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
), a training-free offline metric of alignment between sensory representations and end-effector trajectories. Across VLAs, raw VLMs, and WAMs in simulation, and across real-robot policies,
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
correlates positively with downstream task success, which supports this PRH-inspired view of embodiment.
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
correlates more strongly with success than VQA scores and video-quality metrics, and explains, at the representation level, VLA and WAM phenomena previously seen only in closed-loop behavior: modality dominance, the performance drop from freezing the vision encoder, the small task-success cost of skipping iterative denoising, and the importance of mid-depth blocks for semantic reasoning. We use
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
only offline as a low-cost model-selection and diagnostic tool before closed-loop evaluation, but this correlation motivates optimizing embodied models directly for sensorimotor alignment.
Limitations.
Our study has three main limitations. (1) The positive relationship between
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
and task success is correlational across the tested models; we have not yet demonstrated that sensorimotor alignment can be used directly during training to improve task success rates. (2) Models with similar
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
values can still achieve different success rates, so
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
is best used as a low-cost offline proxy for identifying promising models and VLM backbones before costly fine-tuning or closed-loop testing, which remains the final step of model selection. (3) Our evaluation covers limited model families, benchmarks, and training recipes, few models per comparison, and a single real-robot setting; broader generalization remains to be tested.

article.headline: 运动轨迹对齐可作为机器人策略离线代理
article.lede: 研究者提出免训练指标 S²，用视觉-文本特征与末端轨迹的最近邻重合度离线评估具身模型。
article.problem: 机器人基础模型通常依赖昂贵的闭环 rollout 评估，速度慢、噪声大且依赖基准。现有 VQA 分数或视频质量指标衡量被动感知或生成质量，不直接反映表征是否按动作组织。作者希望找到一个低成本离线代理，在闭环测试前筛选模型。
article.method: S² 从参考数据集采样 episode，把图像与指令编码成感官向量，把未来 h 步末端执行器位置、姿态和夹爪状态作为运动轨迹。感官空间用余弦距离，运动空间用 DTW，比较两者的 k 近邻集合重合度，默认 k=10。该指标无需训练，可直接在不同模型族上计算。
article.results: 在 12 个 VLA 上，S² 与 SimplerEnv 成功率正相关，Pearson r=+0.717（95% CI +0.436 至 +0.912）。8 个原始 VLM 上 r=+0.681（p=0.031），而 VQA 分数 r=-0.154；6 个 WAM 上 r=+0.718（p=0.054），真实机器人 5 个策略 r=+0.831（p=0.041）。在 3 个 WAM 对比中，S² 达 r=+0.999，SSIM、PSNR、FID 分别仅 +0.558、+0.468、+0.680（FID 方向相反）；冻结视觉编码器使 S² 降 41%、成功率降 40%。
article.why_it_matters: 它提供低成本模型筛选和表征级诊断，可在昂贵微调或闭环评估前排除明显不佳的 VLM 主干与策略。
article.limitations: 作者明确承认结果主要是相关性，尚未证明在训练中直接优化 S² 能提升成功率；相似 S² 的模型仍可能成功率不同。评估覆盖的模型族、基准和训练配方有限，每类模型少且仅一个真实机器人设置；真实机器人显著结果来自探索性 h=110，预设 h=7 仅 r=+0.429（p=0.236）。
article.figure_caption_zh: 图：S² 在 VLA、原始 VLM、WAM 和真实机器人策略四个面板中均与下游任务成功率正相关。

figure.caption: {Sensorimotor Alignment ( ) correlates with task success across model families and in simulated and real-world evaluations.} Each panel plots offline ($x$-axis) against downstream task success rate ($y$-axis) for (a) fine-tuned vision-language-action models (VLAs), (b) raw vision-language models (VLMs), (c) world action models (WAMs), and (d) real-robot policies. For raw VLMs, task success is measured after VLA fine-tuning. These correlations (Pearson's $r$; unadjusted one-tailed $p$-values) support as an offline proxy across model families. {fig:pa-predicts-sr-1x3}
