Overview of WeVisOne-VL’s unified object- and
pixel-level perception capabilities.
†

footnotetext:
*
Equal contribution.
†
\dagger
Project leader.
‡
\ddagger
Corresponding author.
WeVisOne-VL: Unified Visual Perception
from Objects to Pixels
Tianming Liang
*
, Junyi Pan
*
, Yuxi Li
*
, Canmiao Fu, Zhipeng Huang,
Chong Sun
†
\dagger
, Chen Li
‡
\ddagger
, Jing Lyu
Affiliation:
WeChat Vision, Tencent Inc.
Abstract
Existing vision-language models (VLMs) remain unreliable for fine-grained visual perception.
In this report, we present
WeVisOne-VL
(WeChat Vision All-in-One), a powerful VLM that unifies object-level and pixel-level perception through structured next-token prediction. It supports multiple visual tasks including object detection, referring localization, counting, OCR, segmentation, and matting, enabling localization at any user-specific granularity, from points and boxes to masks and alpha mattes.
Architecturally, we integrate a lightweight pixel decoder into the VLM via a special
<OBJ>
token to generate instance-level pixel outputs. We train the model with a three-stage curriculum SFT followed by mixed-task RL.
Across over 30 benchmarks, WeVisOne-VL demonstrates leading performance on both object-level and pixel-level tasks, while maintaining robust rejection for object-absent queries.
By releasing WeVisOne-VL to the open-source community, we hope to advance VLMs from broad visual understanding toward truly reliable perception systems for real-world deployment.
1
Introduction
Perceiving and understanding the visual world has long been a central pursuit of computer vision
[
46
,
25
,
70
,
32
,
5
,
45
,
1
,
94
]
. An intelligent visual system must be able to recognize what is present in an image, identify which object a user is referring to, and determine where these objects exist. Such capabilities establish the foundation for a wide range of real-world applications, such as content creation
[
65
]
, industrial inspection
[
37
]
, autonomous driving, and embodied intelligence
[
18
]
.
Over the past decade, computer vision has made remarkable progress toward this goal. From conventional detection and segmentation models (e.g., YOLO
[
86
]
and DETR
[
5
]
), to open-world perception models (e.g., Grounding-DINO
[
67
]
and SAM
[
45
]
), and more recently to large Vision-Language Models (VLMs)
[
1
]
, this field is being driven toward more unified, general, and powerful visual systems. This evolution has substantially broadened the concepts that a model can recognize and the instructions that it can follow. However, when both performance and efficiency are considered, current models are still far from satisfactory for real-world deployment. They often hallucinate non-existent objects, misinterpret user intent when encountering unfamiliar object descriptions, or overlook non-salient instances, leading to incomplete recall.
In this report, we introduce
WeVisOne-VL
(
We
Chat
Vis
ion All-in-
One
), a frontier vision-language model that unifies object-level and pixel-level visual perception through a single natural-language interface. The model casts diverse visual tasks as structured next-token prediction and incorporates a lightweight pixel decoder for generating dense outputs.
Built on Qwen3-VL
[
1
]
, we instantiate our models at two scales: 2B and 4B. We train the models on approximately 100M images with fine-grain annotations using a multi-stage curriculum. The key designs of WeVisOne-VL are summarized as follows.
Data Engine.
We develop a unified data engine that connects semantic discovery with instance-aligned supervision for object detection, referring localization, segmentation, and matting. To guide targeted acquisition and task-specific annotation, the engine organizes category concepts and compositional referring expressions in a shared knowledge graph. It then combines complementary localization experts to generate spatial candidates and consolidates their predictions through visual-language verification of query–instance correspondence. Building on these verified localizations, the engine generates binary masks to extend supervision to the pixel level while preserving target identity across tasks, with manual spot checks for additional quality control. For matting, it further leverages expert predictions and curated data to support a dedicated annotator that provides continuous alpha supervision. Finally, the engine uses reviewed model errors to guide subsequent acquisition, annotation correction, and hard-example sampling, enabling iterative refinement of the training data.
Model Design.
WeVisOne-VL consists of a VLM backbone and a lightweight pixel decoder. Built on Qwen3-VL
[
1
]
, WeVisOne-VL casts a broad range of vision tasks as structured next-token prediction, generating object labels and spatial coordinates autoregressively. For compact and efficient output, we introduce a group of dedicated tokens (from
<0>
to
<1000>
) to encode normalized coordinates
[
40
]
. For dense prediction tasks, the model generates a special
<OBJ>
token after each predicted bounding box, whose hidden state serves as a latent representation of the corresponding instance. The pixel decoder combines this instance representation with multi-level features from the shared ViT to produce predictions over the full image canvas. In this way, WeVisOne-VL supports both discrete and dense predictions without relying on a separate large segmentation model
[
48
,
122
,
68
,
61
]
.
Training Pipeline.
We train WeVisOne-VL in a curriculum pipeline consisting of three-stage Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) followed by mixed-task Reinforcement Learning (RL). Stage 1 establishes task alignment, teaching the model to follow task instructions and produce well-formed structured outputs. Stage 2 introduces high-resolution and dense perception data to improve the recall of small and crowded objects. Stage 3 further incorporates pixel-level tasks, extending the model from discrete localization to dense prediction. For RL, we first select samples on which the SFT model is most uncertain, then apply Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) over the mixture of tasks. This on-policy optimization effectively improves the localization accuracy, while suppressing repeated or hallucinated predictions.
Across multiple visual benchmarks, WeVisOne-VL demonstrates highly competitive performance against both state-of-the-art general-purpose models and specialized vision systems. It exhibits consistently strong capabilities on both object-level and pixel-level tasks, including object detection, fine-grained referring, text recognition and language-guided pixel prediction. In addition, it also shows strong potential in challenging real-world scenarios, such as maintaining high recall in crowded scenes and correctly rejecting queries when the target is absent. By unifying these capabilities into a single model, we offer a powerful, efficient, and versatile vision-language foundation for the open-source community, accelerating the development of truly practical and reliable visual systems.
2
WeVisOne-VL Data Engine
Data construction for unified visual perception must support both category-level recognition and context-dependent target selection, while preserving instance associations across language and spatial supervision. To this end, we build the
WeVisOne-VL Data Engine
(WDE). WDE draws on GRIT
[
78
]
, CC3M
[
90
]
, LAION
[
49
]
, SA-1B
[
45
]
, and several task-specific datasets, and its annotation inventory comprises over 100 million images and approximately 3.6 billion bounding-box annotations.
Figure
2
shows an overview of WDE. We first organize category concepts and referring expressions in a shared knowledge graph, which guides targeted image acquisition (Section
2.1
). The acquired image–query pairs then go through task-specific localization and semantic verification, which establish the correspondence between each query and its target instances (Sections
2.2
and
2.3
). We keep these correspondences when generating binary masks (Section
2.4
), and further extend the instance annotations to continuous alpha supervision with a dedicated matting pipeline (Section
2.6
). Finally, model errors reviewed after each training round guide subsequent acquisition and annotation refinement (Section
2.7
). Below, we describe each component in detail.
Figure 2:
Overview of the WeVisOne-VL Data Engine (WDE).
2.1
Concept Discovery and Targeted Acquisition
Semantic discovery produces two complementary annotations: category-level concepts and compositional referring expressions. For detection, we use an optimized Tokenize Anything model
[
76
]
to discover object categories. For referring tasks, we prompt Qwen3-VL
[
1
]
to generate referring expressions that specify targets through attributes, states, actions, and relations. Category concepts support category-based localization, while referring expressions support selecting particular instances from their context. Both serve as annotation queries, and their correspondence to image regions is established in the subsequent localization stages.
We organize both category concepts and referring expressions in a shared knowledge graph. The graph is initialized from resources including Wikipedia
1
1
1
https://www.wikipedia.org/
and WordNet
[
73
]
, and represents canonical category names, aliases, taxonomic relations, and whole–part relations. A candidate term is first linked to existing nodes through text retrieval and vision-language verification, and is considered for addition to the graph only when it is supported by stable visual evidence. During normalization, we merge equivalent category terms while keeping the descriptive constraints that determine the scope of referring expressions.
This semantic organization also supports targeted acquisition. Concept names and aliases serve as textual retrieval queries, verified instances provide visual retrieval cues, and historical errors indicate where additional coverage is needed. We set sampling priorities according to concept representation, image domain, target scale, and challenging conditions such as occlusion and dense object arrangements, and confusable categories and recurring failures in interpreting referring expressions further inform acquisition. In this way, annotation effort is directed toward both semantic gaps and visual conditions that remain difficult for the current model. The acquired image–query pairs are then sent to the detection or referring annotation pipeline.
2.2
Detection Annotation
Conventional object detectors excel at detecting densely distributed objects but struggle to recognize long-tail categories and open-world concepts. By contrast, VLMs offer strong recognition capabilities but often exhibit low recall in dense object scenarios. Therefore, for each object category, we first utilize detectors to generate exhaustive proposals, and then use a VLM for post verification. Specifically, we obtain proposals in parallel from SAM3
[
4
]
and an in-house open-vocabulary detector based on a DINO-style architecture
[
123
]
, which we refine iteratively. For each image–query pair, the predictions of both models are merged into a shared candidate pool. This design reduces our reliance on any single proposal source and uses the variation across detectors to pursue broader instance coverage.
For detection, we obtain proposals in parallel from two models: SAM3
[
4
]
and an in-house open-vocabulary detector based on a DINO-style architecture
[
123
]
, which we refine iteratively. For each image–query pair, the predictions of both models are merged into a shared candidate pool. This design reduces our reliance on any single proposal source and uses the variation across detectors to pursue broader instance coverage.
We then use Qwen3-VL
[
1
]
to verify whether each proposed region matches the category query given the image content. Based on its judgments, we select candidates, remove duplicates, and resolve conflicting predictions. For the retained instances, we keep the bounding boxes produced by the localization models. These boxes serve as detection supervision and also define the target instances used in the subsequent segmentation annotation.
2.3
Referring Annotation
Referring annotation requires the predicted regions to satisfy the compositional meaning of an expression, including the conditions that distinguish the intended targets within a scene. We build this stage on the SAM3 Agent framework
[
4
]
and add Rex-Omni
[
40
]
as an additional localization expert. Within the same expression-conditioned workflow, SAM3 and Rex-Omni both propose candidate regions, providing complementary localization evidence for the same expression.
Qwen3-VL then consolidates these proposals by checking whether each one matches the expression in its image context. The check covers the attributes, states, actions, and relations stated in the expression, and distinguishes the requested targets from objects that are mentioned only as contextual references. Whether an expression refers to a whole object or one of its parts is likewise determined by the expression itself. Conflicting proposals are resolved through the same semantic check. The accepted results bind each expression to an individual target or a target set, so that the annotation preserves the selection constraints of the query.
2.4
Mask Annotation
For each localized instance, we use SAM2
[
85
]
to predict a binary mask of its visible region. Each mask inherits the query of the box it is generated from. Each instance thus has both a box and a mask under the same query. With category queries, the boxes supervise detection and the masks supervise category-conditioned segmentation. With referring expressions, the boxes supervise referring localization and the masks supervise referring segmentation.
We manually spot-check a subset of these annotations, checking whether each mask and box are linked to the correct instance and whether the masks are accurate. Defects found in this check are corrected through the refinement process in Section
2.7
. We also record the source of every annotation, so that affected labels can be traced and regenerated.
2.5
Hard-Example Construction
Some distinctions may not be adequately represented by broad semantic coverage alone, and we construct hard examples to focus on them. Candidate queries are derived from confusable concepts in the knowledge graph, visually similar categories, controlled changes to descriptive conditions, and observed model failures. These sources provide plausible alternatives that can only be handled by precisely interpreting both the category and the contextual constraints of a query.
A query is negative only when no object in the image satisfies all of its conditions, and this cannot be decided from the query or the detector output alone. For example, changing “red car” to “blue car” does not mean the image contains no blue car, and a detector that returns nothing for a query may simply have missed the target. Therefore, we review each candidate negative against the whole image, checking the attributes, actions, and relations in the query. If a matching target turns out to exist, the query is sent back to positive annotation.
Whether an example is hard is determined by the behavior of the current model. A reviewed negative becomes a hard negative when the model nevertheless predicts a target region for it. Such examples carry an empty target set, so they teach the model to reject the query without introducing any box or pixel targets. We retain the erroneous predictions as evidence of the underlying confusion. Hard positives, in turn, capture missed targets, incorrect referent selection, and difficult localization under crowding or occlusion. We keep their reliable annotations, so that these examples strengthen the model’s sensitivity to true targets while hard negatives teach it to reject. Sample difficulty is reassessed for each model version, and the sampling emphasis is adjusted toward persistent and newly emerging failure modes.

2.7
Training Feedback and Data Refinement
After each training round, we analyze model errors to guide both data acquisition and annotation refinement. We organize the errors by concept, image domain, target scale, occlusion, task, and failure type, and apply clustering and deduplication to select representative cases for review. This concentrates annotation effort on recurring failures and coverage gaps.
The review distinguishes errors in model prediction from errors in supervision. If the annotation is reliable, we keep the example unchanged; it may receive greater sampling emphasis or serve as a retrieval seed for related images. If the review identifies an annotation defect, we correct or regenerate the affected supervision before including it in a subsequent data version. In other words, model disagreement only triggers an investigation, and annotations are changed only after review.
Different failure modes lead to different updates. Missed targets guide additional acquisition and hard-positive sampling. Referent confusion motivates instance contrasts and more descriptive queries, while false positive responses contribute to hard-negative construction. Defects in boxes, masks, or cross-task instance associations are returned to the corresponding annotation stage for correction.
Each data release records the annotation provenance, the model version that exposed each error, and the associated review and revision history. Unresolved cases are excluded from training. Original images, their identified near duplicates, and the derived task records stay within the same data partition across updates. Reviewed feedback data can enter subsequent training versions, whereas a fixed monitoring set is reserved for internal regression and excluded from both training and threshold calibration. Formal benchmarks are kept isolated from training and from feedback-driven data construction, so that evaluation remains independent as WDE evolves.

We train WeVisOne-VL with a three-stage Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
curriculum followed by mixed-task Reinforcement Learning (RL). The curriculum
first establishes a shared output interface, then improves high-resolution and
dense perception, and finally connects autoregressive localization with
pixel-level prediction. After SFT, RL directly optimizes the quality of the
complete prediction rather than the likelihood of individual output tokens.

4.1
Curriculum Supervised Fine-Tuning
Stage 1: Task Alignment.
This stage adapts the model to the new tokens and task-specific structured outputs. Starting from Qwen3-VL with an extended vocabulary, we freeze the vision encoder and visual-language projector and train only the language model on 90M examples covering all target tasks for 13K optimization steps. The model learns to follow different task instructions, produce the structured outputs, and return
None
when the target is absent. For pixel-task examples, we impose only next-token prediction supervision (NTP) without activating the pixel decoder, thereby establishing an initial correspondence between each predicted instance and its
<OBJ>
token. In this stage, we use 16–512 visual tokens per image and limit the context length to 4,096 tokens. Notably, early training can be dominated by extremely dense samples (e.g., containing hundreds of boxes in a single response), making the model highly prone to repetitive output collapse. To mitigate this issue, we primarily use samples with at most 50 boxes or points per category during this stage.
Stage 2: Resolution and Density Scaling.
Building on Stage 1, we unfreeze the vision encoder, projector, and language model. This stage serves two purposes. First, we raise the maximum input resolution to 1,960 visual tokens, preserving the visual details for recognizing small objects. Second, we increase the maximum box/point number within one response to 500, exposing the model to crowded scenes for dense detection. The maximum context length is extended to 8,192 tokens. We train on approximately 40M examples for 9K optimization steps. During this stage, pixel-level examples remain supervised solely by NTP.

As shown in Table

Figure

In the first example, both baselines detect only the foreground elephant, while WeVisOne-VL also recovers the distant elephants partly obscured by dust. Across the carrot and dense fruit examples, the baselines tend to merge adjacent instances into coarse-grained boxes, whereas WeVisOne-VL more often preserves instance-level localization.

In these cases, WeVisOne-VL successfully selects the correct target, while the baselines select distractors or include additional people. The final query specifies a person wearing a white shirt and red shorts, but no one in the image satisfies both conditions. Object counting.
Figure

The remaining queries specify green balls and fake green apples among distractors. The baselines often count objects outside the requested subset or count individual shoes instead of pairs; in the last example, Rex-Omni reports 537 rather than 42. Object pointing.
Figure

In the first example, WeVisOne-VL places points across the heart-shaped balloons, while LocateAnything misses most instances and Rex-Omni produces redundant points on some balloons. The second query asks for two people gazing into each other’s eyes: both baselines select other people, whereas WeVisOne-VL points to the indicated pair. In the third example, Rex-Omni points to multiple pigs and LocateAnything selects a distractor, while WeVisOne-VL identifies the pig facing upward. In the final example, both baselines point to the handle, whereas WeVisOne-VL places its point on the queried curved hook.

OCR.

8
Limitations
In this work, we focus on fundamental visual perception, which entails several trade-offs. First, the limited amount of general-purpose training data may compromise the general capabilities relative to the base model. Second, for inference efficiency, we train the model to directly produce structured outputs without chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning
[
69
,
21
]
, which potentially limits its ability to tackle complex reasoning tasks. Third, our current approach is limited to single-turn prediction. It is promising to integrate an agent framework to progressively refine visual understanding through multi-turn tool interactions
[
38
,
61
]
.
Beyond these limitations, a key challenge lies in the real-world complexity. The object prompts in benchmarks are typically clear, well-formed, and unambiguous. However, real-world user instructions are often vague and hesitant. Variations in contexts or communication styles can make a straightforward task, such as locating the target, significantly more challenging. Therefore, strong intent reasoning is essential for a reliable vision system. In future work, we will continue to improve WeVisOne-VL toward addressing these limitations.
9
Conclusion
We introduced WeVisOne-VL, a vision-language model that unifies object-level (e.g., object detection, referring localization, counting, and OCR) and pixel-level (e.g., referring segmentation, and image matting) tasks through a structured next-token interface. Dedicated coordinate tokens encode instance predictions, while an
<OBJ>
token connects each localized instance to a lightweight pixel decoder for masks and alpha mattes. A three-stage supervised curriculum develops task alignment, high-resolution dense perception, and pixel-level prediction. After that, we apply mixed-task reinforcement learning to optimize the complete grounding outputs. Across the evaluated benchmarks, WeVisOne-VL achieves strong results on both object-level and pixel-level tasks. It improves mean detection F1 and counting accuracy over comparable-scale VLMs, advances text grounding and referring localization, and surpasses the evaluated baselines for referring segmentation and image matting. Qualitative examples further show that the model can localize individual instances in crowded scenes, ground expressions involving multiple objects, and recognize when a requested target is absent. By unifying these capabilities within a single language-guided model, WeVisOne-VL provides a foundation for practical visual systems.

article.headline: WeVisOne-VL：统一对象与像素级感知
article.lede: 腾讯微信视觉团队提出 WeVisOne-VL，用结构化下一 token 预测统一检测、指代定位、计数、OCR、分割与抠图
article.problem: 现有视觉语言模型在细粒度视觉感知上仍不可靠，常会幻觉出不存在的物体、误解不熟悉的指代表达，或漏掉不显著实例。真实部署既需要对象级定位，也需要像素级掩码与 alpha 抠图，单一模型同时做好这两类任务仍具挑战。
article.method: WeVisOne-VL 基于 Qwen3-VL 构建 2B 和 4B 两个规模，用 <0> 到 <1000> 的专用 token 编码归一化坐标，并在每个框后生成 <OBJ> token，将其隐藏状态送入约 9.6M 参数的轻量像素解码器输出掩码或 alpha matte。训练采用三阶段课程式 SFT，再用混合任务 GRPO 强化学习；配套数据引擎覆盖约 1 亿图像和约 36 亿框标注。
article.results: 在 COCO 上，4B 模型 F1@0.5 为 74.0、Mean 为 57.1；LVIS Mean 55.3，Dense200 Mean 71.3，VisDrone Mean 44.7。指代检测 RefCOCOg test 为 81.8，WeRef-Bench 拒绝率 67.4%；计数 PixMo-Count test 为 89.6，MixCount test 为 40.4。指代分割 RefCOCO val cIoU 为 81.4，ReasonSeg test gIoU 为 66.8；抠图 P3M-500-NP 的 2B 模型 MAD 为 6.6，AM-2K 的 4B 模型 MAD 为 5.0。
article.why_it_matters: 它把检测、指代、计数、OCR、分割和抠图收进同一个语言接口，减少对独立大分割模型的依赖，并开源权重与代码，便于社区构建可部署的细粒度视觉系统。
article.limitations: 论文自述的局限包括：通用训练数据有限可能削弱基础模型通用能力；模型直接输出结构化结果、不使用 CoT，且仅支持单轮预测。另一个存疑点是 RL 对分割和抠图只用框级奖励，掩码与 alpha 质量并未在 RL 中直接优化。
